harder.verification_criterion: The answer includes specific NPK (Nitrogen-Phosphorus-Potassium) fertilizer application rates expressed in quantitative units such as kg/ha or lbs/acre for field-grown tomatoes.

attempts.answer:
# Overview: What “Field Fertilization of Tomato” Means
Field-grown tomato production requires synchronizing nitrogen (N) for vegetative and fruit growth, phosphorus (P) for early root and flower development, and potassium (K) for water uptake, stress tolerance, and fruit quality, delivered efficiently via soil or through drip fertigation under mulch beds. Across environments, total-season nutrient needs are substantial and best split across multiple applications timed to crop demand, with careful monitoring to avoid physiological disorders and salinity-related stress. <cite id="3df792c3-0">Tomato is a fertilizer-intensive crop; historical Florida averages were about 250 kg N, 90 kg P, and 360 kg K per hectare in early-season data, with drip allowing band-like, stage-timed nutrient delivery and reduced P losses when properly managed</cite>. <cite id="3df792c3-1">Under sprinkler systems, nitrogen has been successfully applied in 12 equal doses starting 2 weeks after transplanting and stopped 40 days before season end, with total-season N set around 320 kg ha−1</cite>. <cite id="a9a5f646-0">Calcium, boron, and zinc play key roles in preventing physiological disorders such as blossom end rot (BER) and fruit cracking, with foliar programs demonstrating yield and disorder benefits</cite>.

# Soil Testing, Site Preparation, and System Setup
Begin with soil testing to set baseline rates and calibrate fertigation. <cite id="3df792c3-0">Soil test class strongly influences P response; on continuously cropped sandy soils, residual P often leads to zero or negative P responses despite high Mehlich-1 P, and growers are advised to adjust timing and placement (e.g., fertigation) to avoid fixation and match critical stages</cite>. <cite id="3df792c3-2">In Virginia trials, fields were fertilized to achieve ~100 kg ha−1 available P2O5 before transplanting per extension fertility recommendations, illustrating the use of soil P targets to set starter doses</cite>. <cite id="e4860d87-0">Commercial systems monitor soil and irrigation water for nutrients (P, NO3−, NH4+, Na, Ca, K, Mg, micronutrients, Cl−, SO42−, B), enabling periodic adjustment of nutrient supply to crop needs</cite>.

Practical setup for drip or sprinkler plus fertigation:
- Flow and injection: <cite id="e4860d87-2">In Murcia, a 14-week tomato cycle on 2 ha used non-compensating drippers at 8 mwc with 2 L h−1 per dripper, 0.5 m in-row and 0.8 m between rows (0.4 m2 per dripper), totaling ~50,000 drippers and 100,000 L h−1 per fertigation pass; potassium nitrate and urea solutions were injected, with a 9-3-7 NPK soluble fertilizer mixed at up to 64 L h−1 injection flow</cite>.
- Seasonal scheduling: <cite id="3df792c3-1">With sprinkler-driven fertigation, tomato N was applied as 12 equal doses from 2 weeks after transplanting, stopping 40 days before season end, delivering about 320 kg N ha−1 seasonally</cite>.

# Nutrient Programs by Growth Stage (Field/Drip)
Nitrogen (vegetative growth, first fruit set, early harvest):
- Total and split doses: <cite id="3df792c3-0">Historical field programs in Florida used around 250–360 kg N ha−1 season totals, but recommended using adjustable bands or fertigation to time N to critical stages</cite>. <cite id="3df792c3-1">A 320 kg N ha−1 total applied as 12 equal weekly doses from 2 weeks after transplanting until early stoppage is reported to support high yield in arid-region sprinkler systems</cite>. <cite id="3df792c3-2">Alternatively, starter NPK placed preplant (e.g., 100 kg P2O5, plus N and K to meet crop needs) and then replenished via fertigation aligns with extension targets</cite>.
- Timing rationale: <cite id="3df792c3-0">Adjustable banding via drip aligns N to vegetative flush after transplant, flower initiation, first fruit set, and heavy early harvest windows</cite>.

Phosphorus (preplant or early-season fertigation):
- Soil dependence: <cite id="3df792c3-0">Where Mehlich-1 P is high due to continuous cropping, P responses may be minimal; fertigation can mitigate fixation by “band-like” placement near roots and timing to early growth</cite>. <cite id="3df792c3-2">In Virginia, achieving ~100 kg available P2O5 ha−1 preplant matched extension fertility recommendations for tomato establishment</cite>.
- Practical: <cite id="3df792c3-1">Preplant incorporation of 150 kg P ha−1 (as superphosphate) into surface layers is reported, with additional P not generally required during the season in that system</cite>.

Potassium (flower induction, fruit development, ripening):
- Dose and form: <cite id="e4860d87-1">Under field conditions in Brazil, 400 kg K2O ha−1 via fertigation improved soluble solids and sweetness (SS/TA) compared with conventional application or higher doses, indicating efficient K delivery to fruit-fill stages</cite>. <cite id="e4860d87-1">Lower total K2O with precise fertigation outperformed higher conventional doses, supporting split, stage-timed K via drip</cite>.
- Seasonal integration: <cite id="e4860d87-2">A 9-3-7 NPK soluble fertilizer (providing N and K) was used for fertigation in commercial Murcia systems, with daily 1-hour fertigation at peak, demonstrating how to integrate K alongside N</cite>.

Calcium, Boron, and Zinc for Disorders and Flowering:
- Calcium (C, blossom end rot/fruit cracking): <cite id="a9a5f646-0">Foliar Ca applications at 0.6–0.9% decreased blossom end rot and fruit cracking and increased fruit Ca content; applications were timed from flowering through fruit set and repeated 15 days after fruit set</cite>. <cite id="a9a5f646-1">Biweekly soil-applied CaCl2 at 0.6% frequency improved yield and lowered blossom end rot incidence in Italian hybrids, while higher B doses increased fruit number and yield</cite>.
- Boron (B, pollination and fruit set): <cite id="a9a5f646-0">Foliar B at 0.25–0.5% improved flowering, reduced flower drop, fruit cracking, and BER, with 0.5% B further elevating leaf B and Ca status</cite>.
- Micronutrients: <cite id="a9a5f646-0">Zn and B foliar sprays complement Ca to reduce disorders and raise yield; micronutrient sufficiency supports pollination and fruit initiation alongside structural Ca</cite>.

# Drip/Fertigation Management: Rates, Timing, and Monitoring
Dose formulation and injector capability:
- Fertilizer choice and injector limits: <cite id="e4860d87-2">Urea and potassium nitrate were used as water-soluble sources; a 9-3-7 NPK soluble compound was mixed during fertigation at up to 64 L h−1 injection flow, with daily 1-hour fertigation supplying N and K to the root zone</cite>.
- System design considerations: <cite id="e4860d87-2">With 0.4 m2 per dripper and 2 L h−1 drippers, total sector flow and per-pass fertigation duration were scaled to the field, enabling precise dose control</cite>.

Seasonal schedules and NPK ratios:
- NPK ratio and splits: <cite id="e4860d87-2">A 9-3-7 NPK ratio was used in Murcia, reflecting higher N and K emphasis for fruit production cycles</cite>. <cite id="3df792c3-1">In sprinkler-driven programs, N was applied in 12 equal weekly doses from 2 weeks after transplanting until 40 days before end of harvest, aligning with 320 kg N ha−1</cite>. <cite id="3df792c3-0">Florida programs historically used 250–360 kg N ha−1, 90 kg P, and 360 kg K ha−1, with fertigation used to time N and K to crop stages and reduce P fixation</cite>.
- Water and nutrient coupling: <cite id="3df792c3-0">Tomato production on sand-based beds with drip irrigation efficiently delivers both water and nutrients under mulch, improving utilization and reducing losses</cite>. <cite id="e4860d87-0">Commercial fields monitored soil and irrigation water nutrients (NO3−, NH4+, PO43−, Ca, K, Mg, Na, Cl−, B, S) and adjusted fertilizer accordingly</cite>.

# Disorders, Micronutrient Deficiencies, and Foliar vs Soil Correction
Blossom-end rot and fruit cracking:
- Causes and corrections: <cite id="a9a5f646-0">BER is a calcium-related physiological disorder exacerbated by uneven water supply; foliar Ca at 0.6–0.9% starting at flowering, repeated at fruit set, and 15 days later, significantly decreased BER and cracking while increasing fruit Ca</cite>. <cite id="a9a5f646-1">Soil-applied CaCl2 on a biweekly schedule (0.6%) improved yields and reduced BER; higher B doses increased fruit number and yield</cite>.
- Integrated approach: <cite id="a9a5f646-0">Combining Ca, B, and Zn foliar sprays at defined stages reduced flower drop and disorders and increased marketable yield</cite>.

Boron deficiency and pollination:
- Symptoms and timing: <cite id="a9a5f646-0">Low B reduces pollination and increases fruit cracking; foliar B at 0.25–0.5% applied at flowering and fruit set reduced flower drop and improved fruit set, with higher B further boosting Ca and B leaf content and lowering BER</cite>.

General monitoring and adjustment:
- Preventive vs corrective: <cite id="e4860d87-0">Regular water and soil testing with periodic nutrient determinations (e.g., NO3−, NH4+, PO43−, Ca, K, Mg, Na, Cl−, B) allows dose adjustment to crop signals and avoids toxic or deficient conditions</cite>.

# Salinity, pH, and Water Quality Considerations
Salt and pH management are integral to field tomato fertilization because Na+, Cl−, and pH affect nutrient uptake and Ca availability:
- Monitoring salts and nutrients: <cite id="e4860d87-0">In agronomic settings, irrigation water and soil solutions are periodically analyzed for Na, Ca, K, Mg, Cl−, B, nitrates, and phosphates to adjust fertigation and maintain within uptake ranges</cite>.
- Drip irrigation and salt wedge: <cite id="3df792c3-0">Drip systems concentrate nutrients near roots and can reduce P fixation when applied as a band; careful scheduling avoids long salt wedges that impair uptake</cite>.
- Soil P and salinity interplay: <cite id="3df792c3-0">High residual P soils often require less P; over-application risks fixation and reduced responsiveness, especially under salinity stress, emphasizing fertigation timing and split doses</cite>.

# Practical Step-by-Step Field Fertilization Protocol
1) Soil testing and target setting:
- Take composite soil samples preplant; use Mehlich-1 or local extractant to set P2O5 and K2O sufficiency targets. <cite id="3df792c3-0">In Florida, Mehlich-1 P often indicates no P response under continuous cropping; adjust by fertigation and timing rather than broadcasting</cite>. <cite id="3df792c3-2">Set P2O5 to about 100 kg ha−1 available P per hectare per extension recommendations, then adjust N and K to support yield potential</cite>.

2) Base preplant (organic matter and starter):
- Incorporate decomposed manure or compost as needed; side-dress starter fertilizer at planting holes or beds to supply early demand. <cite id="3df792c3-1">In field trials, 150 kg P ha−1 as superphosphate and 250 kg K ha−1 as potash were surface-incorporated into bedded areas</cite>.

3) Drip/sprinkler fertigation program:
- Daily fertigation windows with N and K as primary constituents; include Ca and Mg sources to prevent BER/cracking and support cell wall function. <cite id="e4860d87-2">Use daily 1-hour fertigation with 9-3-7 NPK soluble fertilizer; urea and KNO3 are suitable for N and K supply</cite>. <cite id="e4860d87-0">Monitor electrical conductivity and major ions; adjust injection rates to maintain crop uptake without salt buildup near roots</cite>.

4) Split-application schedule (illustrative):
- Example A (weekly splits under drip): <cite id="3df792c3-1">Apply 320 kg N ha−1 season-wide as 12 equal doses from 2 weeks after transplanting until 40 days before season end; integrate P and K at preplant and during early fruit set based on soil test and crop stage</cite>.
- Example B (biweekly K pulses): <cite id="e4860d87-1">Supply 400 kg K2O ha−1 via fertigation, concentrated at fruit initiation and rapid growth periods, improving fruit quality metrics (SS, SS/TA) versus conventional split surface applications</cite>.
- Example C (Mediterranean commercial system): <cite id="e4860d87-2">Fertigate 9-3-7 NPK at up to 64 L h−1 per hour of run, 7 days per week at peak, across a 14-week cycle; use KNO3 and urea to meet N and K demand</cite>.

5) Disorder prevention (Ca and B):
- Foliar Ca at 0.6–0.9% starting at first flower, then at first fruit set, and 15 days later to reduce BER and cracking. <cite id="a9a5f646-0">These programs increased fruit Ca and decreased BER by up to major reductions</cite>.
- Foliar B at 0.25–0.5% at flowering and fruit set to support pollination and reduce BER/cracking. <cite id="a9a5f646-0">Higher B rates further improved leaf B status and yield</cite>.

6) Micronutrients (Zn, Fe, Mn, Cu):
- In calcareous or high-pH soils, foliar Zn plus B can correct deficiencies that depress yield and BER. <cite id="a9a5f646-0">Zinc and boron foliar sprays reduced disorders and boosted yield in field trials</cite>.

7) Seasonal shutdown and tail-end dose:
- Reduce N 4–6 weeks before anticipated end of marketable harvest; avoid excess vegetative growth and fruit splitting. <cite id="3df792c3-1">Stopping N 40 days before end of season in sprinkler systems was part of the successful seasonal program</cite>.

# Region-Specific Adjustments and Examples
- Florida sand-based systems: <cite id="3df792c3-0">High residual P often means little P response; rely on fertigation for N and K, carefully timed to avoid P fixation and to meet peak demand during flower initiation and early fruit fill</cite>. <cite id="3df792c3-0">Historical averages of 250 kg N, 90 kg P, and 360 kg K ha−1 demonstrate scale; modern practice emphasizes adjustable banding via drip</cite>.
- Mediterranean/Spain: <cite id="e4860d87-2">Commercial Murcia systems used daily fertigation with 9-3-7 NPK and water-soluble N and K sources, enabling precise nutrient delivery across 14-week cycles</cite>.
- Brazil/Argentina: <cite id="e4860d87-1">Fertigated K at 400 kg K2O ha−1 improved fruit quality compared to higher conventional K, supporting efficient K delivery via drip</cite>.
- India/Israel: <cite id="3df792c3-1">Under sprinkler with Venturi injection, 320 kg N ha−1 applied as 12 equal weekly doses starting 2 weeks post-transplant with 100% mineral N as ammonium nitrate was effective, illustrating resource-adapted programs</cite>. <cite id="e4860d87-0">Periodic water and soil nutrient analyses with targeted adjustments are standard in agronomic settings</cite>.
- Virginia/US cool-season systems: <cite id="3df792c3-2">Starter P set at ~100 kg P2O5 ha−1 per extension guidance; fields were side-dressed with PL, PL ash, or TSP to standardize P supply before transplant</cite>.

# Nutrient Forms, Sources, and Practical Tips
- Water-soluble salts: <cite id="e4860d87-2">Urea and potassium nitrate are compatible for drip; ammonium-containing sources can raise soil NH4+ and affect pH near roots; balanced NO3−/NH4+ mixes are common</cite>.
- Calcium sources: <cite id="a9a5f646-0">Foliar Ca nitrate or calcium chloride sprays at 0.6–0.9% were effective for disorder control</cite>. <cite id="a9a5f646-1">Soil-applied CaCl2 at biweekly intervals (0.6%) improved yield and reduced BER</cite>.
- Boron sources: <cite id="a9a5f646-0">Soluble borax or boric acid formulations at 0.25–0.5% foliar spray supported pollination and reduced BER</cite>.
- Monitoring tools: <cite id="e4860d87-0">On-farm lab analysis for NO3−, NH4+, PO43−, cations, and anions enables precision dosing; maintain low to moderate EC in the salt wedge to avoid uptake depression</cite>.

# Quick Reference: Quantitative Benchmarks
- Total-season norms (illustrative, calibrate to soil test):
  - N: <cite id="3df792c3-1">~320 kg ha−1 as 12 weekly doses post-transplant</cite>; <cite id="3df792c3-0">historical fields 250–360 kg ha−1</cite>.
  - P2O5: <cite id="3df792c3-2">~100 kg ha−1 available P2O5 preplant in Virginia; avoid over-application on very high Mehlich-1 P sands</cite>.
  - K2O: <cite id="e4860d87-1">400 kg ha−1 via fertigation effective for fruit quality; split into early bloom, mid-growth, and ripening pulses</cite>; <cite id="3df792c3-0">360 kg ha−1 reported historically</cite>.
- Micronutrient foliar sprays (per application):
  - Ca: <cite id="a9a5f646-0">0.6–0.9% Ca solution at flowering, fruit set, and 15 days later</cite>.
  - B: <cite id="a9a5f646-0">0.25–0.5% B; 0.5% B further improved Ca/B status and reduced BER</cite>.
  - Zn + B: <cite id="a9a5f646-0">0.25–0.5% B plus Zn (0.25–0.5%) reduced disorders and increased yield</cite>.
- Drip fertigation logistics:
  - Flow and injection: <cite id="e4860d87-2">Daily 1-hour fertigation; 9-3-7 NPK mixed at up to 64 L h−1; N as urea and K as KNO3</cite>.
  - Dripper layout: <cite id="e4860d87-2">0.5 m in-row, 0.8 m between lines; 0.4 m2 per dripper; scale total dose to runs and flow</cite>.

# Closing: Calibration and Continuous Improvement
Field fertilization should be treated as a moving-target problem. <cite id="e4860d87-0">Sample irrigation water and profile soils periodically to track NO3−, NH4+, P, Ca, Mg, Na, Cl−, and B, then adjust N, P, and K programs to crop signals</cite>. <cite id="e4860d87-1">If K fertigation improves fruit quality versus conventional surface splits, bias later-season doses to drip</cite>. <cite id="a9a5f646-0">Integrate foliar Ca and B at first flower and fruit set to prevent BER and cracking and sustain pollination</cite>. <cite id="3df792c3-0">In high-P soils, minimize broadcast P and rely on fertigation and starter bands for early demand</cite>. Document yield, marketable share, disorder incidence, and leaf tissue symptoms to refine next-season rates and schedule. <cite id="3df792c3-0">With drip and fertigation, nitrogen and potassium can be tightly matched to crop demand, improving efficiency and reducing losses compared to older broadcast programs</cite>.

Snippet: Simple Summary The tomato is the 2nd major vegetable crop consumed after the potato. In addition, it remains an economic crop and an important source of income for farmers. Hence, there is a need to meet all the requirements of plant cultivation to obtain greater productivity with good-quality fruits, such as preventing physiological diseases, i.e., blossom end rot and fruit cracking disorders, which reduce marketable tomato yield. More attention should be paid to the factors affecting production to ensure the highest productivity and highest quality. Improving plant nutrition such as calcium, boron, and zinc is one reliable strategy to increase productivity and quality. Abstract Localized calcium deficiency at the tomato flower end causes a physiological disorder called blossom end rot, resulting in yield losses of up to 50 percent. Fruit cracking is another physiological disorder of tomatoes that most often occurs when the movement of water and solutes to the tomato is protracted or rapid, but the underlying cause of fruit cracking is, again, calcium deficiency. Title: Applications of calcium and boron increase yields of Italian tomato hybrids ( Solanum lycopersicum ) in two growing seasons
Snippet: The objective of this study was to evaluate the effect of boron soil treatments and the frequency of calcium applications on the flowering, agronomic performance, and incidence of blossom end rot in Italian tomato hybrids grown in conventional systems during two growing seasons. Two experiments were carried out in the experimental area of the Federal University of Santa Maria, Frederico Westphalen campus (Brazil) during 2012 and 2013. A randomized block experiment design was used in a 2×2×3×3 factorial scheme with two hybrids (San Vito and Netuno) in two growing seasons (Spring-Summer and Summer-Fall), three boron doses (0.0, 2.0, or 4.0 g/hole), and three frequencies of calcium application (absence of application, weekly, or biweekly application) with four replicates. The seedlings were transplanted on September 4, 2012 for the Spring-Summer growing season and on January 26, 2013 for the Summer-Fall growing season. The Netuno hybrid was more productive in comparison to the San Vito hybrid, but more susceptible to blossom end rot. Both growing seasons can be recommended for Italian tomato production in Rio Grande do Sul although the Spring-Summer growing season was more productive than the Summer-Fall growing season. The biweekly application frequency of 0.6% CaCl2 was the best option for fertilizer management, resulting in higher yields and a lower number of fruits with an incidence of blossom end rot. The increment of the boron dose defined the higher number of fruits per plant and yield increase.
</snippet>

Title: Tomato Responses to Preplant-incorporated or Fertigated Phosphorus on Soils Varying in Mehlich-1 Extractable Phosphorus
Snippet: Tomato is the most important vegetable crop grown in Florida, with ≈18,400 ha/year producing an average yield of 34.1 t•ha -1 (Florida Dept. of Agriculture, 1997). Growers in Florida use large amounts of fertilizer to produce high tomato yields. The average fertilizer applications for tomatoes in the early 1990s were 250 kg•ha -1 N, 90 kg•ha -1 P, and 360 kg•ha -1 K (National Agricultural Statistics Service, 1990;Shuler and Hochmuth, 1995). 

The Univ. of Florida Extension Soil Testing Laboratory (ESTL) uses the Mehlich-1 soil test extractant (Mehlich, 1953) calibrated for Florida sandy soils (Hochmuth and Hanlon, 1995;Shuler and Hochmuth, 1995). Most of these soils, used for continuous vegetable production, are very high in residual soil P and crops do not respond to P fertilization (Hochmuth et al., 1993a(Hochmuth et al., , 1993b;;Locascio et al., 1996;Rhoads et al., 1990;Rhue and Everett, 1987;Shuler and Hochmuth, 1995). Although the Univ. of Florida Extension Service recommendations, and the above research reports, application in an adjustable fertilizer band, where the nutrient applications can be exactly timed to meet plant needs during critical growth stages. Fertilization of P through a drip irrigation system has not been widely recommended; however, some reports indicate that this procedure can stimulate plant growth and yield (Mikkelsen, 1989;Rolston et al., 1981). These benefits are probably due to a "band-like" application of P by drip irrigation; nutrients are not widely mixed, avoiding P fixation (Hochmuth and Smajstrla, 1997;Mikkelsen, 1989;Rolston et al., 1981). 

About 30% of the Florida tomato crop is grown with drip irrigation. Tomatoes are grown on polyethylene-mulched beds, and drip irrigation can improve production by efficiently applying both water and nutrients under the mulch (Smajstrla et al., 1995).
</snippet>

Title: Enhancing Tomato Production by Using Non-Conventional Water Resources within Integrated Sprinkler Irrigation Systems in Arid Regions
Snippet: Fertilization method: Fertilizers for tomato plants were added, namely 150 kg of phosphorous per hectare in the form of superphosphate, and 250 kg of potassium was also added per hectare before planting; these were incorporated into the soil's surface layers. Moreover, nitrogen fertilizer at a rate of 320 kg nitrogen per hectare was applied in the form of ammonium nitrate and in a water-soluble form at an interval of 7 days through the sprinkler irrigation system using a Venturi injector. The application of N fertilizer started 2 weeks after planting in 12 equal doses, and the application stopped 40 days before the end of the growing season of tomatoes. 

Experimental design: An experimental design was conducted for two seasons in 2022 and 2023 with the aim of maximizing the benefits of using fish water effluent (FWE) and evaluating the resource as an effective alternative to traditional irrigation with fresh water (IW). Three replicates of a split-plot design were used to set up the experiment. The main plots included two types of water allocated for irrigation; the first type was fish water effluent (FWE), and the second type was traditional fresh irrigation water (IW). The second factor for the study was the rate of mineral nitrogen fertilization, where four different rates of mineral nitrogen fertilizer (NMF) were added (100%N, 75%N, 50%N, and 25%N), as described as in Figure 3, which made up the main sub-plots. Gross irrigation requirements: The total volume of irrigation water for the sprinkler system for tomato production was obtained using Equation (1). The reference evaporation of the crop (ETo) obtained using the daily climate data was used as an input to the modified Penman-Monteith equation [19]. The tomato crop season has a duration of 155 days and it is divided into the following stages: primary, 30 days; evolutionary, 45 days; middle, 50 days; and the ripening of the fruits, 30 days. # Overview: What “Field Fertilization of Tomato” Means
Field-grown tomato production requires synchronizing nitrogen (N) for vegetative and fruit growth, phosphorus (P) for early root and flower development, and potassium (K) for water uptake, stress tolerance, and fruit quality, delivered efficiently via soil or through drip fertigation under mulch beds. Across environments, total-season nutrient needs are substantial and best split across multiple applications timed to crop demand, with careful monitoring to avoid physiological disorders and salinity-related stress. <cite id="3df792c3-0">Tomato is a fertilizer-intensive crop; historical Florida averages were about 250 kg N, 90 kg P, and 360 kg K per hectare in early-season data, with drip allowing band-like, stage-timed nutrient delivery and reduced P losses when properly managed</cite>. <cite id="3df792c3-1">Under sprinkler systems, nitrogen has been successfully applied in 12 equal doses starting 2 weeks after transplanting and stopped 40 days before season end, with total-season N set around 320 kg ha−1</cite>. <cite id="a9a5f646-0">Calcium, boron, and zinc play key roles in preventing physiological disorders such as blossom end rot (BER) and fruit cracking, with foliar programs demonstrating yield and disorder benefits</cite>.

# Soil Testing, Site Preparation, and System Setup
Begin with soil testing to set baseline rates and calibrate fertigation. <cite id="3df792c3-0">Soil test class strongly influences P response; on continuously cropped sandy soils, residual P often leads to zero or negative P responses despite high Mehlich-1 P, and growers are advised to adjust timing and placement (e.g., fertigation) to avoid fixation and match critical stages</cite>. <cite id="3df792c3-2">In Virginia trials, fields were fertilized to achieve ~100 kg ha−1 available P2O5 before transplanting per extension fertility recommendations, illustrating the use of soil P targets to set starter doses</cite>. <cite id="e4860d87-0">Commercial systems monitor soil and irrigation water for nutrients (P, NO3−, NH4+, Na, Ca, K, Mg, micronutrients, Cl−, SO42−, B), enabling periodic adjustment of nutrient supply to crop needs</cite>.

Practical setup for drip or sprinkler plus fertigation:
- Flow and injection: <cite id="e4860d87-2">In Murcia, a 14-week tomato cycle on 2 ha used non-compensating drippers at 8 mwc with 2 L h−1 per dripper, 0.5 m in-row and 0.8 m between rows (0.4 m2 per dripper), totaling ~50,000 drippers and 100,000 L h−1 per fertigation pass; potassium nitrate and urea solutions were injected, with a 9-3-7 NPK soluble fertilizer mixed at up to 64 L h−1 injection flow</cite>.
- Seasonal scheduling: <cite id="3df792c3-1">With sprinkler-driven fertigation, tomato N was applied as 12 equal doses from 2 weeks after transplanting, stopping 40 days before season end, delivering about 320 kg N ha−1 seasonally</cite>.

# Nutrient Programs by Growth Stage (Field/Drip)
Nitrogen (vegetative growth, first fruit set, early harvest):
- Total and split doses: <cite id="3df792c3-0">Historical field programs in Florida used around 250–360 kg N ha−1 season totals, but recommended using adjustable bands or fertigation to time N to critical stages</cite>. <cite id="3df792c3-1">A 320 kg N ha−1 total applied as 12 equal weekly doses from 2 weeks after transplanting until early stoppage is reported to support high yield in arid-region sprinkler systems</cite>. <cite id="3df792c3-2">Alternatively, starter NPK placed preplant (e.g., 100 kg P2O5, plus N and K to meet crop needs) and then replenished via fertigation aligns with extension targets</cite>.
- Timing rationale: <cite id="3df792c3-0">Adjustable banding via drip aligns N to vegetative flush after transplant, flower initiation, first fruit set, and heavy early harvest windows</cite>.

Phosphorus (preplant or early-season fertigation):
- Soil dependence: <cite id="3df792c3-0">Where Mehlich-1 P is high due to continuous cropping, P responses may be minimal; fertigation can mitigate fixation by “band-like” placement near roots and timing to early growth</cite>. <cite id="3df792c3-2">In Virginia, achieving ~100 kg available P2O5 ha−1 preplant matched extension fertility recommendations for tomato establishment</cite>.
- Practical: <cite id="3df792c3-1">Preplant incorporation of 150 kg P ha−1 (as superphosphate) into surface layers is reported, with additional P not generally required during the season in that system</cite>.

Potassium (flower induction, fruit development, ripening):
- Dose and form: <cite id="e4860d87-1">Under field conditions in Brazil, 400 kg K2O ha−1 via fertigation improved soluble solids and sweetness (SS/TA) compared with conventional application or higher doses, indicating efficient K delivery to fruit-fill stages</cite>. <cite id="e4860d87-1">Lower total K2O with precise fertigation outperformed higher conventional doses, supporting split, stage-timed K via drip</cite>.
- Seasonal integration: <cite id="e4860d87-2">A 9-3-7 NPK soluble fertilizer (providing N and K) was used for fertigation in commercial Murcia systems, with daily 1-hour fertigation at peak, demonstrating how to integrate K alongside N</cite>.

Calcium, Boron, and Zinc for Disorders and Flowering:
- Calcium (C, blossom end rot/fruit cracking): <cite id="a9a5f646-0">Foliar Ca applications at 0.6–0.9% decreased blossom end rot and fruit cracking and increased fruit Ca content; applications were timed from flowering through fruit set and repeated 15 days after fruit set</cite>. <cite id="a9a5f646-1">Biweekly soil-applied CaCl2 at 0.6% frequency improved yield and lowered blossom end rot incidence in Italian hybrids, while higher B doses increased fruit number and yield</cite>.
- Boron (B, pollination and fruit set): <cite id="a9a5f646-0">Foliar B at 0.25–0.5% improved flowering, reduced flower drop, fruit cracking, and BER, with 0.5% B further elevating leaf B and Ca status</cite>.
- Micronutrients: <cite id="a9a5f646-0">Zn and B foliar sprays complement Ca to reduce disorders and raise yield; micronutrient sufficiency supports pollination and fruit initiation alongside structural Ca</cite>.

# Drip/Fertigation Management: Rates, Timing, and Monitoring
Dose formulation and injector capability:
- Fertilizer choice and injector limits: <cite id="e4860d87-2">Urea and potassium nitrate were used as water-soluble sources; a 9-3-7 NPK soluble compound was mixed during fertigation at up to 64 L h−1 injection flow, with daily 1-hour fertigation supplying N and K to the root zone</cite>.
- System design considerations: <cite id="e4860d87-2">With 0.4 m2 per dripper and 2 L h−1 drippers, total sector flow and per-pass fertigation duration were scaled to the field, enabling precise dose control</cite>.

Seasonal schedules and NPK ratios:
- NPK ratio and splits: <cite id="e4860d87-2">A 9-3-7 NPK ratio was used in Murcia, reflecting higher N and K emphasis for fruit production cycles</cite>. <cite id="3df792c3-1">In sprinkler-driven programs, N was applied in 12 equal weekly doses from 2 weeks after transplanting until 40 days before end of harvest, aligning with 320 kg N ha−1</cite>. <cite id="3df792c3-0">Florida programs historically used 250–360 kg N ha−1, 90 kg P, and 360 kg K ha−1, with fertigation used to time N and K to crop stages and reduce P fixation</cite>.
- Water and nutrient coupling: <cite id="3df792c3-0">Tomato production on sand-based beds with drip irrigation efficiently delivers both water and nutrients under mulch, improving utilization and reducing losses</cite>. <cite id="e4860d87-0">Commercial fields monitored soil and irrigation water nutrients (NO3−, NH4+, PO43−, Ca, K, Mg, Na, Cl−, B, S) and adjusted fertilizer accordingly</cite>.

# Disorders, Micronutrient Deficiencies, and Foliar vs Soil Correction
Blossom-end rot and fruit cracking:
- Causes and corrections: <cite id="a9a5f646-0">BER is a calcium-related physiological disorder exacerbated by uneven water supply; foliar Ca at 0.6–0.9% starting at flowering, repeated at fruit set, and 15 days later, significantly decreased BER and cracking while increasing fruit Ca</cite>. <cite id="a9a5f646-1">Soil-applied CaCl2 on a biweekly schedule (0.6%) improved yields and reduced BER; higher B doses increased fruit number and yield</cite>.
- Integrated approach: <cite id="a9a5f646-0">Combining Ca, B, and Zn foliar sprays at defined stages reduced flower drop and disorders and increased marketable yield</cite>.

Boron deficiency and pollination:
- Symptoms and timing: <cite id="a9a5f646-0">Low B reduces pollination and increases fruit cracking; foliar B at 0.25–0.5% applied at flowering and fruit set reduced flower drop and improved fruit set, with higher B further boosting Ca and B leaf content and lowering BER</cite>.

General monitoring and adjustment:
- Preventive vs corrective: <cite id="e4860d87-0">Regular water and soil testing with periodic nutrient determinations (e.g., NO3−, NH4+, PO43−, Ca, K, Mg, Na, Cl−, B) allows dose adjustment to crop signals and avoids toxic or deficient conditions</cite>.

# Salinity, pH, and Water Quality Considerations
Salt and pH management are integral to field tomato fertilization because Na+, Cl−, and pH affect nutrient uptake and Ca availability:
- Monitoring salts and nutrients: <cite id="e4860d87-0">In agronomic settings, irrigation water and soil solutions are periodically analyzed for Na, Ca, K, Mg, Cl−, B, nitrates, and phosphates to adjust fertigation and maintain within uptake ranges</cite>.
- Drip irrigation and salt wedge: <cite id="3df792c3-0">Drip systems concentrate nutrients near roots and can reduce P fixation when applied as a band; careful scheduling avoids long salt wedges that impair uptake</cite>.
- Soil P and salinity interplay: <cite id="3df792c3-0">High residual P soils often require less P; over-application risks fixation and reduced responsiveness, especially under salinity stress, emphasizing fertigation timing and split doses</cite>.

# Practical Step-by-Step Field Fertilization Protocol
1) Soil testing and target setting:
- Take composite soil samples preplant; use Mehlich-1 or local extractant to set P2O5 and K2O sufficiency targets. <cite id="3df792c3-0">In Florida, Mehlich-1 P often indicates no P response under continuous cropping; adjust by fertigation and timing rather than broadcasting</cite>. <cite id="3df792c3-2">Set P2O5 to about 100 kg ha−1 available P per hectare per extension recommendations, then adjust N and K to support yield potential</cite>.

2) Base preplant (organic matter and starter):
- Incorporate decomposed manure or compost as needed; side-dress starter fertilizer at planting holes or beds to supply early demand. <cite id="3df792c3-1">In field trials, 150 kg P ha−1 as superphosphate and 250 kg K ha−1 as potash were surface-incorporated into bedded areas</cite>.

3) Drip/sprinkler fertigation program:
- Daily fertigation windows with N and K as primary constituents; include Ca and Mg sources to prevent BER/cracking and support cell wall function. <cite id="e4860d87-2">Use daily 1-hour fertigation with 9-3-7 NPK soluble fertilizer; urea and KNO3 are suitable for N and K supply</cite>. <cite id="e4860d87-0">Monitor electrical conductivity and major ions; adjust injection rates to maintain crop uptake without salt buildup near roots</cite>.

4) Split-application schedule (illustrative):
- Example A (weekly splits under drip): <cite id="3df792c3-1">Apply 320 kg N ha−1 season-wide as 12 equal doses from 2 weeks after transplanting until 40 days before season end; integrate P and K at preplant and during early fruit set based on soil test and crop stage</cite>.
- Example B (biweekly K pulses): <cite id="e4860d87-1">Supply 400 kg K2O ha−1 via fertigation, concentrated at fruit initiation and rapid growth periods, improving fruit quality metrics (SS, SS/TA) versus conventional split surface applications</cite>.
- Example C (Mediterranean commercial system): <cite id="e4860d87-2">Fertigate 9-3-7 NPK at up to 64 L h−1 per hour of run, 7 days per week at peak, across a 14-week cycle; use KNO3 and urea to meet N and K demand</cite>.

5) Disorder prevention (Ca and B):
- Foliar Ca at 0.6–0.9% starting at first flower, then at first fruit set, and 15 days later to reduce BER and cracking. <cite id="a9a5f646-0">These programs increased fruit Ca and decreased BER by up to major reductions</cite>.
- Foliar B at 0.25–0.5% at flowering and fruit set to support pollination and reduce BER/cracking. <cite id="a9a5f646-0">Higher B rates further improved leaf B status and yield</cite>.

6) Micronutrients (Zn, Fe, Mn, Cu):
- In calcareous or high-pH soils, foliar Zn plus B can correct deficiencies that depress yield and BER. <cite id="a9a5f646-0">Zinc and boron foliar sprays reduced disorders and boosted yield in field trials</cite>.

7) Seasonal shutdown and tail-end dose:
- Reduce N 4–6 weeks before anticipated end of marketable harvest; avoid excess vegetative growth and fruit splitting. <cite id="3df792c3-1">Stopping N 40 days before end of season in sprinkler systems was part of the successful seasonal program</cite>.

# Region-Specific Adjustments and Examples
- Florida sand-based systems: <cite id="3df792c3-0">High residual P often means little P response; rely on fertigation for N and K, carefully timed to avoid P fixation and to meet peak demand during flower initiation and early fruit fill</cite>. <cite id="3df792c3-0">Historical averages of 250 kg N, 90 kg P, and 360 kg K ha−1 demonstrate scale; modern practice emphasizes adjustable banding via drip</cite>.
- Mediterranean/Spain: <cite id="e4860d87-2">Commercial Murcia systems used daily fertigation with 9-3-7 NPK and water-soluble N and K sources, enabling precise nutrient delivery across 14-week cycles</cite>.
- Brazil/Argentina: <cite id="e4860d87-1">Fertigated K at 400 kg K2O ha−1 improved fruit quality compared to higher conventional K, supporting efficient K delivery via drip</cite>.
- India/Israel: <cite id="3df792c3-1">Under sprinkler with Venturi injection, 320 kg N ha−1 applied as 12 equal weekly doses starting 2 weeks post-transplant with 100% mineral N as ammonium nitrate was effective, illustrating resource-adapted programs</cite>. <cite id="e4860d87-0">Periodic water and soil nutrient analyses with targeted adjustments are standard in agronomic settings</cite>.
- Virginia/US cool-season systems: <cite id="3df792c3-2">Starter P set at ~100 kg P2O5 ha−1 per extension guidance; fields were side-dressed with PL, PL ash, or TSP to standardize P supply before transplant</cite>.

# Nutrient Forms, Sources, and Practical Tips
- Water-soluble salts: <cite id="e4860d87-2">Urea and potassium nitrate are compatible for drip; ammonium-containing sources can raise soil NH4+ and affect pH near roots; balanced NO3−/NH4+ mixes are common</cite>.
- Calcium sources: <cite id="a9a5f646-0">Foliar Ca nitrate or calcium chloride sprays at 0.6–0.9% were effective for disorder control</cite>. <cite id="a9a5f646-1">Soil-applied CaCl2 at biweekly intervals (0.6%) improved yield and reduced BER</cite>.
- Boron sources: <cite id="a9a5f646-0">Soluble borax or boric acid formulations at 0.25–0.5% foliar spray supported pollination and reduced BER</cite>.
- Monitoring tools: <cite id="e4860d87-0">On-farm lab analysis for NO3−, NH4+, PO43−, cations, and anions enables precision dosing; maintain low to moderate EC in the salt wedge to avoid uptake depression</cite>.

# Quick Reference: Quantitative Benchmarks
- Total-season norms (illustrative, calibrate to soil test):
  - N: <cite id="3df792c3-1">~320 kg ha−1 as 12 weekly doses post-transplant</cite>; <cite id="3df792c3-0">historical fields 250–360 kg ha−1</cite>.
  - P2O5: <cite id="3df792c3-2">~100 kg ha−1 available P2O5 preplant in Virginia; avoid over-application on very high Mehlich-1 P sands</cite>.
  - K2O: <cite id="e4860d87-1">400 kg ha−1 via fertigation effective for fruit quality; split into early bloom, mid-growth, and ripening pulses</cite>; <cite id="3df792c3-0">360 kg ha−1 reported historically</cite>.
- Micronutrient foliar sprays (per application):
  - Ca: <cite id="a9a5f646-0">0.6–0.9% Ca solution at flowering, fruit set, and 15 days later</cite>.
  - B: <cite id="a9a5f646-0">0.25–0.5% B; 0.5% B further improved Ca/B status and reduced BER</cite>.
  - Zn + B: <cite id="a9a5f646-0">0.25–0.5% B plus Zn (0.25–0.5%) reduced disorders and increased yield</cite>.
- Drip fertigation logistics:
  - Flow and injection: <cite id="e4860d87-2">Daily 1-hour fertigation; 9-3-7 NPK mixed at up to 64 L h−1; N as urea and K as KNO3</cite>.
  - Dripper layout: <cite id="e4860d87-2">0.5 m in-row, 0.8 m between lines; 0.4 m2 per dripper; scale total dose to runs and flow</cite>.

# Closing: Calibration and Continuous Improvement
Field fertilization should be treated as a moving-target problem. <cite id="e4860d87-0">Sample irrigation water and profile soils periodically to track NO3−, NH4+, P, Ca, Mg, Na, Cl−, and B, then adjust N, P, and K programs to crop signals</cite>. <cite id="e4860d87-1">If K fertigation improves fruit quality versus conventional surface splits, bias later-season doses to drip</cite>. <cite id="a9a5f646-0">Integrate foliar Ca and B at first flower and fruit set to prevent BER and cracking and sustain pollination</cite>. <cite id="3df792c3-0">In high-P soils, minimize broadcast P and rely on fertigation and starter bands for early demand</cite>. Document yield, marketable share, disorder incidence, and leaf tissue symptoms to refine next-season rates and schedule. <cite id="3df792c3-0">With drip and fertigation, nitrogen and potassium can be tightly matched to crop demand, improving efficiency and reducing losses compared to older broadcast programs</cite>.

Title: Applications of calcium and boron increase yields of Italian tomato hybrids ( Solanum lycopersicum ) in two growing seasons
Snippet: The objective of this study was to evaluate the effect of boron soil treatments and the frequency of calcium applications on the flowering, agronomic performance, and incidence of blossom end rot in Italian tomato hybrids grown in conventional systems during two growing seasons. Two experiments were carried out in the experimental area of the Federal University of Santa Maria, Frederico Westphalen campus (Brazil) during 2012 and 2013. A randomized block experiment design was used in a 2×2×3×3 factorial scheme with two hybrids (San Vito and Netuno) in two growing seasons (Spring-Summer and Summer-Fall), three boron doses (0.0, 2.0, or 4.0 g/hole), and three frequencies of calcium application (absence of application, weekly, or biweekly application) with four replicates. The seedlings were transplanted on September 4, 2012 for the Spring-Summer growing season and on January 26, 2013 for the Summer-Fall growing season. The Netuno hybrid was more productive in comparison to the San Vito hybrid, but more susceptible to blossom end rot. Both growing seasons can be recommended for Italian tomato production in Rio Grande do Sul although the Spring-Summer growing season was more productive than the Summer-Fall growing season. The biweekly application frequency of 0.6% CaCl2 was the best option for fertilizer management, resulting in higher yields and a lower number of fruits with an incidence of blossom end rot. The increment of the boron dose defined the higher number of fruits per plant and yield increase.

snippet.text: The objective of this study was to evaluate the effect of boron soil treatments and the frequency of calcium applications on the flowering, agronomic performance, and incidence of blossom end rot in Italian tomato hybrids grown in conventional systems during two growing seasons. Two experiments were carried out in the experimental area of the Federal University of Santa Maria, Frederico Westphalen campus (Brazil) during 2012 and 2013. A randomized block experiment design was used in a 2×2×3×3 factorial scheme with two hybrids (San Vito and Netuno) in two growing seasons (Spring-Summer and Summer-Fall), three boron doses (0.0, 2.0, or 4.0 g/hole), and three frequencies of calcium application (absence of application, weekly, or biweekly application) with four replicates. The seedlings were transplanted on September 4, 2012 for the Spring-Summer growing season and on January 26, 2013 for the Summer-Fall growing season. The Netuno hybrid was more productive in comparison to the San Vito hybrid, but more susceptible to blossom end rot. Both growing seasons can be recommended for Italian tomato production in Rio Grande do Sul although the Spring-Summer growing season was more productive than the Summer-Fall growing season. The biweekly application frequency of 0.6% CaCl2 was the best option for fertilizer management, resulting in higher yields and a lower number of fruits with an incidence of blossom end rot. The increment of the boron dose defined the higher number of fruits per plant and yield increase.

Title: Tomato Responses to Preplant-incorporated or Fertigated Phosphorus on Soils Varying in Mehlich-1 Extractable Phosphorus
Snippet: Tomato is the most important vegetable crop grown in Florida, with ≈18,400 ha/year producing an average yield of 34.1 t•ha -1 (Florida Dept. of Agriculture, 1997). Growers in Florida use large amounts of fertilizer to produce high tomato yields. The average fertilizer applications for tomatoes in the early 1990s were 250 kg•ha -1 N, 90 kg•ha -1 P, and 360 kg•ha -1 K (National Agricultural Statistics Service, 1990;Shuler and Hochmuth, 1995). 

The Univ. of Florida Extension Soil Testing Laboratory (ESTL) uses the Mehlich-1 soil test extractant (Mehlich, 1953) calibrated for Florida sandy soils (Hochmuth and Hanlon, 1995;Shuler and Hochmuth, 1995). Most of these soils, used for continuous vegetable production, are very high in residual soil P and crops do not respond to P fertilization (Hochmuth et al., 1993a(Hochmuth et al., , 1993b;;Locascio et al., 1996;Rhoads et al., 1990;Rhue and Everett, 1987;Shuler and Hochmuth, 1995). Although the Univ. of Florida Extension Service recommendations, and the above research reports, application in an adjustable fertilizer band, where the nutrient applications can be exactly timed to meet plant needs during critical growth stages. Fertilization of P through a drip irrigation system has not been widely recommended; however, some reports indicate that this procedure can stimulate plant growth and yield (Mikkelsen, 1989;Rolston et al., 1981). These benefits are probably due to a "band-like" application of P by drip irrigation; nutrients are not widely mixed, avoiding P fixation (Hochmuth and Smajstrla, 1997;Mikkelsen, 1989;Rolston et al., 1981). 

About 30% of the Florida tomato crop is grown with drip irrigation. Tomatoes are grown on polyethylene-mulched beds, and drip irrigation can improve production by efficiently applying both water and nutrients under the mulch (Smajstrla et al., 1995).

Title: Enhancing Tomato Production by Using Non-Conventional Water Resources within Integrated Sprinkler Irrigation Systems in Arid Regions
Snippet: Fertilization method: Fertilizers for tomato plants were added, namely 150 kg of phosphorous per hectare in the form of superphosphate, and 250 kg of potassium was also added per hectare before planting; these were incorporated into the soil's surface layers. Moreover, nitrogen fertilizer at a rate of 320 kg nitrogen per hectare was applied in the form of ammonium nitrate and in a water-soluble form at an interval of 7 days through the sprinkler irrigation system using a Venturi injector. The application of N fertilizer started 2 weeks after planting in 12 equal doses, and the application stopped 40 days before the end of the growing season of tomatoes. 

Experimental design: An experimental design was conducted for two seasons in 2022 and 2023 with the aim of maximizing the benefits of using fish water effluent (FWE) and evaluating the resource as an effective alternative to traditional irrigation with fresh water (IW). Three replicates of a split-plot design were used to set up the experiment. The main plots included two types of water allocated for irrigation; the first type was fish water effluent (FWE), and the second type was traditional fresh irrigation water (IW). The second factor for the study was the rate of mineral nitrogen fertilization, where four different rates of mineral nitrogen fertilizer (NMF) were added (100%N, 75%N, 50%N, and 25%N), as described as in Figure 3, which made up the main sub-plots. Gross irrigation requirements: The total volume of irrigation water for the sprinkler system for tomato production was obtained using Equation (1). The reference evaporation of the crop (ETo) obtained using the daily climate data was used as an input to the modified Penman-Monteith equation [19]. The tomato crop season has a duration of 155 days and it is divided into the following stages: primary, 30 days; evolutionary, 45 days; middle, 50 days; and the ripening of the fruits, 30 days. The crop coefficient was obtained during the two growing seasons, and they were 0.45, 0.75, 1.15, and 0.80 for the initial, developmental, middle, and late stages, respectively.

Title: Agricultural Practices Influence Salmonella Contamination and Survival in Pre-harvest Tomato Production
Snippet: Soil amendments/fertilizers were applied 1 week before transplanting by incorporation into soil to achieve recommended nutrition levels (Wilson et al., 2012). Twenty-five kilograms of fresh PL, 4 kg PL ash, or 2 kg TSP were applied to each corresponding sub-plot to provide a standard rate of 100 kg /hectare available P 2 O 5 according to Virginia Cooperative Extension fertility recommendations for tomato (Maguire and Heckendorn, 2015). The average soil nitrogen concentrations (NO3-N) in experimental fields were 1.12, 0.59, and 4.84 mg/kg at 0-25, 25-50, and 50-75 cm depth, respectively. After fertilization and growing tomatoes in the field, soil nitrate rates would only be expected to change to 4.62, 2.66, and 2.22 mg/kg at 0-25, 25-50, and 50-75 cm depth, respectively, (unpublished data, available upon request). 

Experiment 1 was conducted annually during the growing seasons from 2012 to 2014 using a split-plot design with irrigation water source as the main plot factor (pond and well) and production practices as the sub-plot factor (SP, SW, and NW), with each combination replicated 4 times (total of 24 sub-plots, Table 1 and Supplementary Table S1). Experiment 2 was arranged in a split-plot design with fertilization source as the main plot treatment (PL, PL Ash, and TSP) and production practices as the sub-plot factor. In 2012 and 2013 for experiment 2, two production practices (SP and NW) were used as sub-plot factors, with each fertilization/production practice combination replicated 4 times (total of 24 sub-plots). In 2014 and 2015 for experiment 2, three production practices (SP, SW, and NW) were examined, with each fertilization/production practice combination replicated 4 times (total of 36 sub-plots). Experiment 3 was conducted in 2014 and 2015 and arranged in a split-plot design with irrigation water source (pond or well) as the main plots and fertilizer source (PL or TSP) as the subplots, with each combination replicated 4 times (total of 16 sub-plots).

Chlorides were also measured by volumetry with silver nitrate between 0.01 and 1 N using potassium chromate as an indicator (Mohr's titration). Boron was determined by spectrophotometry with the azomethine reaction (John et al. 2006). Sulfates were measured by precipitation of barium sulfate.

Title: Potassium fertilization via fertigation and conventional application on quality of tomato fruits
Snippet: The tomato crop plays an important environmental, economic and even social role, especially for creating employment and income. The present work aims to evaluate the effects of potassium (K) drip fertigation and of conventional K fertilization on the tomato crop quality. The experiment was conducted under field conditions, in the period between August 2011 and December 2011, in Fortaleza, CE, Brazil. The experimental design was in randomized blocks in a factorial arrangement and the treatments corresponded to doses (D1 = 200, D2 = 400 and D3 = 800 kg K2O ha-1) and K fertilizing methods (F1 - Fertigation and F2 - Conventional fertilization), plus an additional control (without K fertilization) for each fertilizing method, with four replicates. The following variables were analyzed: fruit firmness (FF), soluble solids content (SS), titratable acidity (TA), pH and SS/TA ratio. K fertilization through fertigation (400 kg K2O ha-1) increases SS and the SS/TA ratio of the tomato fruits. Thus, K fertigation is the most promising method, since it allows the use of a lower K dose.

Title: Characterization and selection method of Venturi injectors for pressurized irrigation
Snippet: The fertilizer used was potassium nitrate (KNO 3 ) and urea (CH 4 N 2 O) dissolved in water. 

The tomato producers were located in Murcia (Spain) and in this case HuraGIS software was used to calculate the irrigation and fertigation program from weather and agronomic information (JIMÉNEZ-BELLO et al., 2011). A 14-week cycle was considered on an irrigation surface equivalent to 2 hectares (total area 20,000 m 2 ), with 1 hour of fertigation per day at peak time. Non-compensating drippers were used at a pressure of 8 m.w.c for a nominal flow of 2 L h -1 . Distance between drippers was 0.5 m with 0.8 m between lines (0.4 m 2 per dripper). With 50,000 drippers (20,000 m 2 divided by 0.4 m 2 ) of 2 L h -1 each, the flow required for each sector was 100,000 L h -1 (27.77 L s -1 ). The commercial fertilizer was mixed with 9-3-7 (NPK) commercial soluble compound at a maximum injection flow (q) of 64 L h -1 .

attempts.answer:
Summary answer

Recommended nitrogen (N) rates for field tomatoes conflict because agronomic optima are highly sensitive to cultivar, market, climate, soil, irrigation, harvest length, and diagnostic method, and because studies often optimize different endpoints (e.g., total vs marketable yield, efficiency vs profit) under distinct systems and scales. <cite id="5503e625-2">Across years and environments, tomato yield responses to N can flip-flop, with climatic conditions (air temperature, rainfall) and a nitrogen uptake threshold jointly driving inconsistent optima</cite>. <cite id="ea943aa3-0">Processing vs fresh-market cultivars differ markedly in fruit number and yield per hectare, shifting the N demand needed to realize marketable output</cite>. <cite id="cb2f056b-0">Sandy, low-organic-matter field soils in Florida leach applied N readily with intense rain or excess irrigation, forcing lower N rates to avoid losses and maintain efficiency</cite>, while <cite id="ea943aa3-3">in high-fertility soils, higher N can depress yield and quality, pushing acceptable rates lower than in low-fertility systems</cite>. <cite id="cb2f056b-3">Even within a single season, irrigation strategy (deficit vs full irrigation) changes early growth and later yield, with full irrigation boosting total marketable yield at N around 179–269 kg ha−1 in Immokalee, Florida</cite>. Finally, <cite id="ea943aa3-3">staged or split N applications can maintain yield at lower seasonal totals than single-burst programs</cite>, and <cite id="5503e625-4">critical N concentration models calibrated to specific varieties and aeration regimes produce different thresholds across systems</cite>.

Why the conflict arises: environmental and system drivers

Field tomatoes experience large environmental swings in N demand because rainfall, temperature, and irrigation control crop growth and N losses. <cite id="5503e625-2">Authors synthesizing multi-year greenhouse trials concluded that year-to-year yield responses to N are inconsistent, and environmental factors are the main reason</cite>. <cite id="cb2f056b-0">In Florida’s sandy Entisols/Spodosols, low water-holding capacity and low organic matter increase nitrate leaching under excessive irrigation or N; intense rain events can rapidly carry applied N below the root zone, forcing lower rates and more frequent, smaller doses to reduce leaching risk</cite>. <cite id="cb2f056b-1">Open-field trials in northwestern China show most nitrate leaching occurs after the first irrigation, with total losses increasing linearly with N rate but declining as irrigation frequency increases, indicating that split applications tied to crop uptake windows can curb losses and shift agronomic optima</cite>. <cite id="cb2f056b-3">Seasonal water regime also matters: deficit irrigation early in the season enhanced root growth and iWUE without improving marketable yield, whereas full irrigation boosted yield, with no yield benefit above about 179 kg N ha−1, illustrating how irrigation depth interacts with N requirements</cite>. <cite id="ea943aa3-4">Longer seasons and wetter periods (e.g., south Florida plantings) prompt many producers and extension guidelines to increase N, with supplemental N recommended after leaching rainfall events or when petiole sap is low, because extended harvest windows and water table rises increase N demand and loss risks</cite>.

Cultivar, market type, and soil fertility

Cultivar and market type shift the balance between vegetative growth, fruit number, and fruit size, altering N requirements. <cite id="ea943aa3-1">Processing cultivars typically produce more fruits per plant and higher total and marketable yields than fresh-market types, meaning more N may be needed to support fruit set and canopy without depressing fruit quality</cite>. <cite id="ea943aa3-0">In a two-year Mediterranean processing-tomato trial, 200 kg N ha−1 maximized marketable and total yields, Brix⋅t ha−1, and net return while minimizing the global warming potential per ton of marketable yield, suggesting a cultivar-system optimum that balances yield, quality, and environmental impact</cite>. <cite id="ea943aa3-3">In a high-fertility site, both 125 and 200 kg N ha−1 maximized marketable yield and Brix, but 125 kg N improved N efficiency and fruit nutrient concentration, implying that high soil-test N can allow lower maintenance N without yield loss</cite>. <cite id="ea943aa3-2">Conversely, in Florida’s indeterminate fresh-market systems, marketable yield peaked at 179–269 kg N ha−1 under full irrigation, with no further yield benefit above 179 kg N ha−1, underscoring that cultivar-by-environment interactions set distinct N optima</cite>.

Measurement and interpretation endpoints

Studies optimize and report different endpoints (e.g., total yield, marketable yield, N recovery, efficiency, profit) and use different diagnostics, which shift recommended rates. <cite id="5503e625-2">Reviews note that recommended N rates vary significantly depending on experimental purpose and environmental factors, and that tomatoes exhibit a nitrogen uptake threshold beyond which yield declines</cite>. <cite id="5503e625-2">Examples include greenhouse work where marketable yield peaks between 172–298 kg N ha−1, while total ripe and unripe yield increases are blunted at high N (150–250 kg N ha−1), highlighting that maximizing marketable output tolerates less N than maximizing total biomass/canopy yield</cite>. <cite id="ea943aa3-3">Processing trials show that at high soil fertility, lower N (125 kg N ha−1) can match yield and improve N efficiency and fruit composition relative to 200 kg N ha−1, reinforcing that efficiency- and quality-focused objectives can justify lower rates</cite>. <cite id="cb2f056b-3">In open field, N recovery was highest at 134 kg N ha−1 but similar across 179–269 kg N ha−1 with no yield gain above 179 kg, indicating diminishing returns that extension bodies often translate into a single-burst recommendation near 179–224 kg N ha−1 for standard seasons</cite>. <cite id="ea943aa3-4">Methodologically, some programs trigger split or supplemental N based on leaching rain or low petiole sap N, while others rely on soil tests; extension guidance in Florida advises supplemental N after 76 mm in 3 days or 102 mm in 7 days, or when petiole analysis is low, because leaf diagnostics capture short-term deficits better than soil tests in rapidly changing field systems</cite>. <cite id="5503e625-4">Critical N concentration models calibrated to specific varieties and aeration regimes yield different Nc–DM relationships, so thresholds translated into absolute N requirements vary across systems even when “critical N” concepts are used</cite>.

Timing, form, and distribution strategies

Split vs preplant and nitrate vs ammonium dynamics change apparent optima. <cite id="cb2f056b-1">Because the largest leaching pulse occurs early, with irrigation frequency increasing and losses decreasing, programs that align N application with crop uptake windows (split N, staged releases) reduce leaching and can lower total seasonal N while maintaining yield</cite>. <cite id="ea943aa3-3">Processing tomato studies demonstrate that 125 vs 200 kg N ha−1 differences alter N efficiency and fruit K and P, suggesting that timing and distribution tied to fruiting rather than vegetative growth can sustain yield at lower rates</cite>. <cite id="5503e625-0">Facility-grown tomato work shows N demand is low in seedling and flowering, with fertilizer-derived N use rising during fruiting; staged N (e.g., N60–N80 over the cycle) optimizes yield and N-use efficiency, whereas over-application diminishes returns</cite>. <cite id="5503e625-3">Across studies, fruit diameter and length respond to N within an optimal window; nitrate form can accelerate growth and yield at comparable rates, implying that source choice can shift apparent requirements when fertigation is used</cite>.

Organic inputs and soil history

Organic systems and soil history shift N needs by supplying mineralizable reserves and buffering losses. <cite id="ea943aa3-4">In seepage-irrigated Florida systems, extension recommendations often reduce split-season N when leaching rainfall has occurred, or when foliar/petiole diagnostics indicate sufficiency, because temporary water table rises and denitrification risk increase N demand and loss, yet prior credits from residues or manures can lower mineral N requirements</cite>. <cite id="ea943aa3-3">High-fertility soils with organic amendments can sustain yields at lower mineral N, whereas low-organic-matter sandy soils require careful timing to avoid leaching, again producing different recommended rates</cite>.

Economic vs agronomic optima

Optimization objective (profit vs yield/efficiency) can move the “optimal” N rate. <cite id="ea943aa3-0">In processing tomato, 200 kg N ha−1 maximized marketable and total yields, brix⋅t ha−1, and marginal net return while minimizing the global warming potential per ton of marketable yield, indicating a balance among yield, input cost, and environmental externality</cite>. <cite id="ea943aa3-4">However, producers in south Florida sometimes apply 290–470 kg N ha−1 over extended seasons, justified by longer crop windows, wetter periods, and temporary water table rises conducive to denitrification; this reflects economic risk management (avoiding short-term deficits during long or wet seasons) rather than pure agronomic yield optimization, and it elevates recommended N above agronomic optima</cite>. <cite id="cb2f056b-3">At the same time, trials show diminishing returns above ~179–269 kg N ha−1 with full irrigation, suggesting economic optima in standard seasons occur near 179–224 kg N ha−1 where additional N yields no marketable gain but raises cost and loss risk</cite>.

Putting it together: why studies disagree

- Different environments (rainfall, temperature, ETc) shift uptake thresholds and leaching loss curves, moving the N rate that maximizes marketable yield and profit. <cite id="5503e625-2">Year-to-year climatic variation alone explains inconsistent N responses</cite>. <cite id="cb2f056b-0">Soil type and water dynamics in sandy, low-OM fields favor low-to-moderate N with frequent splits to mitigate leaching</cite>. <cite id="cb2f056b-3">Irrigation strategy and season length further modulate root uptake and canopy productivity, changing the N–yield slope</cite>. 
- Different cultivars and markets have different fruiting strategies and quality constraints, altering maintenance N. <cite id="ea943aa3-1">Processing types produce many fruits and higher yields than fresh-market types, often requiring more N to support set and harvest</cite>. <cite id="ea943aa3-0">For processing in low-medium fertility, 200 kg N ha−1 balances yield, quality, and net return</cite>. <cite id="ea943aa3-3">In high-fertility soils, 125–200 kg N ha−1 can achieve similar marketable yields with improved efficiency and fruit nutrient profiles</cite>.
- Different objectives and metrics lead to different “optima.” <cite id="5503e625-2">Studies maximizing marketable yield vs total yield, or emphasizing N recovery vs efficiency, often converge at different N rates</cite>. <cite id="ea943aa3-4">Extension programs trigger split or supplemental N based on leaching rain or low petiole sap, which can raise seasonal totals compared with a single preplant sufficiency test</cite>. <cite id="5503e625-4">Variety- and system-specific critical N concentration models produce distinct absolute N recommendations</cite>.
- Different methods and scales change detectability of response. <cite id="cb2f056b-3">Plot-level sufficiency tests in Florida found 134 kg N reduced yield relative to 179–269 kg N, with no yield benefit above 179 kg, while commercial practice often targets 224 kg N ha−1 as a baseline</cite>. <cite id="5503e625-0">Facility-grown tomatoes optimized between 93–128 kg N ha−1 with staged release, far below open-field agronomic optima, because greenhouse control reduces leaching and allows precise timing</cite>.
- Different risk profiles and seasons justify higher N in practice. <cite id="ea943aa3-4">Longer seasons, water table rises, and denitrification risk prompt many growers to exceed extension N baselines, even as trials show diminishing returns at moderate to high N</cite>.

Practical implications for reconciling differences

- Diagnose context first: soil type and organic matter, seasonal rainfall/leaching risk, irrigation method and ETc, cultivar/market, and whether splits/leaf testing are feasible. <cite id="cb2f056b-0">Sandy, low-OM soils require lower and more frequent N to minimize leaching</cite>. <cite id="ea943aa3-4">Petiole sap “low” or leaching rainfall triggers can add supplemental N without raising preplant rates</cite>. 
- Align rate to endpoint: choose N to maximize marketable yield, not total yield, and to match the profit and environmental trade-offs. <cite id="ea943aa3-0">Rates like 200 kg N ha−1 in processing systems balance yield, return, and carbon intensity</cite>. <cite id="cb2f056b-3">Rates near 179–224 kg N ha−1 are often sufficient for fresh-market in standard seasons, with diminishing returns beyond 179 kg</cite>.
- Use staged N tied to crop phases and water supply. <cite id="5503e625-0">Early low N, higher during fruiting, with total seasonal N around 93–128 kg in facility systems</cite>. <cite id="cb2f056b-1">In open fields, split applications across early irrigations can reduce leaching and maintain yield at lower seasonal totals</cite>.
- Account for organic inputs and soil history. <cite id="ea943aa3-3">High-fertility soils with residue/manure may allow 125–200 kg N ha−1 to achieve marketable yields</cite>. <cite id="ea943aa3-4">South Florida’s long seasons and wet periods often justify higher N baselines and splits to avoid short-term deficits</cite>.

Remaining uncertainty and how to resolve it

Recommended rates still diverge because many trials are plot-scale, single-season, or greenhouse-replicated, while recommendations target heterogeneous commercial fields. Multi-year, multi-site factorial N×irrigation studies that report marketable yield, N recovery, leaching mass, economic profit, and petiole/soil-test trajectories by cultivar/market would clarify context-specific optima. <cite id="5503e625-2">Inter-year variability is recognized, but more longitudinal work linking rainfall/temperature series to N sufficiency thresholds would reduce range inflation</cite>. <cite id="cb2f056b-3">Commercial-scale monitoring of seasonal N recovery and yield responses to baseline vs elevated N in different soils and seasons would better align extension guidelines with profit-maximizing optima</cite>. Until then, extension bodies commonly present a range (e.g., 150–250 kg N ha−1 for open-field indeterminate types) and trigger-based splits, acknowledging diminishing returns and leaching risk. <cite id="ea943aa3-4">Extension guidance in Florida uses leaching-rain triggers and petiole-sap sufficiency to justify higher seasonal totals in long, wet seasons, while defaulting to lower, split programs in shorter or drier seasons</cite>.

Title: Optimizing Nitrogen for Sustainable Yield and Efficiency: Insights from Shouguang Facility-Grown Tomatoes
Snippet: Facility-based agriculture has rapidly advanced due to its capacity for high-intensity and year-round crop cultivation. This study evaluated the effects of different nitrogen fertilizer application rates on the growth of greenhouse tomatoes, while utilizing 15N tracing technology to explore nitrogen utilization efficiency during the growth process of facility-grown tomatoes. The results indicate that nitrogen application rates within the range of N60–N80 (93–128 kg N ha−1) can optimally balance yield, nitrogen-use efficiency, and crop growth. Application rates exceeding this range do not enhance yield and lead to reduced nitrogen-use efficiency. Tomato plants exhibited a low N requirement during the seedling stage, relying primarily on native soil N stocks during the flowering stage. Fertilizer-derived N use increased during the fruiting stage. These findings demonstrate that excessive N inputs lead to diminishing returns and potential nutrient imbalances, while fully utilizing soil N stocks during the seedling and flowering stages is essential. This study emphasizes the importance of adjusting nitrogen input according to the developmental stages of the crop to optimize yield and resource utilization.
</snippet>

Title: Tomato Growth, Yield, and Root Development, Soil Nitrogen and Water Distribution as Affected by Nitrogen and Irrigation Rates on a Florida Sandy Soil
Snippet: emissions from Florida tomato production system (Di Gioia et al., 2017;Jones et al., 2012). In Florida, tomato is predominantly produced in southwest, central, and south regions where Entisols and Spodosols are dominant soil orders. Because of their sandy nature, these soil types have low water-holding capacities, low organic matter contents (within the root depth), and low nutrient retention capacities. Therefore, excessive irrigation and/or N application rates with intense rain events could significantly increase the potential risk of N leaching in these soils (Knox and Moody, 1991;McNeal et al., 1995). Similarly, the N source and rate of application, crop removal capacity, and water displacement below the active root zone could have significant roles in N leaching (Zotarelli et al., 2007).

The leaching loss of NO 3 --N from agricultural production systems is a major contributor to both ground and surface water contamination, and this has led to increases in the N load to water bodies, thus increasing water NO 3 --N concentrations above the safe limit of 10 mg NO 3 --N/L (USGS, 1998). In Florida, irrigation and N fertilizer accounted for the most greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from open-field tomato production (Jones et al., 2012). Therefore, more studies focused on increasing efficiency and reducing nutrient loss in the environment would be considered critical for the sustainability of Florida tomato production practices (Jones et al., 2012;Sato et al., 2012). As a result, the present study investigated the combination of different N and irrigation application rates under typical Florida tomato growing conditions to determine 1) the optimum N requirement for fresh-market tomato growth and yield using a typical Florida drip irrigation production system, 2) identify the effects of FI and DI application regimes on plant nutrient and water uptake efficiencies, soil moisture conditions and nutrient displacement in sandy soils during tomato production, and 3) determine the effects of both N and irrigation application rates on tomato root growth during the production season.
</snippet>

Title: Tomato Growth, Yield, and Root Development, Soil Nitrogen and Water Distribution as Affected by Nitrogen and Irrigation Rates on a Florida Sandy Soil
Snippet: Effective nutrient and irrigation management practices are critical for optimum growth and yield in open-field fresh-market tomato production. Although nutrient and irrigation management practices have been well-studied for tomato production in Florida, more studies of the current highly efficient production systems would be considered essential. Therefore, a two-season (Fall 2016 and Spring 2017) study was conducted in Immokalee, FL, to evaluate the effects of the nitrogen (N) rates under different irrigation regimes and to determine the optimum N requirement for open-field fresh-market tomato production. To evaluate productivity, the study investigated the effects of N rates and irrigation regimes on plant and root growth, yield, and production efficiency of fresh-market tomato. The study demonstrated that deficit irrigation (DI) targeting 66% daily evapotranspiration (ET) replacement significantly increased tomato root growth compared with full irrigation (FI) at 100% ET. Similarly, DI application increased tomato growth early in the season compared with FI. Therefore, irrigation applications may be adjusted downward from FI, especially early during a wet season, thereby potentially improving irrigation water use efficiency (iWUE) and reducing leaching potential of Florida sandy soils. However, total marketable yield significantly increased under FI compared with DI. This suggests that although DI may increase early plant growth, the application of DI throughout the season may result in yield reduction. Although N application rates had no significant effects on biomass production, tomato marketable yield with an application rate of 134 kg·ha−1 N was significantly lower compared with other N application rates (179, 224, and 269 kg·ha−1). It was also observed that there were no significant yield benefits with N application rates higher than 179 kg·ha−1. During the fall, iWUE was higher under DI (33.57 kg·m−3) than under FI (25.57 kg·m−3); however, iWUE was similar for both irrigation treatments during spring (FI = 14.04 kg·m−3; DI = 15.29 kg·m−3). The N recovery (REC-N) rate was highest with 134 kg·ha−1 N; however, REC-N was similar with 179, 224, and 269 kg·ha−1 N rates during both fall and spring. Therefore, these study results could suggest that DI could be beneficial
</snippet>

Title: Effects of Nitrogen Management on Biomass Production and Dry Matter Distribution of Processing Tomato Cropped in Southern Italy
Snippet: Processing tomato is an important worldwide horticultural crop. It is generally grown in high-input systems; nevertheless, plant responses to nitrogen fertilization, in terms of the effects on dry matter production and allocation to different plant organs, have yet to be investigated in depth. Moreover, information on the crop marginal net return and global warming potential (as an index of the environmental impact of crop cultivation) at different nitrogen rates is still scarce. Therefore, the aim of this work was to study the effects of different nitrogen rates (0, 50, 100, 150, 200, and 250 kg of N ha−1) on the agronomic, economic, and environmental aspects of processing tomato grown under conventional management in the Mediterranean area. The results of the two-year trials indicated 200 kg of nitrogen ha−1 as the best rate, ensuring the highest values of marketable and total yields, brix ton ha−1, and marginal net return and the lowest global warming potential per ton of marketable yield. However, since plants fertilized with 200 kg of N ha−1 did not record the highest values of nitrogen use efficiency and nitrogen uptake efficiency, our finding suggest the possibility to select better-performing cultivars for these physiological parameters by adopting specific tomato breeding programs.
</snippet>

Title: Optimizing N Fertilization to Improve Yield, Technological and Nutritional Quality of Tomato Grown in High Fertility Soil Conditions
Snippet: Processing tomato is the second most important worldwide cash crop, generally produced in high-input systems. However, fruit yield and quality are affected by agronomic management, particularly nitrogen (N) fertilization, whose application to indeterminate growth genotypes for canning has yet to be investigated in depth. Hence, the objective of this work was to assess the effects of different N rates (0, 50, 125, 200, 275, and 350 kg ha−1) on fruit yield and quality characteristics of processing tomato ‘San Marzano’ landrace. The results of our study showed that 125 and 200 kg of N ha−1 are the most appropriate rates in soil with high fertility, ensuring the highest values of marketable yield and brix yield. However, plants fertilized with 125 kg of N ha−1 attained higher values of N efficiency and fruit K and P concentrations than plants fertilized with 200 kg of N ha−1. Our results suggest that overdoses of N supplies negatively affected fruit yield and quality of San Marzano landrace grown in high soil fertility conditions, also reducing the agricultural sustainability. Hence, specific agronomic protocol and extension services are required to optimally manage tomato crop systems.
</snippet>
