Summary answer

Recommended nitrogen (N) rates for field tomatoes conflict because agronomic optima are highly sensitive to cultivar, market, climate, soil, irrigation, harvest length, and diagnostic method, and because studies often optimize different endpoints (e.g., total vs marketable yield, efficiency vs profit) under distinct systems and scales. <cite id="5503e625-2">Across years and environments, tomato yield responses to N can flip-flop, with climatic conditions (air temperature, rainfall) and a nitrogen uptake threshold jointly driving inconsistent optima</cite>. <cite id="ea943aa3-0">Processing vs fresh-market cultivars differ markedly in fruit number and yield per hectare, shifting the N demand needed to realize marketable output</cite>. <cite id="cb2f056b-0">Sandy, low-organic-matter field soils in Florida leach applied N readily with intense rain or excess irrigation, forcing lower N rates to avoid losses and maintain efficiency</cite>, while <cite id="ea943aa3-3">in high-fertility soils, higher N can depress yield and quality, pushing acceptable rates lower than in low-fertility systems</cite>. <cite id="cb2f056b-3">Even within a single season, irrigation strategy (deficit vs full irrigation) changes early growth and later yield, with full irrigation boosting total marketable yield at N around 179–269 kg ha−1 in Immokalee, Florida</cite>. Finally, <cite id="ea943aa3-3">staged or split N applications can maintain yield at lower seasonal totals than single-burst programs</cite>, and <cite id="5503e625-4">critical N concentration models calibrated to specific varieties and aeration regimes produce different thresholds across systems</cite>.

Why the conflict arises: environmental and system drivers

Field tomatoes experience large environmental swings in N demand because rainfall, temperature, and irrigation control crop growth and N losses. <cite id="5503e625-2">Authors synthesizing multi-year greenhouse trials concluded that year-to-year yield responses to N are inconsistent, and environmental factors are the main reason</cite>. <cite id="cb2f056b-0">In Florida’s sandy Entisols/Spodosols, low water-holding capacity and low organic matter increase nitrate leaching under excessive irrigation or N; intense rain events can rapidly carry applied N below the root zone, forcing lower rates and more frequent, smaller doses to reduce leaching risk</cite>. <cite id="cb2f056b-1">Open-field trials in northwestern China show most nitrate leaching occurs after the first irrigation, with total losses increasing linearly with N rate but declining as irrigation frequency increases, indicating that split applications tied to crop uptake windows can curb losses and shift agronomic optima</cite>. <cite id="cb2f056b-3">Seasonal water regime also matters: deficit irrigation early in the season enhanced root growth and iWUE without improving marketable yield, whereas full irrigation boosted yield, with no yield benefit above about 179 kg N ha−1, illustrating how irrigation depth interacts with N requirements</cite>. <cite id="ea943aa3-4">Longer seasons and wetter periods (e.g., south Florida plantings) prompt many producers and extension guidelines to increase N, with supplemental N recommended after leaching rainfall events or when petiole sap is low, because extended harvest windows and water table rises increase N demand and loss risks</cite>.

Cultivar, market type, and soil fertility

Cultivar and market type shift the balance between vegetative growth, fruit number, and fruit size, altering N requirements. <cite id="ea943aa3-1">Processing cultivars typically produce more fruits per plant and higher total and marketable yields than fresh-market types, meaning more N may be needed to support fruit set and canopy without depressing fruit quality</cite>. <cite id="ea943aa3-0">In a two-year Mediterranean processing-tomato trial, 200 kg N ha−1 maximized marketable and total yields, Brix⋅t ha−1, and net return while minimizing the global warming potential per ton of marketable yield, suggesting a cultivar-system optimum that balances yield, quality, and environmental impact</cite>. <cite id="ea943aa3-3">In a high-fertility site, both 125 and 200 kg N ha−1 maximized marketable yield and Brix, but 125 kg N improved N efficiency and fruit nutrient concentration, implying that high soil-test N can allow lower maintenance N without yield loss</cite>. <cite id="ea943aa3-2">Conversely, in Florida’s indeterminate fresh-market systems, marketable yield peaked at 179–269 kg N ha−1 under full irrigation, with no further yield benefit above 179 kg N ha−1, underscoring that cultivar-by-environment interactions set distinct N optima</cite>.

Measurement and interpretation endpoints

Studies optimize and report different endpoints (e.g., total yield, marketable yield, N recovery, efficiency, profit) and use different diagnostics, which shift recommended rates. <cite id="5503e625-2">Reviews note that recommended N rates vary significantly depending on experimental purpose and environmental factors, and that tomatoes exhibit a nitrogen uptake threshold beyond which yield declines</cite>. <cite id="5503e625-2">Examples include greenhouse work where marketable yield peaks between 172–298 kg N ha−1, while total ripe and unripe yield increases are blunted at high N (150–250 kg N ha−1), highlighting that maximizing marketable output tolerates less N than maximizing total biomass/canopy yield</cite>. <cite id="ea943aa3-3">Processing trials show that at high soil fertility, lower N (125 kg N ha−1) can match yield and improve N efficiency and fruit composition relative to 200 kg N ha−1, reinforcing that efficiency- and quality-focused objectives can justify lower rates</cite>. <cite id="cb2f056b-3">In open field, N recovery was highest at 134 kg N ha−1 but similar across 179–269 kg N ha−1 with no yield gain above 179 kg, indicating diminishing returns that extension bodies often translate into a single-burst recommendation near 179–224 kg N ha−1 for standard seasons</cite>. <cite id="ea943aa3-4">Methodologically, some programs trigger split or supplemental N based on leaching rain or low petiole sap N, while others rely on soil tests; extension guidance in Florida advises supplemental N after 76 mm in 3 days or 102 mm in 7 days, or when petiole analysis is low, because leaf diagnostics capture short-term deficits better than soil tests in rapidly changing field systems</cite>. <cite id="5503e625-4">Critical N concentration models calibrated to specific varieties and aeration regimes yield different Nc–DM relationships, so thresholds translated into absolute N requirements vary across systems even when “critical N” concepts are used</cite>.

Timing, form, and distribution strategies

Split vs preplant and nitrate vs ammonium dynamics change apparent optima. <cite id="cb2f056b-1">Because the largest leaching pulse occurs early, with irrigation frequency increasing and losses decreasing, programs that align N application with crop uptake windows (split N, staged releases) reduce leaching and can lower total seasonal N while maintaining yield</cite>. <cite id="ea943aa3-3">Processing tomato studies demonstrate that 125 vs 200 kg N ha−1 differences alter N efficiency and fruit K and P, suggesting that timing and distribution tied to fruiting rather than vegetative growth can sustain yield at lower rates</cite>. <cite id="5503e625-0">Facility-grown tomato work shows N demand is low in seedling and flowering, with fertilizer-derived N use rising during fruiting; staged N (e.g., N60–N80 over the cycle) optimizes yield and N-use efficiency, whereas over-application diminishes returns</cite>. <cite id="5503e625-3">Across studies, fruit diameter and length respond to N within an optimal window; nitrate form can accelerate growth and yield at comparable rates, implying that source choice can shift apparent requirements when fertigation is used</cite>.

Organic inputs and soil history

Organic systems and soil history shift N needs by supplying mineralizable reserves and buffering losses. <cite id="ea943aa3-4">In seepage-irrigated Florida systems, extension recommendations often reduce split-season N when leaching rainfall has occurred, or when foliar/petiole diagnostics indicate sufficiency, because temporary water table rises and denitrification risk increase N demand and loss, yet prior credits from residues or manures can lower mineral N requirements</cite>. <cite id="ea943aa3-3">High-fertility soils with organic amendments can sustain yields at lower mineral N, whereas low-organic-matter sandy soils require careful timing to avoid leaching, again producing different recommended rates</cite>.

Economic vs agronomic optima

Optimization objective (profit vs yield/efficiency) can move the “optimal” N rate. <cite id="ea943aa3-0">In processing tomato, 200 kg N ha−1 maximized marketable and total yields, brix⋅t ha−1, and marginal net return while minimizing the global warming potential per ton of marketable yield, indicating a balance among yield, input cost, and environmental externality</cite>. <cite id="ea943aa3-4">However, producers in south Florida sometimes apply 290–470 kg N ha−1 over extended seasons, justified by longer crop windows, wetter periods, and temporary water table rises conducive to denitrification; this reflects economic risk management (avoiding short-term deficits during long or wet seasons) rather than pure agronomic yield optimization, and it elevates recommended N above agronomic optima</cite>. <cite id="cb2f056b-3">At the same time, trials show diminishing returns above ~179–269 kg N ha−1 with full irrigation, suggesting economic optima in standard seasons occur near 179–224 kg N ha−1 where additional N yields no marketable gain but raises cost and loss risk</cite>.

Putting it together: why studies disagree

- Different environments (rainfall, temperature, ETc) shift uptake thresholds and leaching loss curves, moving the N rate that maximizes marketable yield and profit. <cite id="5503e625-2">Year-to-year climatic variation alone explains inconsistent N responses</cite>. <cite id="cb2f056b-0">Soil type and water dynamics in sandy, low-OM fields favor low-to-moderate N with frequent splits to mitigate leaching</cite>. <cite id="cb2f056b-3">Irrigation strategy and season length further modulate root uptake and canopy productivity, changing the N–yield slope</cite>. 
- Different cultivars and markets have different fruiting strategies and quality constraints, altering maintenance N. <cite id="ea943aa3-1">Processing types produce many fruits and higher yields than fresh-market types, often requiring more N to support set and harvest</cite>. <cite id="ea943aa3-0">For processing in low-medium fertility, 200 kg N ha−1 balances yield, quality, and net return</cite>. <cite id="ea943aa3-3">In high-fertility soils, 125–200 kg N ha−1 can achieve similar marketable yields with improved efficiency and fruit nutrient profiles</cite>.
- Different objectives and metrics lead to different “optima.” <cite id="5503e625-2">Studies maximizing marketable yield vs total yield, or emphasizing N recovery vs efficiency, often converge at different N rates</cite>. <cite id="ea943aa3-4">Extension programs trigger split or supplemental N based on leaching rain or low petiole sap, which can raise seasonal totals compared with a single preplant sufficiency test</cite>. <cite id="5503e625-4">Variety- and system-specific critical N concentration models produce distinct absolute N recommendations</cite>.
- Different methods and scales change detectability of response. <cite id="cb2f056b-3">Plot-level sufficiency tests in Florida found 134 kg N reduced yield relative to 179–269 kg N, with no yield benefit above 179 kg, while commercial practice often targets 224 kg N ha−1 as a baseline</cite>. <cite id="5503e625-0">Facility-grown tomatoes optimized between 93–128 kg N ha−1 with staged release, far below open-field agronomic optima, because greenhouse control reduces leaching and allows precise timing</cite>.
- Different risk profiles and seasons justify higher N in practice. <cite id="ea943aa3-4">Longer seasons, water table rises, and denitrification risk prompt many growers to exceed extension N baselines, even as trials show diminishing returns at moderate to high N</cite>.

Practical implications for reconciling differences

- Diagnose context first: soil type and organic matter, seasonal rainfall/leaching risk, irrigation method and ETc, cultivar/market, and whether splits/leaf testing are feasible. <cite id="cb2f056b-0">Sandy, low-OM soils require lower and more frequent N to minimize leaching</cite>. <cite id="ea943aa3-4">Petiole sap “low” or leaching rainfall triggers can add supplemental N without raising preplant rates</cite>. 
- Align rate to endpoint: choose N to maximize marketable yield, not total yield, and to match the profit and environmental trade-offs. <cite id="ea943aa3-0">Rates like 200 kg N ha−1 in processing systems balance yield, return, and carbon intensity</cite>. <cite id="cb2f056b-3">Rates near 179–224 kg N ha−1 are often sufficient for fresh-market in standard seasons, with diminishing returns beyond 179 kg</cite>.
- Use staged N tied to crop phases and water supply. <cite id="5503e625-0">Early low N, higher during fruiting, with total seasonal N around 93–128 kg in facility systems</cite>. <cite id="cb2f056b-1">In open fields, split applications across early irrigations can reduce leaching and maintain yield at lower seasonal totals</cite>.
- Account for organic inputs and soil history. <cite id="ea943aa3-3">High-fertility soils with residue/manure may allow 125–200 kg N ha−1 to achieve marketable yields</cite>. <cite id="ea943aa3-4">South Florida’s long seasons and wet periods often justify higher N baselines and splits to avoid short-term deficits</cite>.

Remaining uncertainty and how to resolve it

Recommended rates still diverge because many trials are plot-scale, single-season, or greenhouse-replicated, while recommendations target heterogeneous commercial fields. Multi-year, multi-site factorial N×irrigation studies that report marketable yield, N recovery, leaching mass, economic profit, and petiole/soil-test trajectories by cultivar/market would clarify context-specific optima. <cite id="5503e625-2">Inter-year variability is recognized, but more longitudinal work linking rainfall/temperature series to N sufficiency thresholds would reduce range inflation</cite>. <cite id="cb2f056b-3">Commercial-scale monitoring of seasonal N recovery and yield responses to baseline vs elevated N in different soils and seasons would better align extension guidelines with profit-maximizing optima</cite>. Until then, extension bodies commonly present a range (e.g., 150–250 kg N ha−1 for open-field indeterminate types) and trigger-based splits, acknowledging diminishing returns and leaching risk. <cite id="ea943aa3-4">Extension guidance in Florida uses leaching-rain triggers and petiole-sap sufficiency to justify higher seasonal totals in long, wet seasons, while defaulting to lower, split programs in shorter or drier seasons</cite>. </answer>

Title: Optimizing Nitrogen for Sustainable Yield and Efficiency: Insights from Shouguang Facility-Grown Tomatoes
Snippet: Facility-based agriculture has rapidly advanced due to its capacity for high-intensity and year-round crop cultivation. This study evaluated the effects of different nitrogen fertilizer application rates on the growth of greenhouse tomatoes, while utilizing 15N tracing technology to explore nitrogen utilization efficiency during the growth process of facility-grown tomatoes. The results indicate that nitrogen application rates within the range of N60–N80 (93–128 kg N ha−1) can optimally balance yield, nitrogen-use efficiency, and crop growth. Application rates exceeding this range do not enhance yield and lead to reduced nitrogen-use efficiency. Tomato plants exhibited a low N requirement during the seedling stage, relying primarily on native soil N stocks during the flowering stage. Fertilizer-derived N use increased during the fruiting stage. These findings demonstrate that excessive N inputs lead to diminishing returns and potential nutrient imbalances, while fully utilizing soil N stocks during the seedling and flowering stages is essential. This study emphasizes the importance of adjusting nitrogen input according to the developmental stages of the crop to optimize yield and resource utilization.

Title: Nitrogen and Soil Moisture Optimization for Tomato Crops in Semi-Arid Areas of Ethiopia
Snippet: Table 2 represent the overall data for growth parameters and yield for two cropping seasons. The growth parameters and yields show significant differences for both irrigation levels and nitrogen application rate application. 

Plant height. Plant varies significantly depending on the soil moisture and nitrogen levels applied. The tallest plants were observed under higher soil moisture conditions of 100% and 75% ETc, measuring 62.5 and 62.1 cm respectively, with no significant difference between them. In contrast, plants under 50% ETc irrigation were notably shorter, measuring 59.9 cm. This difference highlights tomatoes' sensitivity to increased soil moisture stress, which leads to reduced plant height. 

There is also a significant difference in plant height depending on nitrogen application rate. Reducing nitrogen levels results in a reduction in plant height, as shown in Table 2. The application of 230 and 184 kg/ha of nitrogen resulted in the tallest tomato plants compared to the application of 138, 92, and 0 kg/ha, without any significant difference. These treatments yielded tomato heights of 65.0 and 64.7 cm, respectively. Applications of 138, 92, and 0 kg/ha also resulted in plant heights of 63.3, 59.4, and 55.1 cm, respectively. The result indicates that plant height increases with an increase in nitrogen rate up to a certain point, and then decreases above optimal levels. Excessive nitrogen application can negatively impact water and nutrient absorption. 

Branch number. Tomato branch numbers show a significant difference when different irrigation levels and nitrogen rates are applied. The largest number of tomato branches was obtained by applying 75% ETc, yielding 9.4 tomato branches, as shown in Table 2. Soil moisture stress at 50% ETc and 100% ETc levels resulted in a lower (8.7) and moderate (9.1) number of tomato branches. Irrigating tomatoes with 75% ETc resulted in 3.19% and 7.44% more tomato branches than irrigating with 100% ETc and 50% ETc, respectively. 

In this study, the largest (9.6) and lowest (8.6) tomato branches were obtained by applying 230 kg/ha and 0 nitrogen rates. The moderate tomato branch numbers 9.3 and 9.1 were achieved with applications of 184 and 138 kg/ha, respectively, showing no significant difference. This suggests that as nitrogen application rates increase, tomato branch number also increase.

Title: Nitrogen Application Can Be Reduced without Affecting Carotenoid Content, Maturation, Shelf Life and Yield of Greenhouse Tomatoes
Snippet: The effect of nitrogen treatments on the yield of tomato fruits was not consistent between the years, and environmental factors may have been the main reason for the lack of this consistency across years. A review reported that the effects of recommended nitrogen rates for tomato fruits varied significantly depending on experimental purposes and environmental factors [42], an observation that is in agreement with our findings. Plants grown in Year 1 exhibited a higher yield compared with Year 2. Many authors have reported that although deviations from the recommended nitrogen levels may not result in a significant difference in yield, climatic conditions (e.g., air temperature, rainfall pattern) significantly affect the yield of tomato fruits [22,[46][47][48][49]. There is a threshold for nitrogen uptake at certain levels, which if exceeded results in decreasing yield. In general, it is assumed that overfertilization of greenhouse tomatoes will provide maximum production, and it has been established as widespread standard practice; however, it has negative environmental effects because it reduces the efficiency of fertilizers [50,51]. Frías-Moreno et al. [52] reported that the yield, weight and diameter of fresh tomato fruits increased as nitrogen supply increased up to an optimum nitrogen level (30 mmol•L −1 ) beyond which growth attributes were reduced. According to a previous study [39], although an increase in nitrogen dose up to a certain level enhances yield, excessive nitrogen has an overall negative effect. Parisi et al. [53] reported that high nitrogen supply (150-250 kg nitrogen ha −1 ) caused no significant increase in the total ripe and unripe yield of tomato. Elia and Conversa [54] evaluated four nitrogen fertilization rates (1, 100, 200 and 300 kg•ha −1 ) and showed that the maximum total yield was obtained with 200 kg•nitrogen ha −1 . Ozores-Hampton et al. [55] showed that maximum marketable yield was achieved by applying nitrogen doses between 172 kg•ha −1 and 298 kg•ha −1 , whereas the application of 470 kg•ha −1 of nitrogen considerably decreased yield. Li et al. [56] stated that higher nitrogen inputs > 300 kg ha −1 did not result in higher yields.

Title: Nitrogen and Soil Moisture Optimization for Tomato Crops in Semi-Arid Areas of Ethiopia
Snippet: Different soil moisture application significant affects tomato branch number. Application of 75% ETc results in highest number of tomato branches. Tesfay et al. (2019), also pointed out that the plots treated with moderate (75% ETc) to full (100% ETc) irrigation had significantly higher numbers of tomato branches. 

On other hand, application of different nitrogen also affects tomato branch number. Increasing nitrogen application rates resulted in the maximum number of tomato branches, while the lowest number of tomato branches was achieved from treatment without any nitrogen application. Degefa et al. (2019) and Iqbal et al. (2011) indicated that an increase in nitrogen application leads to a higher number of branches on tomato plants. 

Fruit diameter. Application of different soil moisture and nitrogen rates significantly affects the diameter of tomato fruits. In this study, the maximum fruit diameter of tomato was achieved with the application of 75% ETc, while the minimum fruit diameter was achieved with higher deficit irrigation. Soil moisture content significantly affects the fruit diameter of tomatoes, with both deficit and saturation leading to a reduction in fruit yield (Bhattarai et al., 2005). 

Fruit diameter increased with the application of a lower nitrogen rate (0 kg/ha) until the optimal rate and then decreased when the nitrogen rate reached its maximum. The influence of nitrogen content on fruit diameter of tomatoes is a complex interaction influenced by various factors and different studies quantify different amounts of nitrogen level. Iqbal et al. (2011) found that applying a nitrogen rate of 120 kg N and 90 kg K resulted in maximum fruit diameter. Lee et al. (2007) also observed an increase in tomato yield with increasing nitrogen fertilization rates, with the highest fruit yield achieved at a N-Fertigation rate of 80. Similarly, Kirimi et al. (2011) reported that an application rate of 80 kg/ha nitrogen produced the highest fruit yield. Qiang et al. (2014) further emphasized the importance of nitrogen form and emphasized that nitrate-N promotes the growth and development of plants, resulting in increased biomass accumulation and fruit yield. Overall, these studies suggest that optimal nitrogen content in combination with the appropriate form of nitrogen is crucial for achieving the maximum diameter of the tomato fruit. 

Fruit length. Fruit length was significantly affected by variations in soil moisture and nitrogen application rates.

Title: Comprehensive Evaluation of Tomato Growth Status under Aerated Drip Irrigation Based on Critical Nitrogen Concentration and Nitrogen Nutrient Diagnosis
Snippet: Nitrogen is the macronutrient for tomatoes, and it is involved in most of the physiological metabolic processes. Reasonable application of nitrogen fertilizer is the key to regulate the growth and development of tomatoes, improve the function of leaf blades, and increase the yield [25][26][27]. However, irrational application of nitrogen fertilizer and low utilization efficiency in the current production is very common, so it is very important to clarify the characteristics of tomato nitrogen demand for reasonable fertilizer application [28]. In studies on critical N concentrations of aboveground dry matter in wheat, oilseed rape, potato, and sorghum [29][30][31][32][33], the critical N concentration model is suitable for different climatic regions and crop varieties. A critical nitrogen dilution model of facility tomatoes at different aeration levels and nitrogen application rates was constructed in this study: A1 (Nc = 15.674DM −0.658 ), A2 (Nc = 101.116DM −0.455 ), A3 (Nc = 119.527DM −0.535 ), N1 (Nc = 33.819DM −0.153 ), N2 (Nc = 127.759DM −0.555 ), and N3 (Nc = 209.696DM −0.683 ). This was consistent with the previous models of critical nitrogen dilution for different crops, but with different parameters. This study showed that the parameter value b under the A1 treatment was the largest, suggesting that DM −b was the smallest one, and the final total dry matter accumulation of tomato plants under the A1 treatment was correspondingly the smallest. The parameter value b under A2 treatment was the smallest, which meaned that DM −b was the largest, indicating that the moderate aerated amount could promote nitrogen uptake and improve the nitrogen holding capacity of tomato plants.

(2011) found that applying a nitrogen rate of 120 kg N and 90 kg K resulted in maximum fruit diameter. Lee et al. (2007) also observed an increase in tomato yield with increasing nitrogen fertilization rates, with the highest fruit yield achieved at a N-Fertigation rate of 80. Similarly, Kirimi et al. (2011) reported that an application rate of 80 kg/ha nitrogen produced the highest fruit yield. Qiang et al. Reasonable application of nitrogen fertilizer is the key to regulate the growth and development of tomatoes, improve the function of leaf blades, and increase the yield [25][26][27]. documents.title: Optimizing Nitrogen for Sustainable Yield and Efficiency: Insights from Shouguang Facility-Grown Tomatoes
documents.snippet: Facility-based agriculture has rapidly advanced due to its capacity for high-intensity and year-round crop cultivation. This study evaluated the effects of different nitrogen fertilizer application rates on the growth of greenhouse tomatoes, while utilizing 15N tracing technology to explore nitrogen utilization efficiency during the growth process of facility-grown tomatoes. The results indicate that nitrogen application rates within the range of N60–N80 (93–128 kg N ha−1) can optimally balance yield, nitrogen-use efficiency, and crop growth. Application rates exceeding this range do not enhance yield and lead to reduced nitrogen-use efficiency. Tomato plants exhibited a low N requirement during the seedling stage, relying primarily on native soil N stocks during the flowering stage. Fertilizer-derived N use increased during the fruiting stage. These findings demonstrate that excessive N inputs lead to diminishing returns and potential nutrient imbalances, while fully utilizing soil N stocks during the seedling and flowering stages is essential. This study emphasizes the importance of adjusting nitrogen input according to the developmental stages of the crop to optimize yield and resource utilization.

Table 2 represent the overall data for growth parameters and yield for two cropping seasons. The growth parameters and yields show significant differences for both irrigation levels and nitrogen application rate application. 

Plant height. Plant varies significantly depending on the soil moisture and nitrogen levels applied. The tallest plants were observed under higher soil moisture conditions of 100% and 75% ETc, measuring 62.5 and 62.1 cm respectively, with no significant difference between them. In contrast, plants under 50% ETc irrigation were notably shorter, measuring 59.9 cm. This difference highlights tomatoes' sensitivity to increased soil moisture stress, which leads to reduced plant height. 

There is also a significant difference in plant height depending on nitrogen application rate. Reducing nitrogen levels results in a reduction in plant height, as shown in Table 2. The application of 230 and 184 kg/ha of nitrogen resulted in the tallest tomato plants compared to the application of 138, 92, and 0 kg/ha, without any significant difference. These treatments yielded tomato heights of 65.0 and 64.7 cm, respectively. Applications of 138, 92, and 0 kg/ha also resulted in plant heights of 63.3, 59.4, and 55.1 cm, respectively. The result indicates that plant height increases with an increase in nitrogen rate up to a certain point, and then decreases above optimal levels. Excessive nitrogen application can negatively impact water and nutrient absorption. 

Branch number. Tomato branch numbers show a significant difference when different irrigation levels and nitrogen rates are applied. The largest number of tomato branches was obtained by applying 75% ETc, yielding 9.4 tomato branches, as shown in Table 2. Soil moisture stress at 50% ETc and 100% ETc levels resulted in a lower (8.7) and moderate (9.1) number of tomato branches. Irrigating tomatoes with 75% ETc resulted in 3.19% and 7.44% more tomato branches than irrigating with 100% ETc and 50% ETc, respectively. 

In this study, the largest (9.6) and lowest (8.6) tomato branches were obtained by applying 230 kg/ha and 0 nitrogen rates. The moderate tomato branch numbers 9.3 and 9.1 were achieved with applications of 184 and 138 kg/ha, respectively, showing no significant difference. This suggests that as nitrogen application rates increase, tomato branch number also increase.

documents.snippet: The effect of nitrogen treatments on the yield of tomato fruits was not consistent between the years, and environmental factors may have been the main reason for the lack of this consistency across years. A review reported that the effects of recommended nitrogen rates for tomato fruits varied significantly depending on experimental purposes and environmental factors [42], an observation that is in agreement with our findings. Plants grown in Year 1 exhibited a higher yield compared with Year 2. Many authors have reported that although deviations from the recommended nitrogen levels may not result in a significant difference in yield, climatic conditions (e.g., air temperature, rainfall pattern) significantly affect the yield of tomato fruits [22,[46][47][48][49]. There is a threshold for nitrogen uptake at certain levels, which if exceeded results in decreasing yield. In general, it is assumed that overfertilization of greenhouse tomatoes will provide maximum production, and it has been established as widespread standard practice; however, it has negative environmental effects because it reduces the efficiency of fertilizers [50,51]. Frías-Moreno et al. [52] reported that the yield, weight and diameter of fresh tomato fruits increased as nitrogen supply increased up to an optimum nitrogen level (30 mmol•L −1 ) beyond which growth attributes were reduced. According to a previous study [39], although an increase in nitrogen dose up to a certain level enhances yield, excessive nitrogen has an overall negative effect. Parisi et al. [53] reported that high nitrogen supply (150-250 kg nitrogen ha −1 ) caused no significant increase in the total ripe and unripe yield of tomato. Elia and Conversa [54] evaluated four nitrogen fertilization rates (1, 100, 200 and 300 kg•ha −1 ) and showed that the maximum total yield was obtained with 200 kg•nitrogen ha −1 . Ozores-Hampton et al. [55] showed that maximum marketable yield was achieved by applying nitrogen doses between 172 kg•ha −1 and 298 kg•ha −1 , whereas the application of 470 kg•ha −1 of nitrogen considerably decreased yield. Li et al. [56] stated that higher nitrogen inputs > 300 kg ha −1 did not result in higher yields.

Title: Tomato Growth, Yield, and Root Development, Soil Nitrogen and Water Distribution as Affected by Nitrogen and Irrigation Rates on a Florida Sandy Soil
Snippet: emissions from Florida tomato production system (Di Gioia et al., 2017;Jones et al., 2012). In Florida, tomato is predominantly produced in southwest, central, and south regions where Entisols and Spodosols are dominant soil orders. Because of their sandy nature, these soil types have low water-holding capacities, low organic matter contents (within the root depth), and low nutrient retention capacities. Therefore, excessive irrigation and/or N application rates with intense rain events could significantly increase the potential risk of N leaching in these soils (Knox and Moody, 1991;McNeal et al., 1995). Similarly, the N source and rate of application, crop removal capacity, and water displacement below the active root zone could have significant roles in N leaching (Zotarelli et al., 2007).

The leaching loss of NO 3 --N from agricultural production systems is a major contributor to both ground and surface water contamination, and this has led to increases in the N load to water bodies, thus increasing water NO 3 --N concentrations above the safe limit of 10 mg NO 3 --N/L (USGS, 1998). In Florida, irrigation and N fertilizer accounted for the most greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from open-field tomato production (Jones et al., 2012). Therefore, more studies focused on increasing efficiency and reducing nutrient loss in the environment would be considered critical for the sustainability of Florida tomato production practices (Jones et al., 2012;Sato et al., 2012). As a result, the present study investigated the combination of different N and irrigation application rates under typical Florida tomato growing conditions to determine 1) the optimum N requirement for fresh-market tomato growth and yield using a typical Florida drip irrigation production system, 2) identify the effects of FI and DI application regimes on plant nutrient and water uptake efficiencies, soil moisture conditions and nutrient displacement in sandy soils during tomato production, and 3) determine the effects of both N and irrigation application rates on tomato root growth during the production season.

Title: Tomato Growth, Yield, and Root Development, Soil Nitrogen and Water Distribution as Affected by Nitrogen and Irrigation Rates on a Florida Sandy Soil
Snippet: Effective nutrient and irrigation management practices are critical for optimum growth and yield in open-field fresh-market tomato production. Although nutrient and irrigation management practices have been well-studied for tomato production in Florida, more studies of the current highly efficient production systems would be considered essential. Therefore, a two-season (Fall 2016 and Spring 2017) study was conducted in Immokalee, FL, to evaluate the effects of the nitrogen (N) rates under different irrigation regimes and to determine the optimum N requirement for open-field fresh-market tomato production. To evaluate productivity, the study investigated the effects of N rates and irrigation regimes on plant and root growth, yield, and production efficiency of fresh-market tomato. The study demonstrated that deficit irrigation (DI) targeting 66% daily evapotranspiration (ET) replacement significantly increased tomato root growth compared with full irrigation (FI) at 100% ET. Similarly, DI application increased tomato growth early in the season compared with FI. Therefore, irrigation applications may be adjusted downward from FI, especially early during a wet season, thereby potentially improving irrigation water use efficiency (iWUE) and reducing leaching potential of Florida sandy soils. However, total marketable yield significantly increased under FI compared with DI. This suggests that although DI may increase early plant growth, the application of DI throughout the season may result in yield reduction. Although N application rates had no significant effects on biomass production, tomato marketable yield with an application rate of 134 kg·ha−1 N was significantly lower compared with other N application rates (179, 224, and 269 kg·ha−1). It was also observed that there were no significant yield benefits with N application rates higher than 179 kg·ha−1. During the fall, iWUE was higher under DI (33.57 kg·m−3) than under FI (25.57 kg·m−3); however, iWUE was similar for both irrigation treatments during spring (FI = 14.04 kg·m−3; DI = 15.29 kg·m−3). The N recovery (REC-N) rate was highest with 134 kg·ha−1 N; however, REC-N was similar with 179, 224, and 269 kg·ha−1 N rates during both fall and spring. Therefore, these study results could suggest that DI could be beneficial

Title: Effects of Nitrogen Rates on Nitrogen, Phosphorous, and Potassium Partitioning, Accumulation, and Use Efficiency in Seepage-irrigated Fresh Market Tomatoes

Despite these BMP recommendations, some tomato producers still apply N rates that range between 290 and 470 kg·ha of Nwhich is well above the UF/IFAS-recommended rate (Cantliffe et al., 2009). These higherN ratesmay be ‘‘justified’’ by: 1) the longer crop seasons (16, 20, or 18 weeks in south Florida for fall, winter, and spring plantings compared with 13 weeks in north Florida for spring plantings), 2) temporary water table rises during heavy rainfall periods and/or for frost protection events, and 3) the soil moisture conditions, more conducive to denitrification (Simonne and Morgant, 2005; Simonne and Ozores-Hampton, 2006). Although, studies on tomato yield response to N rates have been documented in the past and recently compiled by Hochmuth and Hanlon (2014), few studies have estimated the crop N, P, and K accumulation and partitioning, or have used the principle of the critical N concentration (%Ncrit), defined as the minimum N concentration in the aerial biomass required for maximum growth (Greenwood et al., 1991), to evaluate the UF/ IFAS N recommended rate. Yet, very few studies have evaluated and compared tomato crop N response in different growing seasons, which seem to have a big influence on the crop productivity and thus on the demand of nutrients (Ozores-Hampton et al., 2006; Scholberg et al., 2000). Therefore, a field study was conducted in southwest Florida on seepage-irrigated tomatoes comparing the UF/IFAS N rate (224 kg·ha) and a CG N rate (358 kg·ha) for two different (spring and winter) seasons to 1) evaluate the N rate and season effects on plant growth and fruit yield; 2) determineN, P, andK partitioning

Similarly, the N source and rate of application, crop removal capacity, and water displacement below the active root zone could have significant roles in N leaching (Zotarelli et al., 2007).

The leaching loss of NO 3 --N from agricultural production systems is a major contributor to both ground and surface water contamination, and this has led to increases in the N load to water bodies, thus increasing water NO 3 --N concentrations above the safe limit of 10 mg NO 3 --N/L (USGS, 1998). In Florida, irrigation and N fertilizer accounted for the most greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from open-field tomato production (Jones et al., 2012). Therefore, more studies focused on increasing efficiency and reducing nutrient loss in the environment would be considered critical for the sustainability of Florida tomato production practices (Jones et al., 2012;Sato et al., 2012). As a result, the present study investigated the combination of different N and irrigation application rates under typical Florida tomato growing conditions to determine 1) the optimum N requirement for fresh-market tomato growth and yield using a typical Florida drip irrigation production system, 2) identify the effects of FI and DI application regimes on plant nutrient and water uptake efficiencies, soil moisture conditions and nutrient displacement in sandy soils during tomato production, and 3) determine the effects of both N and irrigation application rates on tomato root growth during the production season.

documents.title: Tomato Growth, Yield, and Root Development, Soil Nitrogen and Water Distribution as Affected by Nitrogen and Irrigation Rates on a Florida Sandy Soil
documents.snippet: Effective nutrient and irrigation management practices are critical for optimum growth and yield in open-field fresh-market tomato production. Although nutrient and irrigation management practices have been well-studied for tomato production in Florida, more studies of the current highly efficient production systems would be considered essential. Therefore, a two-season (Fall 2016 and Spring 2017) study was conducted in Immokalee, FL, to evaluate the effects of the nitrogen (N) rates under different irrigation regimes and to determine the optimum N requirement for open-field fresh-market tomato production. To evaluate productivity, the study investigated the effects of N rates and irrigation regimes on plant and root growth, yield, and production efficiency of fresh-market tomato. The study demonstrated that deficit irrigation (DI) targeting 66% daily evapotranspiration (ET) replacement significantly increased tomato root growth compared with full irrigation (FI) at 100% ET. Similarly, DI application increased tomato growth early in the season compared with FI. Therefore, irrigation applications may be adjusted downward from FI, especially early during a wet season, thereby potentially improving irrigation water use efficiency (iWUE) and reducing leaching potential of Florida sandy soils. However, total marketable yield significantly increased under FI compared with DI. This suggests that although DI may increase early plant growth, the application of DI throughout the season may result in yield reduction. Although N application rates had no significant effects on biomass production, tomato marketable yield with an application rate of 134 kg·ha−1 N was significantly lower compared with other N application rates (179, 224, and 269 kg·ha−1). It was also observed that there were no significant yield benefits with N application rates higher than 179 kg·ha−1. During the fall, iWUE was higher under DI (33.57 kg·m−3) than under FI (25.57 kg·m−3); however, iWUE was similar for both irrigation treatments during spring (FI = 14.04 kg·m−3; DI = 15.29 kg·m−3). The N recovery (REC-N) rate was highest with 134 kg·ha−1 N; however, REC-N was similar with 179, 224, and 269 kg·ha−1 N rates during both fall and spring. Therefore, these study results could suggest that DI could be beneficial

The recommendations allow for supplemental applicationsofNandK1) after a leaching rainfall event (defined as 76mmof rain in 3 d or 102mm in 7 d), 2) when the results of foliar analysis or petiole sap testing are ‘‘low,’’ or 3) in case of extended harvest seasons (Olson et al., 2005). Despite these BMP recommendations, some tomato producers still apply N rates that range between 290 and 470 kg·ha of Nwhich is well above the UF/IFAS-recommended rate (Cantliffe et al., 2009). These higherN ratesmay be ‘‘justified’’ by: 1) the longer crop seasons (16, 20, or 18 weeks in south Florida for fall, winter, and spring plantings compared with 13 weeks in north Florida for spring plantings), 2) temporary water table rises during heavy rainfall periods and/or for frost protection events, and 3) the soil moisture conditions, more conducive to denitrification (Simonne and Morgant, 2005; Simonne and Ozores-Hampton, 2006). Although, studies on tomato yield response to N rates have been documented in the past and recently compiled by Hochmuth and Hanlon (2014), few studies have estimated the crop N, P, and K accumulation and partitioning, or have used the principle of the critical N concentration (%Ncrit), defined as the minimum N concentration in the aerial biomass required for maximum growth (Greenwood et al., 1991), to evaluate the UF/ IFAS N recommended rate. Yet, very few studies have evaluated and compared tomato crop N response in different growing seasons, which seem to have a big influence on the crop productivity and thus on the demand of nutrients (Ozores-Hampton et al., 2006; Scholberg et al., 2000). Therefore, a field study was conducted in southwest Florida on seepage-irrigated tomatoes comparing the UF/IFAS N rate (224 kg·ha) and a CG N rate (358 kg·ha) for two different (spring and winter) seasons to 1) evaluate the N rate and season effects on plant growth and fruit yield; 2) determineN, P, andK partitioning

Title: Effects of Nitrogen Management on Biomass Production and Dry Matter Distribution of Processing Tomato Cropped in Southern Italy
Snippet: Processing tomato is an important worldwide horticultural crop. It is generally grown in high-input systems; nevertheless, plant responses to nitrogen fertilization, in terms of the effects on dry matter production and allocation to different plant organs, have yet to be investigated in depth. Moreover, information on the crop marginal net return and global warming potential (as an index of the environmental impact of crop cultivation) at different nitrogen rates is still scarce. Therefore, the aim of this work was to study the effects of different nitrogen rates (0, 50, 100, 150, 200, and 250 kg of N ha−1) on the agronomic, economic, and environmental aspects of processing tomato grown under conventional management in the Mediterranean area. The results of the two-year trials indicated 200 kg of nitrogen ha−1 as the best rate, ensuring the highest values of marketable and total yields, brix ton ha−1, and marginal net return and the lowest global warming potential per ton of marketable yield. However, since plants fertilized with 200 kg of N ha−1 did not record the highest values of nitrogen use efficiency and nitrogen uptake efficiency, our finding suggest the possibility to select better-performing cultivars for these physiological parameters by adopting specific tomato breeding programs.

Title: Effects of variety on yield, physical properties and storability of tomato under ambient conditions
Snippet: The total, unmarketable and marketable fruit number and yield of processing and fresh market types of tomato varieties studied were found to be significantly (P ≤ 0.001) different (Table 2). An overview of Table 2 indicates that the processing cultivars produced more number of fruits per plant compared with the fresh market types. Similarly, total and marketable yield per hectare were found to be more in processing cultivars than in the fresh market types except for Fetane that recorded the highest and comparable yield to the highest yielding processing cultivar (Melkasalsa). This study clearly indicates that fresh market tomato varieties of indeterminate growth were low yielder as compared to determinate types of both fresh market and processing types of tomato varieties tested. Wudiri and Henderson (1985) indicated non processing tomatoes of indeterminate growth habit are low yielding because vegetative growth is favored over reproductive growth. 

Comparison between fresh market tomato varieties showed that Fetane had 47.0 and 55.0% more total and marketable number as well as 47 and 64% more total and marketable weight of fruits than the lowest yielder Marglobe Improved, respectively. Among the processing tomato varieties Melkasalsa had 101 and 103% more total and marketable number as well as 12 and 13% more total and marketable weight of fruits as compared to the lowest yielder Roma VF, respectively. 

The result of the present study indicated that the fresh market tomato variety Fetane had more yield than Roma VF and Melkashola. However, Melkasalsa remained at par with Fetane. The variation in yielding ability of the tomato varieties studied could be attributed to fruit set and number of marketable fruits, which is genetically, controlled which is in agreement with the findings of Gould (1992) and Duguma (2000). It has been observed that a positive correlations exists between marketable yield and clusters per plant (r = 0.615***), fruits per cluster and total number of fruits (r = 0.812***) while a negative correlation were observed between yield and fruit weight (r = -0.713***).

Title: Optimizing N Fertilization to Improve Yield, Technological and Nutritional Quality of Tomato Grown in High Fertility Soil Conditions
Snippet: Processing tomato is the second most important worldwide cash crop, generally produced in high-input systems. However, fruit yield and quality are affected by agronomic management, particularly nitrogen (N) fertilization, whose application to indeterminate growth genotypes for canning has yet to be investigated in depth. Hence, the objective of this work was to assess the effects of different N rates (0, 50, 125, 200, 275, and 350 kg ha−1) on fruit yield and quality characteristics of processing tomato ‘San Marzano’ landrace. The results of our study showed that 125 and 200 kg of N ha−1 are the most appropriate rates in soil with high fertility, ensuring the highest values of marketable yield and brix yield. However, plants fertilized with 125 kg of N ha−1 attained higher values of N efficiency and fruit K and P concentrations than plants fertilized with 200 kg of N ha−1. Our results suggest that overdoses of N supplies negatively affected fruit yield and quality of San Marzano landrace grown in high soil fertility conditions, also reducing the agricultural sustainability. Hence, specific agronomic protocol and extension services are required to optimally manage tomato crop systems.

Title: Nitrogen and Soil Moisture Optimization for Tomato Crops in Semi-Arid Areas of Ethiopia
Snippet: The total marketable yield of tomatoes over a two-year period varied significantly due to the application of different soil moisture and nitrogen rates in the treatments. No significant differences were observed between 100% ETc and 75% ETc, whereas a significant difference was noted when using 50% ETc irrigation levels. In this study, the highest yield of 39.8 and 38.9 tons/ha was obtained by applying 75% ETc and 100% ETc, respectively, without any significant difference. Applying an irrigation level of 50% ETc results in a yield of 35.0 tons/ha, with a statistically significant difference. 

The application of nitrogen rates significantly impacts marketable tomato yields. Appling 184 and 138 kg/ha of nitrogen results in higher marketable tomato yields, with reported yields of 42.1 and 41.1 tons/ha, respectively, showing no significant differences between the two rates. In this study, the maximum nitrogen application of 230 kg/ha did not yield the highest tomato output, resulting in 38 tons/ha. Additionally, the application of 92 kg/ha of nitrogen produced a marketable yield of 34 tons/ha, while no nitrogen application led an even lower yield of 33.1 tons/ha. 

The interactive effect of irrigation level and nitrogen rate on growth parameters and yield is presented in Table 3. The interaction effect of soil moisture and nitrogen content significantly influences plant height, number of branches, fruit diameter, fruit length, and marketable yields of tomato. 

The combination of 75% ETc and 230 kg/ha N resulted the longest plant height of 66.2 cm, while the shortest plant height of 54.1 cm, was observed with the combination of 0 kg/ha N and 50% ETc irrigation level. Combination of 50% ETc resulted in shorter plant height across all nitrogen rates and an increase in plant height within the same irrigation levels. The study found that the highest number of branches in tomatoes was achieved with a combination of 75% ETc and a nitrogen content of 230 kg/ha treatment. These were also followed by a combination of 184 kg/ha and 75% ETc as indicated in 3. Interaction of 75% ETc and 184 kg/ha of N resulted in the largest fruit diameter, followed by the interaction of 75% ETc and 138 kg/ha of N. The smallest fruit diameter was obtained from the interaction of 50% ETc and 0N.

documents.title: Optimizing N Fertilization to Improve Yield, Technological and Nutritional Quality of Tomato Grown in High Fertility Soil Conditions
documents.snippet: Processing tomato is the second most important worldwide cash crop, generally produced in high-input systems. However, fruit yield and quality are affected by agronomic management, particularly nitrogen (N) fertilization, whose application to indeterminate growth genotypes for canning has yet to be investigated in depth. Hence, the objective of this work was to assess the effects of different N rates (0, 50, 125, 200, 275, and 350 kg ha−1) on fruit yield and quality characteristics of processing tomato ‘San Marzano’ landrace. The results of our study showed that 125 and 200 kg of N ha−1 are the most appropriate rates in soil with high fertility, ensuring the highest values of marketable yield and brix yield. However, plants fertilized with 125 kg of N ha−1 attained higher values of N efficiency and fruit K and P concentrations than plants fertilized with 200 kg of N ha−1. Our results suggest that overdoses of N supplies negatively affected fruit yield and quality of San Marzano landrace grown in high soil fertility conditions, also reducing the agricultural sustainability. Hence, specific agronomic protocol and extension services are required to optimally manage tomato crop systems.

Summary answer
Split nitrogen application benefits sandy-field tomatoes more than clay-grown tomatoes primarily because sandy soils have low nutrient retention and nitrate leaches rapidly with wetting fronts, so concentrating and repeatedly replenishing N near the root zone reduces losses and “hungry layers” and better matches the crop’s early and midseason demand; in contrast, clays retain and move N more slowly, tolerate larger swings, and are less prone to leaching, so single larger preplant doses or less frequent splits can still support yield unless immobilization, compaction, or drainage issues restrict early uptake or create uneven availability. <cite id="6ac58fe6-1">Because of their sandy nature, these soils have low water-holding capacities, low organic matter, and low nutrient retention capacities, increasing the potential risk of N leaching with excessive irrigation or N; nitrate has high diffusivity and moves with the wetting front in sands</cite> <cite id="6ac58fe6-4">Nitrate is highly mobile and prone to loss in sandy soils; warm, well-aerated production conditions favor rapid nitrification, increasing leaching risk</cite> <cite id="06b1e511-0">Frequent small doses of N reduce variation of nutrient concentration in the root zone, increase availability, and reduce N leaching risk, especially in sandy loam to sandy soils; fertigation at the start of irrigation best matches uptake in sands and loams</cite> <cite id="06b1e511-2">On fine sands and fine sandy loams, total yields were higher with split (40% preplant + 60% trickle) than all preplant; split applications increased extra-large and late-season yields on sand</cite> <cite id="bacefd46-4">In a sandy loam, splitting N weekly increased N uptake from 44% to 58% and halved leaching to 13% compared to a three-split schedule, but too frequent or too infrequent splits can create deficits or excess accumulation; optimized, frequent fertigation maximized uptake and minimized losses</cite>. For clays, higher cation exchange capacity and slower nitrate movement reduce immediate leaching risk, and field studies in high-organic-matter clay loams show yields similar with preplant plus fertigation splits as with less frequent splits, though timing effects were small and early-season growth was slower in clays in some trials, indicating a greater tolerance for larger N pulses when losses are not a constraint <cite id="06b1e511-1">Even in a 60% clay, high-OM soil, a strategy of 10–20% preplant and equal fertigation splits provided initial N, minimized losses, and facilitated management</cite> <cite id="06b1e511-2">On a fine sandy loam, time of fertilizer application had no effect on yield, but split yielded more than all preplant</cite> <cite id="bacefd46-2">Across environments, split N improved plant N uptake relative to single sidedress in coarser-textured, lower-CEC soils and when precipitation was uneven, whereas single N did better in soils with higher total N and C:N (retentive profiles)</cite> <cite id="bacefd46-3">Tomato plants grown in compost (high OM) outperformed those in clay and sandy soils for vegetative growth, reflecting nutrient availability and aeration; clays can become compacted and poorly aerated when wet, limiting early-season N uptake</cite>.

Mechanisms: soil texture, nutrient retention, and nitrate mobility
Sandy soils have low organic matter and cation exchange capacity, so applied ammonium/nitrate is adsorbed poorly and nitrate (NO3−) moves with irrigation water and rainfall, creating high losses when not maintained in the active root zone. Early-season irrigation events on sands can flush applied N below the root zone, lowering available N and increasing leaching losses; this is reflected in open-field tomato systems where most leaching occurred after the first irrigation, with substantial fractions of total loss captured in that event, and total leaching reduced sharply by optimizing timing and rates <cite id="6ac58fe6-0">Nitrogen leaching in open-field tomato peaked after the first irrigation and accounted for roughly half of total leached TN and NO3− over the season; optimized timing reduced total leached TN, NO3−, and NH4+ by 30–52%</cite> <cite id="6ac58fe6-1">Sandy Entisols/Spodosols in Florida have low nutrient retention; excessive irrigation/N increases N leaching risk, with nitrate moving with the wetting front</cite> <cite id="6ac58fe6-4">Nitrate’s high diffusivity in sandy soils and rapid nitrification in warm, well-aerated tomato soils increase leaching risk</cite>. Split applications, especially via drip fertigation, replenish N as it is depleted, keep concentrations in the rhizosphere, and reduce leaching while improving tomato tissue N and yields on sands and fine sands <cite id="06b1e511-0">Daily fertigation of N in sandy soils increased root-zone availability, improved yield/quality, and reduced N and K losses</cite> <cite id="06b1e511-2">On a fine sand in Gainesville, split N plus appropriate water quantity improved leaf tissue N and increased fruit yields versus all preplant</cite> <cite id="bacefd46-4">In a sandy loam, shifting from three split doses to weekly fertigation increased N uptake by 13–15 percentage points and cut leaching in half; optimized schedules achieved 71% N uptake with only 11% leaching below the root zone</cite>.

By contrast, clay soils have higher CEC and stronger sorption of ammonium and nitrate, slower vertical movement, and often higher organic matter, which together reduce leaching risk and allow larger, less frequent N applications without large yield penalties in many systems. Modeling and management studies show loamy and silty clays retain and accumulate nitrate in the root zone longer, with lower leaching fractions than sands even when nitrate penetrates deeper, indicating that clays buffer N supply and timing effects less than sands <cite id="bacefd46-4">Nitrate uptake was higher in loamy soil than in silty clay, with lower leaching and nitrate accumulation in the root zone despite deeper leaching in loam; higher leachability in sandy loam drove greater losses and necessitated more frequent splits to meet plant demand</cite>. Field work in a high-organic-matter, 60% clay soil found that a split strategy still provided practical advantages (initial availability via preplant, loss minimization via fertigation splits, and management simplicity), yet yields were robust even with less frequent splits, consistent with clays’ ability to hold N and supply it slowly, especially when early-season aeration is adequate <cite id="06b1e511-1">In a 60% clay, 34 g dm−3 OM soil, 10–20% preplant plus equal fertigation splits provided initial N, minimized losses, and facilitated management</cite>. However, in compacted or waterlogged clays, restricted aeration and uneven rooting can create early-season “hungry layers” or uneven supply, making split early-season N or improved aeration beneficial to match crop demand windows; this is why split strategies are still recommended to avoid immobilization risks or uneven distribution and to align with tomato’s critical vegetative and bloom periods <cite id="06b1e511-0">Frequent small doses stabilize root-zone concentrations and reduce leaching risk; this is especially relevant when N is in nitrate form and susceptible to leaching</cite> <cite id="bacefd46-2">Split N outperforms single applications in coarser-textured or lower-CEC soils and under uneven rainfall; single applications do better in high-retention soils</cite>.

Crop biology and timing: tomato N demand windows and split alignment
Tomatoes have a pronounced early and midseason demand for N to support rapid vegetative growth, flowering, and fruit set, with losses early in the season on sands directly reducing available supply. Field studies show that on sandy and fine sandy loam soils, distributing N as 40% preplant and 60% through trickle irrigation increased leaf tissue N and total yields relative to all-preplant, with especially strong effects on extra-large and mid–late fruit; timing effects were smaller on the finer loam, consistent with its greater buffering capacity, yet splits still improved outcomes <cite id="06b1e511-2">Split applications (40% preplant + 60% with trickle) produced higher tissue N and higher yields than all preplant on fine sands and fine sandy loams; split improved extra-large and mid-season yields on sand</cite>. Open-field tomato systems in northwestern China similarly found that optimizing N timing across irrigations (i.e., splitting effective dose across events) significantly reduced leaching and maintained high yields, while excessive rates or poorly timed events reduced yield at the highest rate, underscoring the need to align supply with uptake windows and avoid early flush losses <cite id="6ac58fe6-0">Most leaching occurred after the first irrigation; optimized timing reduced TN, NO3−, and NH4+ losses by 30–52%</cite> <cite id="6ac58fe6-2">Yields peaked at moderate N rates and declined at 375 kg ha−1; optimal strategies reduced leaching without reducing yield</cite>. Reviews and management guides emphasize that frequent, small N doses via fertigation stabilize root-zone concentrations, matching tomato crop uptake dynamics and reducing losses—particularly in sands where nitrate is mobile—and that timing at the start of irrigation events is optimal for sandy loams/loams to capture runoff/ infiltration efficiently <cite id="06b1e511-0">Frequent small N doses reduce variability in root-zone concentration, increase availability, improve yield/quality via drip, and reduce losses in sandy soils; fertigation at the beginning of irrigation is best for sandy loam/loam</cite>.

Why clay-grown tomatoes show smaller gains from splitting
- Retention and slow release: Clays adsorb NH4+ and retain nitrate, reducing the need to replenish as frequently and lowering the penalty of a single large pulse that would otherwise leach on sands. <cite id="6ac58fe6-1">Sandy soils’ low nutrient retention increases leaching risk; clays do not share this deficit</cite> <cite id="bacefd46-4">Loamy soils showed higher N uptake and lower leaching than silty clay, reflecting better retention and distribution</cite>.
- Buffering of environmental variability: In high-CEC, high-OM clays, uneven rainfall or irrigation between splits is less likely to create a supply deficit, whereas on sands, the same event can cause rapid loss and a hungry layer. <cite id="bacefd46-2">Single N applications perform well in soils with greater capacity to retain water and nutrients; split benefits are larger when precipitation is uneven and soils are coarse</cite>.
- Practical split advantages in clays can be modest unless distribution/availability is impaired: In high-OM clay loams, yields similar across split and less-frequent strategies indicate that clays can meet demand without aggressive splitting; management simplicity and initial availability via preplant can substitute for frequent fertigation splits. <cite id="06b1e511-1">Even in 60% clay with high OM, a 10–20% preplant plus equal fertigation splits strategy was recommended for initial availability and loss minimization</cite> <cite id="06b1e511-2">On a fine sandy loam, split improved yields, but timing effects were small</cite>.
- Constraints in clays can negate even split benefits if early-season aeration and root growth are impaired: Compaction/waterlogging slow uptake, making early-season N availability variable; organic media outperform clays and sands for vegetative growth, highlighting the role of aeration and nutrient supply in determining how much splitting is needed. <cite id="bacefd46-3">Plants in compost outperformed clay and sandy soils for vegetative growth, with clays being slow to grow when wet due to poor aeration; high N availability in compost improved vegetative growth and flowering/fruiting progression</cite>.

Practical implications for growers
- Sands: Prefer preplant plus frequent fertigation splits aligned to tomato critical windows (pre-bloom, midseason fruit set), with ammonium sources early to leverage short-term immobilization/turnover, and nitrate-dominated splits later when roots are deep and uptake capacity is high; monitor leaching via salinity cues and irrigation scheduling to avoid excess water co-moving nitrate below the root zone. <cite id="6ac58fe6-1">Sandy soils’ low CEC/organic matter increase leaching risk under excessive irrigation/N</cite> <cite id="06b1e511-0">Frequent small N doses reduce leaching and improve uptake in sandy soils</cite> <cite id="bacefd46-4">Weekly fertigation in sandy loam boosted uptake and cut leaching; avoid either too few or too many splits to prevent deficits or accumulation</cite>.
- Clays: Use split only when needed—e.g., to jump-start early vegetative growth, to overcome compacted layers, or to ensure even supply under uneven rainfall/irrigation. High-OM clays with good aeration can sustain yield with moderate preplant plus a couple of later splits; rely on soil health practices (cover crops, organic amendments) to maintain CEC and structure. <cite id="06b1e511-1">In high-OM clay loam, 10–20% preplant plus equal fertigation splits provided initial N, minimized losses, and simplified management</cite> <cite id="bacefd46-2">Single N can be adequate on high-retention soils, while split N is advantageous on coarse-textured or uneven-weather soils</cite>.

Uncertainties and research needs
Direct head-to-head tomato trials comparing identical N rates as single vs split applications across sandy vs clay soils are limited; most evidence comes from region-specific field systems, modeling, and adjacent crops, suggesting that split benefits are strongest where leaching risk and uneven distribution dominate (sands), while clays show smaller gains unless early-season availability or aeration is constrained. <cite id="6ac58fe6-0">Leaching risk and timing strongly influence tomato N outcomes in sandy systems</cite> <cite id="06b1e511-2">On fine sands/loams, split outperformed all preplant, but timing effects were smaller on loam</cite> <cite id="bacefd46-4">Coarse-textured soils require more frequent splits to meet peak demand and minimize losses, with optimized fertigation greatly improving uptake</cite>. Future trials quantifying tomato N uptake dynamics and leaching across textures with identical rates and split vs single timing would clarify genotype-by-soil interactions and the optimal number/frequency of splits per texture. <cite id="6ac58fe6-2">Yield declines at excessive N and optimized timing reduced leaching without yield loss, highlighting the need to balance rate and timing by soil and crop</cite>.

In Florida, irrigation and N fertilizer accounted for the most greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from open-field tomato production (Jones et al., 2012). Therefore, more studies focused on increasing efficiency and reducing nutrient loss in the environment would be considered critical for the sustainability of Florida tomato production practices (Jones et al., 2012;Sato et al., 2012). As a result, the present study investigated the combination of different N and irrigation application rates under typical Florida tomato growing conditions to determine 1) the optimum N requirement for fresh-market tomato growth and yield using a typical Florida drip irrigation production system, 2) identify the effects of FI and DI application regimes on plant nutrient and water uptake efficiencies, soil moisture conditions and nutrient displacement in sandy soils during tomato production, and 3) determine the effects of both N and irrigation application rates on tomato root growth during the production season.

Title: Tomato Growth, Yield, and Root Development, Soil Nitrogen and Water Distribution as Affected by Nitrogen and Irrigation Rates on a Florida Sandy Soil
Snippet: Nutrient and irrigation management practices are key aspects of tomato production for optimum yield and fruit quality. Tomato is a vegetable crop with high nutrient demands (Hartz and Hochmuth, 1996). Therefore, effective irrigation and nutrient management practices are essential to maintain N within the crop root extraction zone and mitigate against potential environmental contaminations. The present N recommendation is 224 kg · ha -1 for a tomato growing season in Florida (Hochmuth and Hanlon, 2014;Liu et al., 2016). Vegetable growers in Florida often apply fertilizer at rates higher than recommended due to the risk of yield reduction in unfavorable weather conditions (Everett, 1976;Hochmuth and Hanlon, 2014;Rhoads et al., 1996). This rate can be an average of 417 kg · ha -1 (Shukla et al., 2014) or higher (up to 470 kg · ha -1 ) (Cantliffe et al., 2009) for a single production season. Although N is considered to be the most limiting nutrient for most nonleguminous production systems, excessive applications of fertilizer and/or water could lead to nutrient losses from a cropping system (Marchi et al., 2016;Zotarelli et al., 2007). This is because N in the form of nitrate (NO 3 --N) has a high diffusivity rate in soil solution (Sato et al., 2009), resulting in high mobility in the soil, especially under saturated conditions. In sandy soils, NO 3 --N moves with the wetting front; therefore, N leaching is a factor of the soil water dynamics (Zotarelli et al., 2007).

Production conditions (warm temperature, good soil aeration, etc.) in the southeastern United States favor rapid conversion of most soil N to NO 3 --N (Jansson and Persson, 1982); hence, there are significant contributions of nitrification and denitrification to greenhouse gas emissions from Florida tomato production system (Di Gioia et al., 2017;Jones et al., 2012). Title: Water Quantity and Time of N and K Application for Trickle-irrigated Tomatoes
Snippet: Tomatoes (Lycopersicon esculentum Mill.) were grown during two seasons at two locations on fine sands and fine sandy loam soils to study the influence of water quantity, frequency of water application, and timing of N and K application for polyethylene-mulched, trickle-irrigated fresh-market tomatoes. Water quantities were 0.50 and 1.0 times pan evaporation applied one or three times daily. Nitrogen and K were applied 100% preplant or 40% applied preplant and 60% applied with trickle irrigation. Higher tomato leaf tissue N and K concentrations in one of the two seasons and higher fruit yields were obtained with 0.5 than with 1.0 time pan water evaporation on a fine sand at Gainesville, Fla. On a fine sandy loam soil at Quincy, fruit yields were higher in a relatively dry season with the higher water quantity and not influenced by the water quantity applied in the second relatively wet season. The number of daily water applications (one vs. three) at both locations had no effect on N and K uptake or fruit yields. Time of N and K applications had no effect on early yields, but total yields were higher with split than all preplant-applied N and K on the fine sandy soil. Split applications of fertilizer resulted in greater yields of extra-large fruit at mid-season and of extra large and large fruit at late harvest than all preplant-applied fertilizer. On the fine sandy loam soil, time of fertilizer application had no effect on yield.
