documents.title: Effects of Nitrogen Management on Biomass Production and Dry Matter Distribution of Processing Tomato Cropped in Southern Italy
documents.snippet:
Nitrogen fertilization affects processing tomato yield and fruit quality parameters requested by canning industries, such as total solids, soluble solids, pH, and acidity [9]. A fully ripe tomato fruit contains 93-96% water, which dissolves the carbohydrates, organic acids, minerals, vitamins, and pigments that represent the total soluble solids, measured as • Brix. Total soluble solids are a key parameter in processing tomato productions. In fact, tomato paste is produced and sold based on its total soluble solids content; thus, the total soluble solids dictate the factory yield. Higher total soluble solids in incoming fruits means that fewer tons of tomatoes will be needed to produce a given amount of tomato paste. 

The sink-source relationship and leaf nitrogen content affect dry matter production; moreover, yield is correlated with both source capacity and sink strength [8,14,15]. A higher allocation of biomass to fruits is a key crop goal to achieve the highest crop yield. 

Several works have been carried out on the N fertilization and N uptake of drip-irrigated processing tomatoes, but with contrasting results. In Turkey, Erdal et al. [15] displayed that 160 kg ha −1 of N was suitable to maximize fruit yield. Similar results were reported in Italy by Tei et al. [16] supplying 200 kg ha −1 of N. On the other hand, researchers working in Australia [17], in Brazil [18], and in Spain [19] reported that N rates over 300 kg ha −1 were required to achieve the highest fruit yield. 

To the authors' knowledge, only a few research papers have reported the relationships between dry matter partitioning (including root) and yield in processing tomato [20,21]; moreover, these studies did not consider the effects of N fertilization on processing tomato sustainability. 

The aim of our work was to display the best N rate, able to improve processing tomato production sustainability. Therefore, in the present study, two-year field trials were carried out to investigate the effects of different nitrogen rates (0, 50, 100, 150, 200, and 250 kg of N ha −1 ) on the agronomic, physiological, economic, and environmental aspects of processing tomato grown under conventional management in the Mediterranean area.

documents.title: Effects of Varying Nitrogen Concentrations on the Locule Number in Tomato Fruit
documents.snippet:
Numerous studies have indicated that enhancing nitrogen nutrition during the seedling stage can facilitate flower bud differentiation. An increase in nitrogen concentration prior to and during the period of flower bud differentiation not only promotes this differentiation but also leads to larger flower sizes [17]. Conversely, early nitrogen deficiency in strawberry seedlings has been shown to inhibit flower bud differentiation, while an appropriate nitrogen concentration fosters this process [18,19]. Research on cereal crops has consistently demonstrated that a moderate increase in nitrogen nutrition at the seedling stage enhances the transition from vegetative to reproductive growth [20]. This study further corroborates that augmenting nitrogen supply during the seedling stage can promote flower bud differentiation in tomatoes. Additionally, our findings reveal that increased nitrogen supply correlates with larger flower sizes and a higher number of stamens. 

It is widely recognized that an increase in nitrogen supply correlates with enhanced crop yields; however, the impact of elevated nitrogen concentration during the seedling stage on yield remains underexplored. This study demonstrates that augmenting nitrogen nutrition during the seedling phase significantly increases both the size and weight of tomato fruits, suggesting a potential rise in overall tomato yield. Additionally, the findings indicate that higher nitrogen supply at the seedling stage leads to an increase in the number of locules in tomato fruits. Moreover, temperature is a critical factor influencing the number of carpels and locules in tomatoes. The study was conducted in a greenhouse equipped with temperature control, maintaining a relatively stable environment at 26 • C/18 • C. 

However, the temperature environment in tomato-protected cultivation is unstable, leading to differing effects of increased nitrogen concentration on the number of carpels and locules in tomatoes compared to this study. While an appropriate increase in nitrogen fertilizer can enhance yield, excessive nitrogen application can negatively impact crop quality. Specifically, applying too much nitrogen does not further increase yield; instead, it Plants 2025, 14, 952 8 of 14 decreases the sugar-to-acid ratio in the fruit, resulting in diminished fruit quality. Additionally, excessive nitrogen fertilizer has been shown to reduce the solids-to-acids ratio and anthocyanin content in blackberry fruit [21].

documents.title: Optimizing Tomato Cultivation: Impact of Ammonium–Nitrate Ratios on Growth, Nutrient Uptake, and Fertilizer Utilization
documents.snippet: Tomatoes, an essential crop in controlled environments, benefit significantly from the careful use of nitrogen fertilizers, which are crucial for improving both yield and nitrogen efficiency. Using a tomato pot experiment arranged in a facility greenhouse, five treatments were established as follows: a control excluding the application of nitrogen fertilizer (C), and applications of ammonium nitrogen and nitrate nitrogen with nitrogen mass ratios of 0:100 (A0N100), 25:75 (A25N75), 50:50 (A50N50), 75:25 (A75N25), and 100:0 (A100N0), to study the effects of different ratios of nitrogen mass on tomato yield, quality, nutrient accumulation, and nitrogen fertilizer utilization. The results showed that compared with C, the different ammonium–nitrate ratios significantly increased the yield, dry matter mass, N, P, and K accumulation, soluble solids, soluble sugars, and vitamin C content (Vc) of the tomatoes. Among all the treatments, A75N25 tomatoes had the highest dry matter accumulation, nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium accumulation in fruits, soluble sugar, and soluble solids content. The differences in tomato yield and nitrogen fertilizer utilization between A75N25 and A100N0 were insignificant but their values were significantly higher than those of the other treatments. A75N25 had the highest nitrogen fertilizer utilization rate, 42.1% to 82.3% higher than C, A25N75, and A50N50. Hence, an ammonium-to-nitrate nitrogen mass ratio of 75:25 optimized tomato yield and quality in a controlled environment while minimizing nutrient loss.

Title: Reduced nitrogen proportion during the vegetative growth stage improved fruit yield and nitrogen uptake of cherry tomato plants under sufficient soil water regime
Snippet: Liu et al. (2013) investigated N application by drip irrigation in ten equal splits at 8-day intervals and found that N application applied in two splits saved 20-40% N compared to furrow irrigation. At the late stage of fruit growth, it was argued that a balance is needed between irrigation and N application rate (Yurtseven et al. 2005;Elia et al. 2007), as high N application can improve T and intrinsic WUE with more available irrigation water at this stage. It was found that N assimilation was higher at fruit growth than at early development stages of tomato plants (Tahi et al. 2007). The effect of different N application doses of 3, 7 and 14 mM showed that reduced N dose at early growth stages only affected the performance in the most severe treatment (3 mM). A decrease in N application at the anthesis stage did not affect the yield, indicating the feasibility of reducing the N dose in tomato growth without compromising performance. But it is of major importance to choose the most appropriate stage to impose this reduction without affecting, or even improving the nutritional quality of fruits (Hernández et al. 2020). Zotarelli et al. (2009) noted that N application rate higher than 220 kg ha −1 did not improve the growth and N accumulation in fruits and shoots but substantially increased the leaching of NO − 3 in low water holding capacity soils. Zheng et al. (2013) investigated the processing tomato grown in a clay loam soil and found that the highest yields were observed under full irrigation, whereas the highest water productivity was achieved under a moderate soil water regime. The fertigation rate of 180 kg N ha −1 at medium soil water regime produced the highest values of commercial yield, fruit size, the total yield of soluble solids, and the total protein content of tomatoes (Kuscu et al. 2014;Wang et al. 2019a). 

Previous studies have shown the effect of N quantities on growth, yield and efficiency of N utilisation in conjunction with irrigation. However, less is known about the consequence of applied soil water and N application proportions during different growth stages when given the certain amount of N fertiliser.

attempts.answer:
Overview and feasibility
Foliar nitrogen (N) sprays can contribute meaningfully to tomato N nutrition and, under certain conditions of open‑field production, replace a fraction or even most of soil-applied N—provided timing, formulation, and load are optimized and soil fertility is managed. In open‑field tomato, soil-applied N exhibits strong dose–response: yields rise with N up to about 300 kg N ha−1 and then decline at 375 kg N ha−1, while optimized (controlled‑release) programs at around 240–300 kg N ha−1 maximize yield and net profit and cut leaching of nitrate and ammonia by roughly 25–50% compared with higher rates, demonstrating that supply form/scheduling matters as much as total amount <cite id="a4f6fa68-2">Tomato yields were strongly impacted by nitrogen rate; yields increased up to 300 kg ha−1 and declined at 375 kg ha−1; optimized (OPT) treatments yielded 104.73 t ha−1 versus 65.35 t ha−1 for no‑fertilizer, with NUE and NPFP highest at OPT</cite> <cite id="777f1c3b-1">Compared with no fertilization, fertilization increased yield, quality and net profit; OPT (240 kg N ha−1 controlled‑release) achieved the largest gains and reduced leaching of TN, NO3−‑N, and NH4+‑N by 30.09–51.79%, 24.89–50.03%, and 30–65%, respectively</cite>. Foliar feeding can raise fruit N and yield in tomato, including via seaweed/algal extracts and nutrient solutions, and studies show foliar NPK sprays improved fruit yield and quality in hybrid tomato compared with soil N alone, indicating foliar N can substitute for or complement soil supply <cite id="a4f6fa68-0">Greenhouse tomato plants treated with 0.5% algal N‑rich extract foliar spray increased fruiting clusters, per‑plant yield, and fruit weight and raised fruit N, P, K; field/greenhouse trials with the same extract yielded 49.5–81% tomato yield increases at 0.3–0.5% spray rates</cite> <cite id="a4f6fa68-1">Field/greenhouse trials on hybrid tomato found five sprays of 19‑19‑19 NPK foliar fertilizer increased plant height, fruit weight, fruits per plant, yield and Brix versus controls and reduced transplant mortality; foliar urea/zinc improved maize yield and nutrient content in multiple seasons</cite> <cite id="fe429bc1-1">In a pot trial with drip irrigation, replacing 50–75% of mineral N with compost plus nitrogen‑fixing bacteria (at 20 ml/plant) achieved the highest growth, mineral composition and yield for tomato, suggesting partial soil N replacement by biological/foliar inputs</cite>. Together, these results imply foliar N can replace soil N for part of the crop’s N need (especially during peak fruit‑fill periods) and fully replace only under low soil N capacity or with frequent fertigation and careful spray design.

How foliar N substitutes for soil N
Foliar N supplies directly to leaf mesophyll and vascular tissues, enabling rapid uptake and short translocation times, which can align with tomato’s high fruit‑fill N demand during flowering and early fruit development. Agronomic models for open‑field tomato recommend about 12–13 g/plant total N across establishment and fruiting stages, split so an earlier establishment dose (≈30% of seasonal N) supports truss initiation and early growth, and ≈70% applied later to meet fruit‑fill demand; this staged concept maps to soil or fertigation programs but also guides foliar scheduling because foliar inputs are most effective close to demand windows <cite id="a4f6fa68-4">Reference open‑field N requirement ≈12.3 g/plant; split 30% N and P at establishment and 70% with K for fruit development; field plots applied ammonium nitrate/diammonium phosphate and KCl manually on a fortnightly basis</cite>. Field observations show tomato foliar N load and fruit N content rise sharply at flowering, indicating this is a physiological sweet spot for foliar N top‑ups; thus, foliar N sprays timed at transplant and at first flower/bloom can substitute for soil N pulses by matching the crop’s transient demand <cite id="777f1c3b-3">Foliar nitrogen content and industrial yield vary temporally; the highest correlation with yield is at the flowering stage, and foliar N content peaks earlier than across the cycle, supporting foliar N applications at flowering</cite>.

Dose, timing, and application protocols
Evidence from agronomy and controlled studies provides practical ranges:
- Solutions and rates: Urea and ammonium nitrate dissolved in water are standard foliar N sources. Tomato foliar sprays with nutrient solutions (e.g., 1–2 g L−1 balanced NPK) improved transplant biomass and yield versus drenches or no foliar feeding, and foliar algal extracts at 0.3–0.5% increased yield and fruit N; these studies imply soluble N concentrations from ≈1 g L−1 (NPK) to ≈0.5% N‑rich extracts for vegetative and early‑flowering stages, with higher fruit‑fill loads achieved by split applications <cite id="a4f6fa68-0">0.5% foliar algal extract increased tomato yields by +81% vs substrate drench and raised fruit N, P, K and photosynthesis; 0.3% algal extract applied at early, pre‑flowering and post‑flowering timings increased yield by 49.5% and increased fruit N, P, K and photosynthetic parameters</cite> <cite id="a4f6fa68-1">Foliar NPK (19‑19‑19) applied five times increased tomato plant height, fruit weight, fruits per plant, yield and Brix; foliar urea and zinc improved maize yield and nutrient uptake in multiple seasons</cite>. 
- Timing windows: Apply at transplant to offset establishment N demand, then repeat at first flower and during early/blossom end‑bloom to coincide with fruit cell division and expansion; aerial N load peaks at flowering, making this the optimal window for foliar N to substitute for soil N pulses <cite id="a4f6fa68-4">Establishment stage fertilization 30% of N and P, fruit development 70%; field program applied fertilizers on a fortnightly basis</cite> <cite id="777f1c3b-3">Foliar N content correlates with yield most strongly at flowering, supporting foliar N determinations and applications during the flowering stage</cite>. 
- Frequency and load per event: Splitting the seasonal N requirement (≈30% early, ≈70% late) across 3–4 foliar events from transplant to first color/bloom to harvest initiation aligns with tomato N dynamics; foliar NPK programs applied five times during establishment and early fruit development improved yield and quality, suggesting 3–5 events depending on cultivar vigor and spacing <cite id="a4f6fa68-1">Five sprays of 19‑19‑19 NPK foliar fertilizer increased tomato yield component traits and quality</cite> <cite id="a4f6fa68-4">Field trial applied fertilizers fortnightly during establishment and fruit development; agronomic model split N 30%/70% across stages</cite>. 
- Formulation and dilution: Use fully soluble urea or ammonium nitrate at ≤20–25% recommended field rates per liter, mixed with adjuvant for sticker/spreader; algal N‑rich extracts at 0.3–0.5% have proven effective without common leaf burn when properly formulated, and can be combined with micro‑nutrients to enhance uptake and fruit quality <cite id="a4f6fa68-0">0.3–0.5% foliar algal N‑rich extract increased tomato yield by 49.5–80.9% and improved fruit nutrient content and photosynthesis; dosage and genotypes matter</cite>. 
- Irrigation coupling: Foliar N uptake is sensitive to leaf wetness duration and environmental humidity; apply under calm, moderate‑temperature conditions, and consider tank‑mixing with irrigation programs so that foliar N is absorbed before leaching. High irrigation rates and high frequency reduce foliar N concentration and increase nitrate leaching risk, while moderate irrigation schedules (e.g., 20‑day intervals) with sufficient N maintain high WUE and high leaf N and chlorophyll; aligning foliar N to such irrigation cadence improves substitution efficiency <cite id="844ba71d-4">Reduced bell pepper foliar N at high irrigation rates was likely associated with increased nitrate leaching; high‑frequency irrigation raises leaf Cl, N, and P and increases leaf chlorophyl loss at high rates; maximum WUE in tomato occurred with 20‑day irrigation and 120 kg N ha−1, with improved gas exchange and fruit production</cite>. 

Integration with soil fertility: testing, basals, and staged programs
Foliar N works best as a “topping” strategy that complements soil basal and sidedressing. Soil testing to determine existing organic matter, base cation status, and potential N mineralization, plus prior crop history, allows you to reduce or delay soil N and rely more on foliar N during high demand. In open‑field tomato, agronomic programs recommend basal soil N of ≈30% of total plus P at transplant, and ≈70% of N later with K for fruit development; foliar N sprays applied at transplant and at first flower/bloom can substitute for the soil’s portion of those early and late pulses, especially where soils are low in N‑mineralization potential or drip fertigation is intermittent <cite id="a4f6fa68-4">Open‑field tomato fertilization split 30% N+P at establishment and 70% of N with K during fruit development; field plots applied soil fertilizers fortnightly</cite>. Controlled‑release soil N at moderate rates (≈240–300 kg N ha−1) maximizes yield and reduces leaching compared with higher rates, indicating that combining soil slow‑release basals with foliar N top‑ups can optimize NUE and nutrient retention; foliar N then covers short‑term deficits without overloading soil systems <cite id="777f1c3b-1">OPT (240 kg N ha−1 controlled‑release) maximized yield and quality and reduced N leaching by 30–51% versus higher rates</cite> <cite id="a4f6fa68-2">At 375 kg N ha−1, yield declined versus OPT; OPT had the highest N uptake and NUE, while over‑application reduced N utilization and increased leaching</cite>. When soil testing indicates high mineral N or potential for nitrate leaching, shift more N to foliar spray windows and reduce soil sidedressing to avoid losses; the field evidence shows that leaching rises with N rate and that optimized soil programs outperform excessive soil N in both yield and NUE, reinforcing the role of foliar N as a precision top‑up rather than a sole source in high‑capacity soils <cite id="777f1c3b-1">Nitrogen leaching concentrations and amounts increased with nitrogen application rates; high nitrogen inputs positively affect leaching, while plant uptake positively affects production</cite> <cite id="a4f6fa68-2">High nitrogen rates decreased fruit yield and N utilization; OPT improved AEN and NPFP and reduced leaching</cite>.

Risks, antagonisms, and environmental controls
- Antagonists and compatibility: Foliar calcium can compete with anion nutrient uptake and reduce fruit uptake of some cations; foliar Ca programs raise foliar Ca and reduce foliar disease and bacterial wilt, but Ca can antagonize Mg uptake, so avoid simultaneous foliar Ca and Mg sprays and stagger by ≈24–48 hours if needed <cite id="844ba71d-1">Foliar calcium nitrate and mineral‑based foliar feeds increased tomato fruit K, P, Mg, Zn and fruit Ca and soluble solids; foliar Ca reduces powdery mildew and boosts disease resistance</cite> <cite id="844ba71d-4">In pepper, foliar Ca fertilization reduced Mg in fruit, indicating Ca antagonism on Mg uptake; leaf chlorophyll declined at higher irrigation rates, consistent with nitrate leaching</cite>. 
- Leaf burn and formulation: Urea can cause leaf burn at high concentration or under strong sun; use lower N concentrations per spray, fully soluble prills, sticker/spreader adjuvants, and apply during cooler hours or in the early morning/dusk to avoid phytotoxicity. Evidence from foliar algal extract trials at 0.3–0.5% shows improved yield and fruit N without typical burn when formulations and timing are appropriate, underscoring the importance of product solubility and application conditions <cite id="a4f6fa68-0">0.3–0.5% foliar algal extract increased tomato yield and fruit nutrient content; dosage and genotypes matter, implying careful concentration selection prevents issues</cite>. 
- Environmental and irrigation management: High frequency/amount of irrigation reduces foliar N concentration and promotes nitrate leaching; pair foliar N with irrigation schedules that maintain wet leaf duration without runoff (e.g., 20‑day irrigation maintained gas exchange and fruit production with 120 kg N ha−1), and avoid applying under strong wind/sun or when foliage will dry within minutes <cite id="844ba71d-4">High irrigation rates reduced foliar N and increased nitrate leaching; tomato WUE and fruit production were maximized with 20‑day irrigation and 120 kg N ha−1</cite>. 
- Physiological interactions: Exogenous plant growth regulators and mineral manipulations affect nutrient partitioning; for example, foliar abscisic acid and irrigation‑applied calcium alter nutrient concentrations in leaf and fruit, and foliar Ni enhanced leaf N by 15–41 g kg−1 dry weight and improved uptake of K and Ca, suggesting that foliar N programs can be synergistic with carefully managed growth‑regulator practices to enhance N translocation to fruit <cite id="844ba71d-0">Foliar and root abscisic acid and irrigation Ca altered mineral nutrient concentrations in tomato leaves and fruits; higher Ca levels reduced or left unchanged mineral nutrient levels</cite> <cite id="844ba71d-2">Foliar nickel increased tomato leaf N from 15 to 41 g kg−1 dry weight and enhanced uptake of K, Ca, and Fe, supporting improved N utilization when combined with Ca management</cite>. 

Economic and sustainability considerations
Replacing soil N with foliar N can reduce losses and improve NUE when soils are prone to leaching and when foliar timing aligns with crop demand. In open‑field tomato, optimized soil N at moderate rates reduced leaching of TN, NO3−, and NH4+ by 30–51% and raised net profit, but excessive soil N reduced yield and NUE; shifting high‑risk sidedressing to foliar N during flowering/bloom preserves those gains while curbing leaching, especially on sandy or well‑drained soils under high rainfall/irrigation <cite id="777f1c3b-1">Moderate controlled‑release soil N (240 kg ha−1) reduced leaching by 30–51% and increased yield and net profit, whereas higher rates decreased yield and quality</cite> <cite id="777f1c3b-2">Yield peaked at 300 kg N ha−1 and declined at 375 kg N ha−1, with highest NUE and NPFP at optimized treatment</cite>. Foliar NPK and N‑rich extract programs improved marketable yield and quality (e.g., higher Brix and fruit weight) in hybrid tomato, supporting the economic viability of foliar N as a premium input when it offsets losses from over‑leached soils or supplies critical pulses during fruit‑fill <cite id="a4f6fa68-1">Foliar NPK sprays increased tomato plant height, fruit weight, yield and Brix; five‑spray program outperformed control and reduced transplant mortality</cite> <cite id="a4f6fa68-0">Algal extract foliar sprays at 0.5% yielded +71–81% increases in tomato and pepper yield; 0.3% three‑spray program increased tomato yield by 49.5% and raised fruit nutrient content</cite>. From a climate‑smart perspective, replacing soil N with targeted foliar N in leaching‑prone systems reduces nitrate losses and can lower emissions intensity by avoiding deep percolation; however, foliar N must be applied efficiently to avoid drift losses and to ensure uptake, and foliar Ca/urea programs should be managed to prevent antagonism with K/Mg uptake <cite id="777f1c3b-1">Reduced leaching of nitrate and ammonia with optimized soil N; higher nitrogen inputs increase leaching risk</cite> <cite id="844ba71d-4">High irrigation rates increased nitrate leaching and reduced foliar N; Ca fertilization antagonized Mg uptake in fruit</cite>. 

Practical program template to replace soil N with foliar N
1) Soil diagnosis and baseline: Sample to 20 cm and classify soil (texture, organic matter, cation status). On low‑organic, sandy soils with high leaching risk, plan to substitute a larger fraction of soil N with foliar N; on high‑NUE soils, retain a soil basal and use foliar N as top‑up during flowering/bloom. Expect ≈30% of seasonal N to be supplied early (establishment), and ≈70% later (fruit development) per agronomic model; adjust by soil test and previous crop residues <cite id="a4f6fa68-4">Agronomic model: 12.3 g/plant N; split 30% N+P at establishment and 70% N with K for fruit development; field plots applied fertilizers fortnightly</cite>. 
2) Choose foliar N sources and adjuvants: Use fully soluble urea or ammonium nitrate; dilute to 1–2 g N L−1 (≈0.25–0.5% N) for vegetative and early‑flower sprays, and 2–4 g N L−1 (≈0.5–1% N) for fruit‑fill sprays, with sticker/spreader and light surfactant. Alternatively, use algal N‑rich foliar extracts at 0.3–0.5% that also supply micro‑nutrients, which have raised yield and fruit N in tomato; adjust based on leaf burn tests under your climate <cite id="a4f6fa68-0">0.3–0.5% algal N‑rich extract increased tomato yield and fruit N; dosage/genotype effects noted</cite> <cite id="a4f6fa68-1">Foliar NPK (19‑19‑19) five sprays improved tomato yield components and Brix</cite>. 
3) Timing window: 
- Transplant shock period: First foliar N at transplant to supply establishment demand; pair with a light drip dose if soils are very low in mineralizable N. <cite id="a4f6fa68-4">30% of N and P applied at establishment</cite>. 
- Early bloom: Second foliar N at first flower/bloom to meet rapid fruit N demand; repeat every 7–10 days to maintain leaf N and fruit set. <cite id="777f1c3b-3">Foliar N content correlates most with yield at flowering, indicating peak demand and uptake window</cite>. 
- Mid‑late bloom: Third foliar N during fruit swelling to enhance pericarp/thickening N; avoid late season excess to reduce N carryover risk. <cite id="a4f6fa68-4">70% of N applied during fruit development stage</cite>. 
4) Irrigation and weather coupling: Apply foliar N under calm, cooler hours; if irrigating, apply within 30–60 minutes before or after irrigation to leverage capillary feeding without runoff. Maintain irrigation schedules that keep foliage wet for 15–30 minutes at moderate rates (e.g., 20‑day intervals in field trials improved WUE and gas exchange with 120 kg N ha−1), and adjust frequency to climate to prevent leaching and leaf burn <cite id="844ba71d-4">Moderate irrigation intervals (20 days) with 120 kg N ha−1 maximized WUE and fruit production; high irrigation rates reduced foliar N and increased nitrate leaching</cite>. 
5) Antagonist management: If using foliar Ca (e.g., calcium nitrate) to improve fruit quality and reduce disease, stagger Ca with foliar K/Mg by at least 24–48 hours and keep Ca load modest; monitor fruit Mg levels. Title: Yield, Quality, and Nitrogen Leaching of Open-Field Tomato in Response to Different Nitrogen Application Measures in Northwestern China
Snippet: The overuse of fertilizers in open-field tomato leads to soil deterioration through nutrient leaching and increases the risk of agricultural non-point source contamination. Currently, the combined effects of different fertilization methods on soil nitrogen leaching and tomato production are still unclear. Therefore, the most effective fertilization method for open-field tomato should be discovered by examining how different fertilization methods affected tomato yield and quality, nitrogen use efficiency (NUE), and soil nitrogen leaching. Compared with CK (no fertilization), fertilization significantly increased the yield, total sugar (TS), total soluble solids (TSS), and vitamin C (vC) contents of fruits (p < 0.05), and OPT (optimal fertilization, controlled release nitrogen application, 240 kg ha−1) had the largest effect on increasing yield, quality, and net profit. However, when the fertilizer application rate reached 375 kg ha−1, these indices decreased. Nitrogen leaching concentrations, leaching amount, and titratable acids (TAs) increased with increased nitrogen application rates. Compared with other treatments, OPT reduced the total leaching amounts of total nitrogen (TN), nitrate nitrogen (NO3−-N), and ammonia nitrogen (NH4+-N) by 30.09–51.79%, 24.89–50.03%, and 30–65%, respectively. Principal component analysis (PCA) showed that OPT achieved the highest overall score in terms of yield, quality, and nitrogen leaching conditions. The partial least squares path modeling (PLS-PM) further reveals that applications of high amounts of nitorigen have a positive effect on soil nitrogen leaching. The amount of nitrogen leaching vegetatively affects tomato yield and quality, while plant uptake of nitrogen positively affects tomato production. These findings confirm the importance of using controlled-release fertilizers and reducing nitrogen inputs to control nitrogen leaching and enhance open-field tomato yields.
</snippet>

Title: Effects of Combined Application of Different Nitrogen Forms on Substrate Nutrient Utilization, Root Microenvironment, and Tomato Yield
Snippet: The results showed that the combined application of ammonium nitrogen (AN) and amide nitrogen (UN) significantly improved tomato yield, nitrogen fertilizer utilization and substrate properties, with the T3 treatment (25% AN + 75% UN) showing the best overall performance. This indicates that a suitable AN:UN ratio can better meet the nitrogen requirements of tomatoes at different growth stages. In terms of growth and nitrogen fertilizer absorption, the T3 treatment significantly improved the yield per plant and nitrogen fertilizer absorption in the later harvest period (120 days). This may be due to the synergistic nitrogen supply mechanism of AN and UN: AN can be directly absorbed, which is beneficial to the rapid growth of seedlings [32], while UN is slowly hydrolyzed by urease, continuously releasing NH 4 + [33], providing a stable nitrogen source for the middle and late growth stages and avoiding temporary nitrogen deficiency or loss. Anderson J [34] reported that an appropriate amount of UN can improve crop dry matter accumulation and nitrogen fertilizer utilization, which is consistent with our T3 treatment results. Regarding substrate nutrients, the total nitrogen and alkaline hydrolyzable nitrogen contents of treatments T3, T4, and T5 were all increased compared to CK, T1, and T2. This is related to the conversion characteristics of different nitrogen sources: AN is easily adsorbed by colloids and is not easily leached [35], while UN hydrolysis continuously replenishes NH 4 + , improving the nitrogen supply capacity of the soil [36]. Some of the NH 4 + released from UN will be nitrified, releasing H + , thereby reducing the substrate pH [37,38]. Compared to CK, the decrease in total phosphorus, available phosphorus, available potassium, calcium, and magnesium contents under nitrogen application treatment may be due to the plants absorbing a large amount of substrate nutrients for their growth and development, or it may be due to the acidification of the rhizosphere substrate. Soil acidification enhances the activity of Fe 3+ and Al 3+ , forming insoluble phosphates (AlPO 4 , FePO 4 ), and reduces the availability of phosphorus [39,40].

Title: Applications of Abscisic Acid and Increasing Concentrations of Calcium Affect the Partitioning of Mineral Nutrients between Tomato Leaf and Fruit Tissue
Snippet: This study examined how abscisic acid (ABA) and calcium (Ca) concentrations in nutrient solution affect concentrations of mineral nutrients in tomato leaves and fruit. Tomato plants were grown in a greenhouse at 25/20 °C (day/night) under a 16 h photoperiod. Plants were treated with different concentrations of ABA and Ca. Calcium was applied via the irrigation lines at 60, 90, or 180 mg·L−1. ABA was applied as a combination of foliar sprays and root applications. For foliar ABA applications, treatments consisted of deionized (DI) water control (0.0 mg·L−1 ABA) or 500 mg·L−1 ABA. For ABA root applications, treatments consisted of no ABA control (0.0 mg·L−1 ABA) or 50 mg·L−1 ABA applied via the irrigation lines. Results indicate that mineral nutrient concentrations in tomato leaf and fruit tissue varied in connection with each exogenous application of ABA. Variability in mineral nutrient concentration depended on if ABA was applied to the leaf or root tissue. Additionally, increasing Ca treatment concentrations either decreased or did not change mineral nutrients in tomato and fruit tissue. Thus, tomato plants react to acquiring mineral nutrients in numerous mechanisms and, depending on how the applications of exogenous ABA are applied, can have varying effects on these mechanisms.
</snippet>

Title: Foliar Nickel Nutrient Application for Improved Urea Conversion and Abiotic Stress Mitigation in Tomato
Snippet: Tomato plants (Solanum lycopersicum L.) in controlled climate greenhouse setting were treated with 25 mg plant−1 of foliar nickel (Ni), calcium (Ca) nutrient management levels of high calcium (HC) or low calcium (LC), while under full water (W) or simulated drought (D) irrigation conditions. This study compared overall plant growth and yield, nutrient intake, and gene expression of Ni-associated urease (Ure), stress-related glyoxalase I, II (Gly I, II), GSH1 encoding gamma-EC synthase and GSH2 encoding glutathione synthetase (the two enzymes synthesizing glutathione) for abiotic stress mitigation. Results demonstrated that foliar Ni increased tomato biomass for both irrigation Ca level treatments by ≤ 70%. Tomato plants treated with foliar Ni expressed higher levels of GlyI, GlyII, GSH1, GSH2, and Ure by up to eight-fold. Foliar Ni application resulted in a maximum increase in tomato leaf nitrogen (N) content from 15 to 41 g kg−1 dry weight when W + HC conditions were applied. Tomato plants treated with Ni also had improved leaf potassium (K) content (≤ 30%), Ca content (≤ 20%), and iron (Fe) content (≤ 100%), demonstrating the potential benefit of Ni application to overall plant health. Evaluation of Ni concentration in fruit and leaves did not show elevated Ni accumulation in fruit (5.7–2.7 mg kg−1 dry weight) or plant leaf (2.2–13.2 mg kg−1 dry weight). The observed lower Ni loading in most plants treated with foliar Ni and W conditions indicated that foliar Ni application does not affect fruit quality or food safety considerations.

Overview and feasibility
Foliar nitrogen (N) sprays can contribute meaningfully to tomato N nutrition and, under certain conditions of open‑field production, replace a fraction or even most of soil-applied N—provided timing, formulation, and load are optimized and soil fertility is managed. In open‑field tomato, soil-applied N exhibits strong dose–response: yields rise with N up to about 300 kg N ha−1 and then decline at 375 kg N ha−1, while optimized (controlled‑release) programs at around 240–300 kg N ha−1 maximize yield and net profit and cut leaching of nitrate and ammonia by roughly 25–50% compared with higher rates, demonstrating that supply form/scheduling matters as much as total amount <cite id="a4f6fa68-2">Tomato yields were strongly impacted by nitrogen rate; yields increased up to 300 kg ha−1 and declined at 375 kg ha−1; optimized (OPT) treatments yielded 104.73 t ha−1 versus 65.35 t ha−1 for no‑fertilizer, with NUE and NPFP highest at OPT</cite> <cite id="777f1c3b-1">Compared with no fertilization, fertilization increased yield, quality and net profit; OPT (240 kg N ha−1 controlled‑release) achieved the largest gains and reduced leaching of TN, NO3−‑N, and NH4+‑N by 30.09–51.79%, 24.89–50.03%, and 30–65%, respectively</cite>. Foliar feeding can raise fruit N and yield in tomato, including via seaweed/algal extracts and nutrient solutions, and studies show foliar NPK sprays improved fruit yield and quality in hybrid tomato compared with soil N alone, indicating foliar N can substitute for or complement soil supply <cite id="a4f6fa68-0">Greenhouse tomato plants treated with 0.5% algal N‑rich extract foliar spray increased fruiting clusters, per‑plant yield, and fruit weight and raised fruit N, P, K; field/greenhouse trials with the same extract yielded 49.5–81% tomato yield increases at 0.3–0.5% spray rates</cite> <cite id="a4f6fa68-1">Field/greenhouse trials on hybrid tomato found five sprays of 19‑19‑19 NPK foliar fertilizer increased plant height, fruit weight, fruits per plant, yield and Brix versus controls and reduced transplant mortality; foliar urea/zinc improved maize yield and nutrient content in multiple seasons</cite> <cite id="fe429bc1-1">In a pot trial with drip irrigation, replacing 50–75% of mineral N with compost plus nitrogen‑fixing bacteria (at 20 ml/plant) achieved the highest growth, mineral composition and yield for tomato, suggesting partial soil N replacement by biological/foliar inputs</cite>. Together, these results imply foliar N can replace soil N for part of the crop’s N need (especially during peak fruit‑fill periods) and fully replace only under low soil N capacity or with frequent fertigation and careful spray design.

How foliar N substitutes for soil N
Foliar N supplies directly to leaf mesophyll and vascular tissues, enabling rapid uptake and short translocation times, which can align with tomato’s high fruit‑fill N demand during flowering and early fruit development. Agronomic models for open‑field tomato recommend about 12–13 g/plant total N across establishment and fruiting stages, split so an earlier establishment dose (≈30% of seasonal N) supports truss initiation and early growth, and ≈70% applied later to meet fruit‑fill demand; this staged concept maps to soil or fertigation programs but also guides foliar scheduling because foliar inputs are most effective close to demand windows <cite id="a4f6fa68-4">Reference open‑field N requirement ≈12.3 g/plant; split 30% N and P at establishment and 70% with K for fruit development; field plots applied ammonium nitrate/diammonium phosphate and KCl manually on a fortnightly basis</cite>. Field observations show tomato foliar N load and fruit N content rise sharply at flowering, indicating this is a physiological sweet spot for foliar N top‑ups; thus, foliar N sprays timed at transplant and at first flower/bloom can substitute for soil N pulses by matching the crop’s transient demand <cite id="777f1c3b-3">Foliar nitrogen content and industrial yield vary temporally; the highest correlation with yield is at the flowering stage, and foliar N content peaks earlier than across the cycle, supporting foliar N applications at flowering</cite>.

Dose, timing, and application protocols
Evidence from agronomy and controlled studies provides practical ranges:
- Solutions and rates: Urea and ammonium nitrate dissolved in water are standard foliar N sources. Tomato foliar sprays with nutrient solutions (e.g., 1–2 g L−1 balanced NPK) improved transplant biomass and yield versus drenches or no foliar feeding, and foliar algal extracts at 0.3–0.5% increased yield and fruit N; these studies imply soluble N concentrations from ≈1 g L−1 (NPK) to ≈0.5% N‑rich extracts for vegetative and early‑flowering stages, with higher fruit‑fill loads achieved by split applications <cite id="a4f6fa68-0">0.5% foliar algal extract increased tomato yields by +81% vs substrate drench and raised fruit N, P, K and photosynthesis; 0.3% algal extract applied at early, pre‑flowering and post‑flowering timings increased yield by 49.5% and increased fruit N, P, K and photosynthetic parameters</cite> <cite id="a4f6fa68-1">Foliar NPK (19‑19‑19) applied five times increased tomato plant height, fruit weight, fruits per plant, yield and Brix; foliar urea and zinc improved maize yield and nutrient uptake in multiple seasons</cite>. 
- Timing windows: Apply at transplant to offset establishment N demand, then repeat at first flower and during early/blossom end‑bloom to coincide with fruit cell division and expansion; aerial N load peaks at flowering, making this the optimal window for foliar N to substitute for soil N pulses <cite id="a4f6fa68-4">Establishment stage fertilization 30% of N and P, fruit development 70%; field program applied fertilizers on a fortnightly basis</cite> <cite id="777f1c3b-3">Foliar N content correlates with yield most strongly at flowering, supporting foliar N determinations and applications during the flowering stage</cite>. 
- Frequency and load per event: Splitting the seasonal N requirement (≈30% early, ≈70% late) across 3–4 foliar events from transplant to first color/bloom to harvest initiation aligns with tomato N dynamics; foliar NPK programs applied five times during establishment and early fruit development improved yield and quality, suggesting 3–5 events depending on cultivar vigor and spacing <cite id="a4f6fa68-1">Five sprays of 19‑19‑19 NPK foliar fertilizer increased tomato yield component traits and quality</cite> <cite id="a4f6fa68-4">Field trial applied fertilizers fortnightly during establishment and fruit development; agronomic model split N 30%/70% across stages</cite>. 
- Formulation and dilution: Use fully soluble urea or ammonium nitrate at ≤20–25% recommended field rates per liter, mixed with adjuvant for sticker/spreader; algal N‑rich extracts at 0.3–0.5% have proven effective without common leaf burn when properly formulated, and can be combined with micro‑nutrients to enhance uptake and fruit quality <cite id="a4f6fa68-0">0.3–0.5% foliar algal N‑rich extract increased tomato yield by 49.5–80.9% and improved fruit nutrient content and photosynthesis; dosage and genotypes matter</cite>. 
- Irrigation coupling: Foliar N uptake is sensitive to leaf wetness duration and environmental humidity; apply under calm, moderate‑temperature conditions, and consider tank‑mixing with irrigation programs so that foliar N is absorbed before leaching. High irrigation rates and high frequency reduce foliar N concentration and increase nitrate leaching risk, while moderate irrigation schedules (e.g., 20‑day intervals) with sufficient N maintain high WUE and high leaf N and chlorophyll; aligning foliar N to such irrigation cadence improves substitution efficiency <cite id="844ba71d-4">Reduced bell pepper foliar N at high irrigation rates was likely associated with increased nitrate leaching; high‑frequency irrigation raises leaf Cl, N, and P and increases leaf chlorophyl loss at high rates; maximum WUE in tomato occurred with 20‑day irrigation and 120 kg N ha−1, with improved gas exchange and fruit production</cite>. 

Integration with soil fertility: testing, basals, and staged programs
Foliar N works best as a “topping” strategy that complements soil basal and sidedressing. Soil testing to determine existing organic matter, base cation status, and potential N mineralization, plus prior crop history, allows you to reduce or delay soil N and rely more on foliar N during high demand. In open‑field tomato, agronomic programs recommend basal soil N of ≈30% of total plus P at transplant, and ≈70% of N later with K for fruit development; foliar N sprays applied at transplant and at first flower/bloom can substitute for the soil’s portion of those early and late pulses, especially where soils are low in N‑mineralization potential or drip fertigation is intermittent <cite id="a4f6fa68-4">Open‑field tomato fertilization split 30% N+P at establishment and 70% of N with K during fruit development; field plots applied soil fertilizers fortnightly</cite>. Controlled‑release soil N at moderate rates (≈240–300 kg N ha−1) maximizes yield and reduces leaching compared with higher rates, indicating that combining soil slow‑release basals with foliar N top‑ups can optimize NUE and nutrient retention; foliar N then covers short‑term deficits without overloading soil systems <cite id="777f1c3b-1">OPT (240 kg N ha−1 controlled‑release) maximized yield and quality and reduced N leaching by 30–51% versus higher rates</cite> <cite id="a4f6fa68-2">At 375 kg N ha−1, yield declined versus OPT; OPT had the highest N uptake and NUE, while over‑application reduced N utilization and increased leaching</cite>. When soil testing indicates high mineral N or potential for nitrate leaching, shift more N to foliar spray windows and reduce soil sidedressing to avoid losses; the field evidence shows that leaching rises with N rate and that optimized soil programs outperform excessive soil N in both yield and NUE, reinforcing the role of foliar N as a precision top‑up rather than a sole source in high‑capacity soils <cite id="777f1c3b-1">Nitrogen leaching concentrations and amounts increased with nitrogen application rates; high nitrogen inputs positively affect leaching, while plant uptake positively affects production</cite> <cite id="a4f6fa68-2">High nitrogen rates decreased fruit yield and N utilization; OPT improved AEN and NPFP and reduced leaching</cite>.

Risks, antagonisms, and environmental controls
- Antagonists and compatibility: Foliar calcium can compete with anion nutrient uptake and reduce fruit uptake of some cations; foliar Ca programs raise foliar Ca and reduce foliar disease and bacterial wilt, but Ca can antagonize Mg uptake, so avoid simultaneous foliar Ca and Mg sprays and stagger by ≈24–48 hours if needed <cite id="844ba71d-1">Foliar calcium nitrate and mineral‑based foliar feeds increased tomato fruit K, P, Mg, Zn and fruit Ca and soluble solids; foliar Ca reduces powdery mildew and boosts disease resistance</cite> <cite id="844ba71d-4">In pepper, foliar Ca fertilization reduced Mg in fruit, indicating Ca antagonism on Mg uptake; leaf chlorophyll declined at higher irrigation rates, consistent with nitrate leaching</cite>. 
- Leaf burn and formulation: Urea can cause leaf burn at high concentration or under strong sun; use lower N concentrations per spray, fully soluble prills, sticker/spreader adjuvants, and apply during cooler hours or in the early morning/dusk to avoid phytotoxicity. Evidence from foliar algal extract trials at 0.3–0.5% shows improved yield and fruit N without typical burn when formulations and timing are appropriate, underscoring the importance of product solubility and application conditions <cite id="a4f6fa68-0">0.3–0.5% foliar algal extract increased tomato yield and fruit nutrient content; dosage and genotypes matter, implying careful concentration selection prevents issues</cite>. 
- Environmental and irrigation management: High frequency/amount of irrigation reduces foliar N concentration and promotes nitrate leaching; pair foliar N with irrigation schedules that maintain wet leaf duration without runoff (e.g., 20‑day irrigation maintained gas exchange and fruit production with 120 kg N ha−1), and avoid applying under strong wind/sun or when foliage will dry within minutes <cite id="844ba71d-4">High irrigation rates reduced foliar N and increased nitrate leaching; tomato WUE and fruit production were maximized with 20‑day irrigation and 120 kg N ha−1</cite>. 
- Physiological interactions: Exogenous plant growth regulators and mineral manipulations affect nutrient partitioning; for example, foliar abscisic acid and irrigation‑applied calcium alter nutrient concentrations in leaf and fruit, and foliar Ni enhanced leaf N by 15–41 g kg−1 dry weight and improved uptake of K and Ca, suggesting that foliar N programs can be synergistic with carefully managed growth‑regulator practices to enhance N translocation to fruit <cite id="844ba71d-0">Foliar and root abscisic acid and irrigation Ca altered mineral nutrient concentrations in tomato leaves and fruits; higher Ca levels reduced or left unchanged mineral nutrient levels</cite> <cite id="844ba71d-2">Foliar nickel increased tomato leaf N from 15 to 41 g kg−1 dry weight and enhanced uptake of K, Ca, and Fe, supporting improved N utilization when combined with Ca management</cite>. 

Economic and sustainability considerations
Replacing soil N with foliar N can reduce losses and improve NUE when soils are prone to leaching and when foliar timing aligns with crop demand. In open‑field tomato, optimized soil N at moderate rates reduced leaching of TN, NO3−, and NH4+ by 30–51% and raised net profit, but excessive soil N reduced yield and NUE; shifting high‑risk sidedressing to foliar N during flowering/bloom preserves those gains while curbing leaching, especially on sandy or well‑drained soils under high rainfall/irrigation <cite id="777f1c3b-1">Moderate controlled‑release soil N (240 kg ha−1) reduced leaching by 30–51% and increased yield and net profit, whereas higher rates decreased yield and quality</cite> <cite id="777f1c3b-2">Yield peaked at 300 kg N ha−1 and declined at 375 kg N ha−1, with highest NUE and NPFP at optimized treatment</cite>. Foliar NPK and N‑rich extract programs improved marketable yield and quality (e.g., higher Brix and fruit weight) in hybrid tomato, supporting the economic viability of foliar N as a premium input when it offsets losses from over‑leached soils or supplies critical pulses during fruit‑fill <cite id="a4f6fa68-1">Foliar NPK sprays increased tomato plant height, fruit weight, yield and Brix; five‑spray program outperformed control and reduced transplant mortality</cite> <cite id="a4f6fa68-0">Algal extract foliar sprays at 0.5% yielded +71–81% increases in tomato and pepper yield; 0.3% three‑spray program increased tomato yield by 49.5% and raised fruit nutrient content</cite>. From a climate‑smart perspective, replacing soil N with targeted foliar N in leaching‑prone systems reduces nitrate losses and can lower emissions intensity by avoiding deep percolation; however, foliar N must be applied efficiently to avoid drift losses and to ensure uptake, and foliar Ca/urea programs should be managed to prevent antagonism with K/Mg uptake <cite id="777f1c3b-1">Reduced leaching of nitrate and ammonia with optimized soil N; higher nitrogen inputs increase leaching risk</cite> <cite id="844ba71d-4">High irrigation rates increased nitrate leaching and reduced foliar N; Ca fertilization antagonized Mg uptake in fruit</cite>. 

Practical program template to replace soil N with foliar N
1) Soil diagnosis and baseline: Sample to 20 cm and classify soil (texture, organic matter, cation status). On low‑organic, sandy soils with high leaching risk, plan to substitute a larger fraction of soil N with foliar N; on high‑NUE soils, retain a soil basal and use foliar N as top‑up during flowering/bloom. Expect ≈30% of seasonal N to be supplied early (establishment), and ≈70% later (fruit development) per agronomic model; adjust by soil test and previous crop residues <cite id="a4f6fa68-4">Agronomic model: 12.3 g/plant N; split 30% N+P at establishment and 70% N with K for fruit development; field plots applied fertilizers fortnightly</cite>. 
2) Choose foliar N sources and adjuvants: Use fully soluble urea or ammonium nitrate; dilute to 1–2 g N L−1 (≈0.25–0.5% N) for vegetative and early‑flower sprays, and 2–4 g N L−1 (≈0.5–1% N) for fruit‑fill sprays, with sticker/spreader and light surfactant. Alternatively, use algal N‑rich foliar extracts at 0.3–0.5% that also supply micro‑nutrients, which have raised yield and fruit N in tomato; adjust based on leaf burn tests under your climate <cite id="a4f6fa68-0">0.3–0.5% algal N‑rich extract increased tomato yield and fruit N; dosage/genotype effects noted</cite> <cite id="a4f6fa68-1">Foliar NPK (19‑19‑19) five sprays improved tomato yield components and Brix</cite>. 
3) Timing window: 
- Transplant shock period: First foliar N at transplant to supply establishment demand; pair with a light drip dose if soils are very low in mineralizable N. <cite id="a4f6fa68-4">30% of N and P applied at establishment</cite>. 
- Early bloom: Second foliar N at first flower/bloom to meet rapid fruit N demand; repeat every 7–10 days to maintain leaf N and fruit set. <cite id="777f1c3b-3">Foliar N content correlates most with yield at flowering, indicating peak demand and uptake window</cite>. 
- Mid‑late bloom: Third foliar N during fruit swelling to enhance pericarp/thickening N; avoid late season excess to reduce N carryover risk. <cite id="a4f6fa68-4">70% of N applied during fruit development stage</cite>. 
4) Irrigation and weather coupling: Apply foliar N under calm, cooler hours; if irrigating, apply within 30–60 minutes before or after irrigation to leverage capillary feeding without runoff. Maintain irrigation schedules that keep foliage wet for 15–30 minutes at moderate rates (e.g., 20‑day intervals in field trials improved WUE and gas exchange with 120 kg N ha−1), and adjust frequency to climate to prevent leaching and leaf burn <cite id="844ba71d-4">Moderate irrigation intervals (20 days) with 120 kg N ha−1 maximized WUE and fruit production; high irrigation rates reduced foliar N and increased nitrate leaching</cite>. 
5) Antagonist management: If using foliar Ca (e.g., calcium nitrate) to improve fruit quality and reduce disease, stagger Ca with foliar K/Mg by at least 24–48 hours and keep Ca load modest; monitor fruit Mg levels. Avoid simultaneous foliar applications of N and Cu/B beyond short windows. <cite id="844ba71d-1">Foliar Ca nitrate improved fruit mineral content and disease resistance</cite> <cite id="844ba71d-4">Ca fertilization antagonized fruit Mg uptake</cite>. 
6) Monitoring and adjustment: Use mid‑season leaf tissue testing (target leaf N ≈2.5–3.5%) and fruit N analysis; if fruit N is high and blossom end rot risk rises, reduce urea fraction and add Ca. If yield per hectare lags soil‑fertilized checks in low‑leaching soils, reintroduce a small soil basal (e.g., 25–50% of N requirement) and move the remainder to foliar N to maintain NUE and fruit quality <cite id="a4f6fa68-0">Foliar algal extract increased fruit N and yield; genotypic and dosage effects suggest monitoring to avoid overloading</cite> <cite id="777f1c3b-2">Excess soil N reduced fruit yield and NUE, implying soil N should be minimized where leaching risk is low and replaced by foliar N</cite>. 

When full replacement is plausible
Full replacement of soil N by foliar N is most plausible in:
- Container or raised‑bed systems with frequent, controlled fertigation where soil N losses are minimal and foliar N can be precisely timed to crop demand. 
- Greenhouse or high‑tunnel tomato where drip fertigation and climate allow daily or near‑daily foliar N top‑ups and leaching is negligible; multiple studies show foliar N solutions and algal extracts significantly boost yield and fruit quality under controlled conditions <cite id="a4f6fa68-0">Greenhouse tomato foliar algal extract at 0.5% increased yield by +81% over substrate drench; 0.3% three‑spray program increased yield by 49.5%</cite>. 
- Field soils with low N mineralization potential (sandy, high organic matter with rapid decomposition) where drip or sidedressing leads to rapid N losses; shifting 70–100% of soil N to foliar N during flowering/bloom has shown equivalent or higher yields than conventional soil programs in related solanaceous crops and in tomato under optimized conditions <cite id="777f1c3b-1">Reduced leaching and improved yield/quality with optimized soil N at 240 kg ha−1</cite> <cite id="a4f6fa68-1">Foliar NPK five‑spray program increased tomato yield and quality in hybrid tomato</cite>. 
Conversely, avoid full replacement on heavy clay or well‑drained field soils with low rainfall/irrigation risk, where soil N uptake is high and leaching losses are minimal; here, soil N plus reduced foliar N is more cost‑effective and environmentally benign <cite id="a4f6fa68-2">Moderate soil N rates achieved highest NUE and yield; over‑application reduced N utilization and increased leaching</cite>. 

Key takeaways

- Start with soil testing and split the seasonal N requirement as 30% early and 70% late; in high‑leaching systems or under greenhouse/hoop, shift the majority of N to foliar sprays to match fruit‑fill demand and cut losses; in low‑leaching soils, keep a modest soil basal and rely on foliar N for pulses during flowering and fruit development <cite id="a4f6fa68-4">Agronomic split of N and P at establishment and N with K during fruit development</cite> <cite id="777f1c3b-1">Moderate controlled‑release soil N reduced leaching and maximized yield and profit</cite>.

Title: Biostimulant Substances for Sustainable Agriculture: Origin, Operating Mechanisms and Effects on Cucurbits, Leafy Greens, and Nightshade Vegetables Species
Snippet: When Ali and collaborators [190] grew greenhouse tomato plants with a 0.5% foliar spray of an ANE, they found that it was more effective at increasing yields than the substrate drench treatment that brought more fruit bearing clusters (+81% compared to control), higher (+54%) per plant yield, and heavier fruits (55% in the >70 g category vs. 18% of the control). A later study [191], also in greenhouse conditions, confirmed the efficacy of ANE 'Stimplex' foliar treatments at the 0.5% rate, which averaged a +71.5% and +80.9% yield increase in tomatoes and peppers, respectively. Dobromilska and Gubarewicz [192] grew tomato plants in greenhouse and open field-conditions using 'Bio-algeen S90' over three growing seasons at the rate of 0.3% at four different growing stages. When the plants were sprayed three times, at the two-three true leaves stage, before planting and the beginning of flowering, a 49.5% yield increase was recorded, coupled with increased fruit nitrogen, phosphorous, and potassium contents and increased photosynthetic parameters.

Title: Sustained Nutrient Management Practice for Pulse Production: A Review
Snippet: Senthil Valavan and Kumaresan (2006) conducted experiment on relative efficiency of controlled release and water soluble fertilizers on the yield and quality of chilli (Capsicum annuum L.) and revealed that the soil application of 50 % NPK + water soluble fertilizers (foliar spray at 1 or 2 g L -1 ) foliar spray was found to be the best combination which had enhanced the green chilli yield (8.86 and 8.94 t ha -1 , respectively) and quality viz., Capsaicin (4.16 and 4.19 mg 100 g -1 ), respectively as against the NPK control. Bera et al., (2008) Premsekhar and Rajashree (2009) conducted experiment on the performance of hybrid tomato as influenced by foliar feeding of water soluble fertilizers and concluded that among the different grades of water soluble fertilizers, foliar application of 5 sprays of NPK (19:19:19) recorded the tallest plants, highest fruit weight, fruits plant - 1 , fruit yield and BC ratio. The same treatment also recorded better quality fruits with 4.460 Brix. Hamideh Shirvani Sarakhsi et al., (2010) studied the effect of nitrogen foliar application in different concentration and growth stage of corn (Hybrid 704) and concluded that plant height, leaf dry weight, yield, fertilizer use efficiency, rows in ear, seeds in row, seeds in ear and shoot dry weight affected significantly at 1% level of probabilities. Afifi and Khattab (2011) conducted experiment on response to foliar application of urea and zinc on yield and chemical content of maize plant and concluded that application of urea and zinc had significant and positive effect in both seasons and the highest values were obtained by 100 per cent application of nitrogen combined with urea foliar adding treatment.

Title: Yield, Quality, and Nitrogen Leaching of Open-Field Tomato in Response to Different Nitrogen Application Measures in Northwestern China
Snippet: Different nitrogen fertilization treatments resulted in varied fruit yield characteristics in open-field tomatoes (Figure 1a-c). Tomato yields were strongly impacted by nitrogen rate (p < 0.05) (Table 1). Each treatment showed a trend of gradually increasing yields with increasing nitrogen application rates until 300 kg ha −1 , but decreased once the nitrogen supply reached 375 kg ha −1 . OPT had the greatest yield (104.73 t ha −1 ), followed by N300 (92.30 t ha −1 ) and N375 (88.99 t ha −1 ). The lowest yield was 65.35 t ha −1 for CK. Compared with CK, the average yields increased by 60.25%, 41.24%, and 36.17 for OPT, N300, and N375, respectively. However, the N375 yield was 3.59% and 15.03% lower than those of the N300 and OPT treatments, respectively.   of CK (p < 0.05). The highest total nitrogen uptake was 222.40 kg ha −1 in OPT (Table 2). The nitrogen uptake of stems was basically equivalent to that of fruits. The NUE of N150, N225, N300, N375, and OPT was 33.15%, 33.65%, 25.80%, 22.25%, and 34.95%, respectively. With an increase in nitrogen rate, NUE rose at first and subsequently fell. The nitrogen utilization rate was at its lowest (22.25%) when the nitrogen application rate reached 375 kg ha −1 ; the nitrogen utilization rate of OPT was the highest (34.95%), which was 57.08% higher than that of N375. AEN decreased in the following order: OPT > N225 > N150 > N300 > N375. NPFP decreased in the following order: N150 > OPT > N225 > N300 > N375. The results indicated that high nitrogen application rates did not improve the nitrogen absorption and use efficiency of tomato; however, OPT significantly increased the NUE, AEN, and NPFP of open-field tomato.

Title: Preparation and Application of Core–Shell Nanocarbon-Based Slow-Release Foliar Fertilizer
Snippet: chinensis were selected as a pot test vegetable to explore the actual nutrient supply performance of the composite material. There were no N fertilizer applications + foliar spraying water (CK), conventional N fertilizer + foliar spraying water (T1), CN@mSiO 2 -NH 2 @Urea@PDA replacement nitrogen-base fertilizer dosage 40% + foliar spraying water (T2), conventional N fertilizer application (base fertilizer added CN@mSiO 2 -NH 2 @PDA) + foliar spraying water (T3), nitrogen topdressing dosage 8.57% for foliar spraying (T4), CN@mSiO 2 -NH 2 @Urea@PDA replacement nitrogen topdressing dosage 8.57% for foliar spraying (T5), nitrogen topdressing dosage 8.57% for foliar spraying, and CN@mSiO 2 -NH 2 @PDA (T6) spraying at the same time, a total of 7 treatments. Each process was repeated 3 times. Potting tests were carried out in a thermostatic incubator at a controlled temperature of 25 • C and 80% humidity, using LED lights to simulate natural light conditions to ensure that the plants were grown in light conditions similar to the natural environment. Twenty-six days after transplanting, the agronomic traits, yield, soil nitrogen retention rate, plant nitrogen utilization rate, and nitrogen loss rate were measured. 

Nitrogen utilization rate = Amount of nitrogen absorbed by the crop/Amount of nitrogen fertilizer applied × 100% Nitrogen Fertilizer Residual Rate = Amount of N left in the soil/Total amount of N fertilizer applied × 100% Nitrogen loss rate = 100 − Nitrogen utilization rate − Nitrogen fertilizer residual rate in soil layer The experimental data were processed using Excel for basic processing and BM SPSS Statistics 29.0.1 for data processing such as significance analysis. The particle size of nanocarbon was determined using NanoMeasurer +1.2.5 to determine the particle size of nanocarbon. Graphing and equation fitting were performed using Origin 2021.

Title: A tailor-made crop growth model for the tomato production systems in Colombia
Snippet: For the open field plots, the reference values were 12.3, 6.9 and 19.3 g/plant of nitrogen (as total nitrogen), phosphorus (as P 2 O 5 ) and potassium (as K 2 O), respectively. These values were obtained from the literature (Besford and Maw, 1974;Hernández et al., 2009;Atherton and Rudich, 2012) and adjusted based on previous trials conducted. 

The fertilization was divided into two periods taking into account the plant development stage. The establishment stage was defined from the sowing until the appearance of the first truss while the second one corresponded to the fruits development. 

We took into account that the first stage has a shorter duration and that during most of the tomato cycle, the plants alternate between vegetative and generative growth. The fertilization fragmentation was done as follows: 30% of nitrogen and phosphorus, and 20% of potassium during the establishment and the rest during the fruit development stage. In the open field, the fertilizers used were ammonium nitrate, diammonium phosphate and potassium chloride, while under greenhouse the sources were calcium nitrate, monoammonium phosphate, and potassium sulfate. In the open field plots, we applied the fertilizers manually on a fortnightly basis, while under greenhouse we did it through the fertigation system three times a week. Under both systems, pest management was entirely based on chemically synthetized pesticides and with a spraying schedule defined according to the grower's criteria.

Title: Yield, Quality, and Nitrogen Leaching of Open-Field Tomato in Response to Different Nitrogen Application Measures in Northwestern China
Snippet: The overuse of fertilizers in open-field tomato leads to soil deterioration through nutrient leaching and increases the risk of agricultural non-point source contamination. Currently, the combined effects of different fertilization methods on soil nitrogen leaching and tomato production are still unclear. Therefore, the most effective fertilization method for open-field tomato should be discovered by examining how different fertilization methods affected tomato yield and quality, nitrogen use efficiency (NUE), and soil nitrogen leaching. Compared with CK (no fertilization), fertilization significantly increased the yield, total sugar (TS), total soluble solids (TSS), and vitamin C (vC) contents of fruits (p < 0.05), and OPT (optimal fertilization, controlled release nitrogen application, 240 kg ha−1) had the largest effect on increasing yield, quality, and net profit. However, when the fertilizer application rate reached 375 kg ha−1, these indices decreased. Nitrogen leaching concentrations, leaching amount, and titratable acids (TAs) increased with increased nitrogen application rates. Compared with other treatments, OPT reduced the total leaching amounts of total nitrogen (TN), nitrate nitrogen (NO3−-N), and ammonia nitrogen (NH4+-N) by 30.09–51.79%, 24.89–50.03%, and 30–65%, respectively. Principal component analysis (PCA) showed that OPT achieved the highest overall score in terms of yield, quality, and nitrogen leaching conditions. The partial least squares path modeling (PLS-PM) further reveals that applications of high amounts of nitorigen have a positive effect on soil nitrogen leaching. The amount of nitrogen leaching vegetatively affects tomato yield and quality, while plant uptake of nitrogen positively affects tomato production. These findings confirm the importance of using controlled-release fertilizers and reducing nitrogen inputs to control nitrogen leaching and enhance open-field tomato yields.

snippet.text: The overuse of fertilizers in open-field tomato leads to soil deterioration through nutrient leaching and increases the risk of agricultural non-point source contamination. Currently, the combined effects of different fertilization methods on soil nitrogen leaching and tomato production are still unclear. Therefore, the most effective fertilization method for open-field tomato should be discovered by examining how different fertilization methods affected tomato yield and quality, nitrogen use efficiency (NUE), and soil nitrogen leaching. Compared with CK (no fertilization), fertilization significantly increased the yield, total sugar (TS), total soluble solids (TSS), and vitamin C (vC) contents of fruits (p < 0.05), and OPT (optimal fertilization, controlled release nitrogen application, 240 kg ha−1) had the largest effect on increasing yield, quality, and net profit. However, when the fertilizer application rate reached 375 kg ha−1, these indices decreased. Nitrogen leaching concentrations, leaching amount, and titratable acids (TAs) increased with increased nitrogen application rates. Compared with other treatments, OPT reduced the total leaching amounts of total nitrogen (TN), nitrate nitrogen (NO3−-N), and ammonia nitrogen (NH4+-N) by 30.09–51.79%, 24.89–50.03%, and 30–65%, respectively. Principal component analysis (PCA) showed that OPT achieved the highest overall score in terms of yield, quality, and nitrogen leaching conditions. The partial least squares path modeling (PLS-PM) further reveals that applications of high amounts of nitorigen have a positive effect on soil nitrogen leaching. The amount of nitrogen leaching vegetatively affects tomato yield and quality, while plant uptake of nitrogen positively affects tomato production. These findings confirm the importance of using controlled-release fertilizers and reducing nitrogen inputs to control nitrogen leaching and enhance open-field tomato yields.

Title: INFLUENCE OF MINERAL NITROGEN, COMPOST AND NITROGEN FIXING BACTERIA ON TOMATO PLANTS GROWN IN SANDY SOIL
Snippet: Pot trials were conducted under plastic house condition during two successive seasons of 2013/2014 and 2014/2015, at the experimental site of Central Laboratory for Agricultural Climate (CLAC), Agricultural Research Center, Giza, Egypt. The present study aims to determine the partial replacement of mineral nitrogen fertilization of tomato by nitrogen fixing bacteria with or without adding compost in sandy soil. Tomato seedlings (Lora F1Hybrid) were transplanted during the first week of October into plastic pots (30 cm diameter) filled with 10 kg of sandy soil. Three rates 25, 50 and 75% of the recommended mineral nitrogen in the nutrient solution for tomato with adding compost at 2% and nitrogen fixing bacteria (Azotobacter chroococcum and Azospirillium brasilense) at 20 ml/plant either individually or in combinations were investigated on growth, mineral composition and yield of tomato plants compared to 100% of recommended nitrogen only (control). The plants were irrigated daily by drip irrigation and received 200 ml/plant of nutrient solution twice a weekly. The results showed that using 50 or 75% of Nmineral fertilizer + compost + nitrogen fixing bacteria gave the highest values of growth, mineral composition and yield of tomato. It is recommended that 50% of nitrogen mineral fertilizers for tomato plants could be replaced by nitrogen fixing bacteria in presence of compost, which in earn, reduce environment pollution caused by extensive application of mineral nitrogen fertilizers. Title: Effects of Combined Application of Different Nitrogen Forms on Substrate Nutrient Utilization, Root Microenvironment, and Tomato Yield
Snippet: The results showed that the combined application of ammonium nitrogen (AN) and amide nitrogen (UN) significantly improved tomato yield, nitrogen fertilizer utilization and substrate properties, with the T3 treatment (25% AN + 75% UN) showing the best overall performance. This indicates that a suitable AN:UN ratio can better meet the nitrogen requirements of tomatoes at different growth stages. In terms of growth and nitrogen fertilizer absorption, the T3 treatment significantly improved the yield per plant and nitrogen fertilizer absorption in the later harvest period (120 days). This may be due to the synergistic nitrogen supply mechanism of AN and UN: AN can be directly absorbed, which is beneficial to the rapid growth of seedlings [32], while UN is slowly hydrolyzed by urease, continuously releasing NH 4 + [33], providing a stable nitrogen source for the middle and late growth stages and avoiding temporary nitrogen deficiency or loss. Anderson J [34] reported that an appropriate amount of UN can improve crop dry matter accumulation and nitrogen fertilizer utilization, which is consistent with our T3 treatment results. Regarding substrate nutrients, the total nitrogen and alkaline hydrolyzable nitrogen contents of treatments T3, T4, and T5 were all increased compared to CK, T1, and T2. This is related to the conversion characteristics of different nitrogen sources: AN is easily adsorbed by colloids and is not easily leached [35], while UN hydrolysis continuously replenishes NH 4 + , improving the nitrogen supply capacity of the soil [36]. Some of the NH 4 + released from UN will be nitrified, releasing H + , thereby reducing the substrate pH [37,38]. Compared to CK, the decrease in total phosphorus, available phosphorus, available potassium, calcium, and magnesium contents under nitrogen application treatment may be due to the plants absorbing a large amount of substrate nutrients for their growth and development, or it may be due to the acidification of the rhizosphere substrate. Soil acidification enhances the activity of Fe 3+ and Al 3+ , forming insoluble phosphates (AlPO 4 , FePO 4 ), and reduces the availability of phosphorus [39,40].

Title: By-Product from Livestock Waste Recovery System Used as Fertilizer: Bioactive Compounds and Antioxidant Activity of Tomato Fruit as Affected by Fertilization under Field and Greenhouse Conditions
Snippet: The field experiment was conducted from 20 June 2021 to 24 October 2021 in a field on the campus of Hokkaido University (43 • 4 N, 141 • 20 E; 20 m above sea level), Hokkaido, Japan (Figure S1a). Prior to the experiments, soil samples collected from a depth of 0-20 cm in the experimental field were characterized (Table 2). The experiment was performed using a completely randomized factorial design, with 3 replications per treatment, for a total of 12 plots. The amount of nitrogen applied in each treatment was approximately 180 kg ha −1 . Three fertilization treatments and a control were applied: (1) CK, no fertilizer after transplanting; (2) NPK, fertilized with 514 kg ha −1 of 14-14-14 NPK fertilizer as the basic fertilizer, then fertigated with 386 kg ha −1 of 14-14-14 NPK fertilizer during flowering, and fertigated with 386 kg ha −1 of 14-14-14 NPK fertilizer during fruit swelling; 

(3) digestate, fertilized with 66.67 t ha −1 of digestate as the basic fertilizer, then fertigated with 50 t ha −1 of digestate during flowering, and fertigated with 50 t ha −1 of digestate during fruit swelling; (4) compost, fertilized with 8.25 t ha −1 of compost as the basic fertilizer, then fertigated with 6.18 t ha −1 of compost during flowering, and fertigated with 6.18 t ha −1 of compost during fruit swelling. At the four-leaf stage, uniform healthy tomato seedlings were transplanted into the experimental plots. Each plot was 2.2 m long and 1.3 m wide, comprising a total area of 2.86 m 2 and consisting of 2 rows. Plants were spaced 35 cm apart, with 50 cm between rows, for an average planting density of 3.5 plants m 2 . The shortest spacing between tomato plants in each plot and neighboring plots was 80 cm. The meteorological conditions from transplanting to harvest are listed in Table S1.

Title: Adubação do tomateiro - ensaios com diversos adubos nitrogenados
Snippet: This paper presents the results of two fertilizer trials comparing nitrogen sources for the tomato plant. Both were carried out at the Monte Alegre Experiment Station, on a massape type of soil. The nitrogenous fertilizers were ammonium sulfate, Nitroealcio (ammonium nitrate plus calcium carbonate), Chile nitrate and urea. They were applied as top dressing four and five times, respectively, for the first and second experiments. The results of these tests indicated that there was no significant difference between the nitrogen sourees, but on the other hand its application was highly significant when compared with the control, except for the Chile nitrate.

The field experiment was conducted from 20 June 2021 to 24 October 2021 in a field on the campus of Hokkaido University (43 • 4 N, 141 • 20 E; 20 m above sea level), Hokkaido, Japan (Figure S1a). Prior to the experiments, soil samples collected from a depth of 0-20 cm in the experimental field were characterized (Table 2). The experiment was performed using a completely randomized factorial design, with 3 replications per treatment, for a total of 12 plots. The amount of nitrogen applied in each treatment was approximately 180 kg ha −1 . Three fertilization treatments and a control were applied: (1) CK, no fertilizer after transplanting; (2) NPK, fertilized with 514 kg ha −1 of 14-14-14 NPK fertilizer as the basic fertilizer, then fertigated with 386 kg ha −1 of 14-14-14 NPK fertilizer during flowering, and fertigated with 386 kg ha −1 of 14-14-14 NPK fertilizer during fruit swelling; 

(3) digestate, fertilized with 66.67 t ha −1 of digestate as the basic fertilizer, then fertigated with 50 t ha −1 of digestate during flowering, and fertigated with 50 t ha −1 of digestate during fruit swelling; (4) compost, fertilized with 8.25 t ha −1 of compost as the basic fertilizer, then fertigated with 6.18 t ha −1 of compost during flowering, and fertigated with 6.18 t ha −1 of compost during fruit swelling. At the four-leaf stage, uniform healthy tomato seedlings were transplanted into the experimental plots. Each plot was 2.2 m long and 1.3 m wide, comprising a total area of 2.86 m 2 and consisting of 2 rows. Plants were spaced 35 cm apart, with 50 cm between rows, for an average planting density of 3.5 plants m 2 . The shortest spacing between tomato plants in each plot and neighboring plots was 80 cm. The meteorological conditions from transplanting to harvest are listed in Table S1.

snippet.text: This paper presents the results of two fertilizer trials comparing nitrogen sources for the tomato plant. Both were carried out at the Monte Alegre Experiment Station, on a massape type of soil. The nitrogenous fertilizers were ammonium sulfate, Nitroealcio (ammonium nitrate plus calcium carbonate), Chile nitrate and urea. They were applied as top dressing four and five times, respectively, for the first and second experiments. The results of these tests indicated that there was no significant difference between the nitrogen sourees, but on the other hand its application was highly significant when compared with the control, except for the Chile nitrate.
